news.title: Kamala Harris's husband opposes another White House bid: Report
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 10 (IANS) Former US Vice President Kamala Harris is considering another presidential run in 2028, but her husband, Doug Emhoff, has privately expressed reservations about the prospect, while some Democratic donors have warned that another campaign would face significant challenges, according to a media report. The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that Emhoff has told people privately he would prefer Harris not to seek the presidency again, although those close to him expect he would support her if she decides to enter the race. The report, citing people familiar with the conversations, said Harris has been taking steps that could lay the groundwork for another White House campaign, including meeting major donors, hiring political staff and travelling to battleground states to campaign for Democratic candidates ahead of the November midterm elections. Harris, the daughter of an Indian mother and Jamaican father, has publicly maintained that she has not decided whether to make another attempt to become America's first woman president. "I have not decided if I’m going to run again," Harris said at an NAACP event in Michigan last month, according to the newspaper. "I do sincerely believe ’28 won’t matter if we don’t get through ’26," she added, emphasising the importance of the upcoming congressional elections. A spokesman for Harris declined to comment on the Journal's report. Harris was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 and lost to Republican Donald Trump. According to the newspaper, some Democratic donors have privately questioned whether Harris should seek the nomination again, while several party figures believe Democrats should consider a fresh candidate in 2028. The report said Emhoff's concerns come after years of supporting Harris through demanding political campaigns and intense public scrutiny. In her memoir, "107 Days," Harris described the personal toll of the 2024 campaign on their marriage, including the pressure created by political attacks and public criticism. Since leaving Washington, Emhoff has resumed practising law in Los Angeles, while the couple have purchased a home in Malibu. Despite uncertainty surrounding her presidential ambitions, Harris has remained politically active. The Journal reported that she has participated in several private fundraisers in California, including events supporting Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate David Crowley and Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford. She also joined a Democratic National Committee mobilisation call involving more than 2,000 volunteers, encouraging campaign workers to reach voters in competitive states. Harris is expected to campaign in Nevada and Georgia, including on behalf of Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election. She has also strengthened her political operation, working with advisers including former ambassador Candace Bond and communications director Eduardo Negrón. The report said Harris has maintained ties with Democratic strategist Brian Fallon, who worked on her 2024 presidential campaign. Her political activities come as several prominent Democrats weigh potential presidential bids. California Governor Gavin Newsom, another possible contender, has said he would not run if Harris entered the race, according to the newspaper. Harris continues to have support among important Democratic constituencies, particularly Black women, and has been campaigning to mobilise voters in competitive states. Democratic strategist Donna Brazile, who remains in contact with Harris, told the Journal that the former vice president was concentrating on helping Democratic candidates in the November elections. Harris served as vice president from 2021 to 2025 under Biden, becoming the first woman, first Black American and first person of South Asian descent to hold the office. Before that, she represented California in the US Senate and served as the state's attorney general.

news.title: Trump takes suit against Hillary Clinton over 2016 election to Supreme Court
news.text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring ​along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year’s election by linking his campaign to Russia.

The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers for bringing a “frivolous” suit. A US appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions.

In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida.

Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a “false narrative” that he ‌and his campaign colluded with ‌Russia. The lengthy suit alleged “racketeering” and a “conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood,” among other ​claims.

Trump ‌defeated ⁠Clinton in ​that ⁠election, despite losing the national popular vote, and served his first term in office from 2017 to 2021.

US government officials have accused Russia of meddling in the 2016 election, and an investigation led by former FBI chief Robert Mueller documented extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in his favor. Trump has called the idea of Russian interference a “hoax.”

Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that year’s election. Trump regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, and has continued to make those false claims.

’Political manifesto’

US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump’s lawsuit against ⁠Clinton, citing numerous inadequacies, including that Trump waited too long to bring some of the ‌claims. The judge likened Trump’s lawsuit to a “two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against ‌those that have opposed him.”

Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and his lead attorney in the ​case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees ‌and costs, imposing the sanctions for bringing a case that the judge said was intended “to dishonestly advance a political narrative.” The judge ‌also faulted Trump and his lawyers for a “continuing pattern of misuse of the courts.”

Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit used abusive litigation tactics, contained “knowingly false” factual allegations and asserted “frivolous” legal theories.

The Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge’s rulings in 2025, including the sanctions.

“Many of Trump’s and Habba’s legal arguments were indeed frivolous,” the 11th Circuit stated.

In court papers, lawyers for Trump and Habba have said that the ‌decisions by the lower courts are having a “profound impact on the presidency, and the nation as a whole.”

Mueller, serving as a special counsel appointed by the Justice Department, issued ⁠a 2019 report on his ⁠investigation. The report stated that Russia “interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion,” but stated that “the investigation did not establish that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities.”

Mueller said in his report that he found “numerous links” and that the Trump campaign “expected it would benefit” from Russia’s effort to tilt the ballot in Trump’s favor.

Trump’s then-Attorney General William Barr appointed a different special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to look into potential missteps by the FBI.

In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the FBI lacked “actual evidence” to investigate Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and relied too heavily on tips provided by Trump’s political opponents to fuel the probe.

Trump’s Justice Department last year indicted Comey, one of several adversaries of the president hit with criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after he was accused of lying about authorizing leaks to the news media. A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor who Trump handpicked to prosecute ​Comey had been unlawfully appointed.

Steele, working for an opposition ​research firm that was hired by a law firm on behalf of the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier that alleged ties between Trump’s campaign and Russia as well as other salacious accusations, all of which Trump denied.

The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers for bringing a “frivolous” suit. news.title: GOP's Best Pickup Opportunity May Be in Democratic Stronghold Oregon
news.text: Democratic Governor Tina Kotek and Republican state Senator Christine Drazan are locked in a tight race for the Oregon governor's seat, a new poll shows, keeping alive what may be the GOP's best shot this year at flipping a governor's mansion in a state it hasn't won since 1982. Kotek drew 46 percent and Drazan 44 percent in the survey of 549 likely voters, conducted by DHM Research for The Oregonian/OregonLive from September 24 to October 1. Pacific Green Party candidate Brett Smith got 3 percent and 7 percent were undecided. The margin of error is 4.2 percentage points. It's the first independent poll since spring with Kotek in front, and an internal survey for her campaign has her up 4. Drazan's lead in public polling had been narrowing for months, from 4 points in June to a single point in late September. John Horvick, senior vice president of DHM Research, told The Oregonian that the trend, the echo of 2022 and four decades of Democratic governors made a late Kotek shift "hard for me to ignore." Still, a Drazan win would be among the stranger results of a midterm cycle that has broken mostly for Democrats. Half of likely voters in an Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) poll released last week said they voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024; 38 percent said President Donald Trump. Kotek's campaign told Newsweek in a statement that voters are turning against Drazan as they learn more about her. "As voters hear more about both candidates and their values, it is clear that they are seeing Christine Drazan as the out-of-touch, MAGA extremist that she is," Federico Araujo, the campaign's communications director, said. "There's only one candidate who's willing to tackle Oregon's toughest challenges, and voters know that it's clearly Governor Kotek." The Drazan campaign seized on Kotek's poor favorability ratings as proof voters want new leadership. "Poll after poll is showing that Oregonians of all political stripes are fed up with Tina Kotek's failed leadership and finding more and more reasons to support Christine Drazan," Trey Rosser, a campaign strategist, told Newsweek last week. Republicans Eye a Historic Oregon Comeback Oregon is one of the few governor's races where Republicans are on offense in a reliably blue state, and arguably their most realistic shot at a pickup in a year when the party is mostly playing defense. A Drazan win would make her Oregon's first Republican governor since Victor Atiyeh, who won his second term in 1982 and served from 1979 to 1987. It would also end a decadelong statewide drought for the party. Dennis Richardson's 2016 victory for secretary of state remains the last statewide race a Republican has won in Oregon. Before that, former Senator Gordon Smith was the last Republican to win statewide, in 2002. No Republican presidential candidate has carried Oregon since Ronald Reagan in 1984, and Harris beat Trump there 55 percent to 41 percent in 2024. The window to change the race is closing fast. County officials begin mailing ballots for the November 3 election next week, and Oregon votes entirely by mail. What Polls Have Shown So Far Early in the year, Kotek looked safe. An FM3 Research poll sponsored by Charlie Health had her 10 points ahead of former NBA player Chris Dudley, then running in the Republican primary, 45 percent to 35 percent. By mid-May, the race was even, at 45 percent apiece in a Hoffman Research Group poll for Dudley's campaign. Drazan's own pollster, Public Opinion Strategies, put her up 48 percent to 44 percent in late June. DHM Research has handled the three latest independent surveys: Drazan up 2 for the business group Grow Oregon in early September, up 1 for OPB later that month and now Kotek up 2. Average them and both candidates land around 45 percent, with every result inside its margin of error. A poll for Kotek's campaign shows her with a bigger lead. The GBAO survey of 800 likely voters, taken October 1 to October 4, had the governor at 46 percent and Drazan at 42 percent, with Smith at 6 percent and 6 percent undecided. Like Drazan's June poll, it was paid for by one of the campaigns. Horvick said the movement could come from Democrats who dislike Kotek but won't back Drazan and are settling on the governor as Election Day approaches. In 2022, Drazan also led some polls late in the race before Kotek pulled ahead and won 47 percent to 43.5 percent, in a three-way contest that included unaffiliated candidate Betsy Johnson. The Cook Political Report moved its rating to "Lean Democrat" in September, describing Oregon as one of the rare races drifting toward Republicans this cycle. Sabato's Crystal Ball has it at "Likely Democrat." What to Know About Oregon's Governor Race The race is a rematch of 2022. With no third candidate splitting conservative and centrist votes this time, Drazan has spent more time in the state's population centers. Neither candidate is especially popular. In the Oregonian poll, 39 percent of respondents had a positive impression of Drazan and 47 percent a negative one. Kotek fared worse, at 36 percent positive and 60 percent negative. The electorate splits along familiar lines. Kotek led 56 percent to 33 percent in the Portland area and did better with women and college graduates. Drazan ran stronger with men and voters without a college degree. The reasons voters gave for rejecting each candidate mirror the campaigns' own messages. Democrats and liberals who would not commit to Kotek most often cited her record and a lack of accomplishments. Republicans and conservatives who would not back Drazan most often cited opposition to the GOP and its allies. Undecided voters lean toward Drazan's issues. Among the 41 undecided respondents, 30 percent named the economy as Oregon's most important problem and 27 percent named homelessness, both well above the overall sample. The OPB poll found voters sour on the state's direction. Only 29 percent said Oregon is headed the right way, while 58 percent said it is on the wrong track and 73 percent rated the state's economy as poor. Yet 69 percent described their own finances as good, a gap that points to frustration with state government more than with household budgets. Asked to name the state's top problem, OPB respondents most often cited cost of living at 18 percent, followed by high taxes at 16 percent, homelessness at 13 percent and poor leadership at 11 percent. Oregon voters also give Republicans an edge on the economy, despite the party's national headwinds on the issue. Forty-four percent said they would prefer a conservative governor to handle it, compared with 32 percent who wanted a liberal one. The numbers reverse on social issues, 42 percent to 37 percent, and Kotek has leaned on abortion access and LGBTQ+ rights in her campaign. Kotek Aims to Tie Drazan to Trump Kotek has made tying Drazan to Trump the center of her campaign. The polling suggests the strategy has limits, even in a deep-blue state. In the OPB survey, Trump was viewed favorably by 37 percent of likely voters, 1 point behind Kotek at 38 percent. Sixty-three percent viewed the president negatively, compared with 60 percent for the governor. The contrast was on display at the candidates' first debate on October 1 at the University of Oregon in Eugene. Kotek invoked the president 13 times, according to Willamette Week. Drazan accused the governor of "pushing everything off on the federal administration" and kept returning to housing, schools and costs. Drazan also distanced herself from one of the president's most unpopular moves in the state. "Let me be clear, I don't want National Guard troops in Oregon," she said during the debate. Her record on the issue is mixed. When Trump moved to send the National Guard to Portland last year, Drazan, then the House Republican leader, blamed state and local leaders for allowing "violent mobs and domestic terrorists" to assault federal agents at the city's U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility. Weeks later, a House Republican spokesperson said she opposed deploying Guard members from other states, then asked to retract the statement. The race has drawn neither a Trump endorsement nor significant spending from the Republican Governors Association, a contrast with 2022, when the group treated Drazan as a priority pickup. Data Centers and AI The fight over artificial intelligence infrastructure has become one of the race's sharpest flashpoints. Oregon ranks among the top 10 U.S. markets for data centers, according to Pew Research. On September 3, Drazan released an ad accusing Kotek of giving data centers $1 billion in tax breaks while raising taxes on Oregonians by more than $6 billion. Democrats answered by branding her "Data Center Drazan," and Kotek has hit her for voting against the POWER Act, a 2025 law requiring tech companies to pay higher electricity rates to cover data centers' energy use. Within days, both candidates hardened their positions. Kotek appeared at an anti-data center rally in Salem and backed a moratorium on new facilities. Hours later, Drazan said she also supported an immediate pause, weeks after telling OPB she did not support ending existing tax breaks for the industry. Voters care about the issue more than they rank it. Only 2 percent of OPB respondents named data centers or AI as the state's top problem, yet 72 percent said the candidates' positions on data centers would matter to their vote. A July DHM poll found 71 percent of Oregonians view data centers negatively. Newsweek's AI Policy Scorecard, which rates members of Congress from 1, or AI Skeptic, to 5, or AI Booster, gives Oregon's eight-member delegation an average score of 2.5. The only member on the Booster side is Republican Representative Cliff Bentz, at 3.6, whose eastern Oregon district includes Umatilla County, home to about a fifth of the state's data centers. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: New poll shows Tina Kotek and Christine Drazan neck-and-neck, with Republicans eyeing Oregon's first governor's win since 1982.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: The Midterm Spending Bonanza Is Threatening Democracy Like Never Before
news.text:
Big money has long dominated American politics, with wealthy donors, corporations, and special interests dumping tons of cash into presidential and congressional elections. This year is no exception. But what’s different is that the quid pro quo of campaign money for preferential government treatment is more brazen than ever before and has become part of the cornucopia of corruption running through the Trump administration. 

In this new episode of Stress Test campaign finance reporter Russ Choma joins hosts David Corn and Garrison Hayes to analyze the $1.7 billion that has been poured into the election so far—including hundreds of millions from crypto and sports betting, industries that were barely on the political map in 2020. “There’s no sign of deceleration,” Russ says in the episode. “There’s no sign of slowing down, it’s only acceleration.”

So much of what’s happening is hidden from public scrutiny, because super PACs can obscure donors, and issue ads and targeted turnout operations can go unreported. It’s like “dark matter in the universe that you can’t see,” David observes. The threat to democracy is real, because donors get to cash in by having the administration align with their deregulatory goals, or, in the case of Elon Musk, can gain control of an agency or decimate whole sections of government. “They’re getting more than total access,” Russ explains. “They’re getting inclusion.”

“There have always been a lot of people who believe that the government was corrupt,” Russ says. “But the problem is that now they’re right.” And this cynicism isn’t just a side effect of all this money. It’s a goal. After all, the most effective thing a campaign can buy, Russ notes, is a negative ad, designed “to make you not vote.”

But there could be some hope. Voters are telling pollsters they see more corruption these days, and when that collides with a sour economy, apathy can curdle into anger. Just ask Viktor Orbán, voted out in Hungary after 16 years in power due to a combo of a poor economy and rampant corruption. Might such synergy be happening in the United States?

That’s all in today’s episode of Stress Test. Find it on our YouTube channel at youtube.com/MotherJones.

And want more on how money is warping American politics? Russ Choma covers Trump’s crypto fortune, his financial conflicts, and the cash behind the midterms. Check out his latest.

This transcript was generated with automated tools and may contain errors.

David Corn: This is Stress Test from Mother Jones. I’m David Corn.

Garrison Hayes: And I’m Garrison Hayes. Welcome to the third episode of the show, David. Oh, no, no, to our audience. Welcome to you. And also welcome to you, David. How are you doing today?

DC: Well, welcome to you, Garrison. It’s great to be back with you. And I hear that when I was gone, you did a great show with Tim Murphy about the backlash to data centers and how that’s become a bipartisan issue during this campaign.

GH: Yeah, yeah, yeah. We had a great conversation about how this is a rare bipartisan issue where you’re seeing backlash and pushback and real anger from both Democrats and Republicans and really everyone in between and beyond, especially in the state of Texas. Our colleague Tim Murphy has been out in Texas a few times, and he has another trip upcoming, where he’s been reporting from the ground on the way that these data centers and the backlash to them are really shaping the political atmosphere there. In fact, he told me about how the governor, Greg Abbott, has made this huge 180 kind of turn from being a champion of data centers to being against them.

DC: Wow, I wonder why. It couldn’t be principle, could it?

GH: You know, he actually invited, you know, Google. They had this big press conference where Google’s spending $40 billion on multiple campuses across the state. It will be their largest data center kind of AI footprint in the country, maybe even in the world. There are other huge projects out there, and none of those projects are actually coming to an end, even though the governor is talking about a pause or a moratorium on data centers going forward.

So there’s a lot to dig in there. If you missed that episode, I really encourage you to go back and watch it. It’s such an important issue during these midterms. You can catch it on our YouTube channel. That’s the Mother Jones YouTube channel. Make sure you subscribe to our channel so you don’t miss any of the episodes coming up.

Okay, listen, today’s gonna be a good show. We’re talking about money in politics, specifically campaign money—in other words, what you can and cannot buy in American politics. And we’re gonna talk about some of the big spenders, some of the big receivers of that money, who wishes they had more money, perhaps, who has more money than they need.

DC: Yeah, everybody.

GH: Everyone. Okay, so that’s an inclusive list. But we’re also gonna talk about Trump and how he and the vice president, JD Vance, are hitting the campaign trail. David, you’ve covered many, many, many, many—

DC: Don’t remind me.

GH: You’ve covered many elections, my friend. So talk to me about what you’ve seen and whether what you’re seeing from the Trump administration—so President Trump and Vice President JD Vance—is this stuff normal, the way they’re hitting the campaign trail?

DC: Well, in a way, yes, but also no. You can tell a lot about a campaign and how things are going politics by looking at a politician’s travel itinerary, right? Because right now we see JD Vance and Donald Trump hitting the campaign trail, but they’re going to places where they shouldn’t be—where they shouldn’t have to be going. Oklahoma, for instance. They’re going to states and districts where usually the Republicans would have a lock on that election by this point. So it shows that they see what everybody else is seeing: a possible gigantic blue tsunami heading right toward the White House.

There are races across the country that, quite frankly, are amazing political experts because they’re competitive: Senate race in Iowa, Senate race in Kansas, in Texas, and even the governor’s race in Texas might be within a few points. So Republicans are in, I think, the technical term, freaking out, and they’re worrying about races. And that means—you know, listen, the president, who’s not quite an asset for the Republican Party at this point in time, when he’s at 31 percent approval rating, according to the AP, still has limited amount of time and places he can go in the five weeks left in the election here, or less than that maybe. And so it makes a big—it’s a big deal where you decide to deploy him and JD Vance.

The same with money. We see Republicans taking their money out of certain states, like North Carolina, where they thought they were competitive in the Senate race there, and shoveling it into South Carolina, where they shouldn’t be competitive, and also to Texas. So that’s how you can tell what they’re thinking, by looking where the money and the president is going.

But I have to say this: When he’s at such a low approval rating, the Trump brand ain’t so strong, and you have to wonder to what degree his campaigning helps people. Now, it may help people in deep—candidates in deep-red states if you can gin up Republican turnout there. But at the same time, a lot of Republicans are running away from the president, and they don’t want their voters in their states to be thinking about Trump.

And listen, he’s out there, and I have some notes here to the side. You know, in one campaign stop recently, he said he knows more about inflation than anyone else, and he knows more about everything than anyone else. When people already are not thinking highly of you, talking about how well you know inflation when inflation is a concern to them is really not smart.

But I think this topped it for me, at least. At one rally, he said you need to be a student at the top of your class at MIT to turn on a lawnmower nowadays, you know? But I got rid of all that stuff. Now you can have a lawnmower. What the heck is he talking about? I have yet to see one focus group where people are complaining about lawnmowers. But don’t take it from me. Let’s hear directly from the president of the United States.

[Clip plays.]

GH: Inspiring. Inspiring stuff.

DC: Garrison, these are not what you call ringing endorsements, right? And it’s always about him. Pretend I’m on a ballot. Most Republicans running right now would rather he not be on the ballot, would rather he be put in exile in Mar-a-Lago.

GH: Yeah, it’s hard to kind of—it’s almost distills down so well the fear that I heard from so many Republicans in the 2024 cycle that Trump was really tanking the party, that he was more or less a dead end for the Republican Party. That, yes, he’s very popular; yes, he has this magic way with the American people to get them to vote for him. He has all this charisma, but really there is no viable succession plan. There is no real plan for after Trump.

And we have, as you see on the screen, Vice President JD Vance. But even with Vance, you know, so many voters have said online, and I’ve heard them myself, that he just doesn’t quite have the it factor. And I think it really does present a real problem for Republicans going forward. And we will see. I mean, talk about stress test. This midterm will actually be a real stress test for the Republican Party to see how they chart a path forward after Trump.

DC: Let’s talk about one of the big issues in any campaign, and it only keeps getting bigger, and that is big money. I talked a moment ago about how Republicans are shifting and, you know, where they’re putting their dollars, but we’re talking about tens of millions and hundreds of millions of dollars. I mean, campaigns keep getting more and more expensive, and that just gives more power to the people who can provide those dollars. So fortunately, we have with us today Russ Choma, a reporter from—for Mother Jones, who’s one of the experts on campaign finances. He’s been covering this almost as long as I have. So let’s bring on Russ.

Russ Choma: Well, thanks for having me, guys. There’s obviously a lot to talk about this year. The money gets bigger every year, and we’re here again, and it’s even bigger.

GH: It’s even bigger. One thing that’s really stood out to me is just how much AI and crypto and Polymarket and these betting markets and all of that—how much of that money is actually going into this election. We saw in New York there was a big kind of AI race there. And some of these things are kind of constantly popping up in the conversation. It feels like these industries are funneling a ton of money into politics. And I’m curious if that sense is true and what you’re seeing as you’re reporting on this.

RC: Yeah, no, I mean, it’s more than a feeling. It’s what’s actually happening. And it’s interesting because for years and years there were always sort of the same set of special interest groups. And, you know, sometimes with new technology, some, you know, new interest groups would be added, but it’s amazing how instantly both prediction, sports betting, crypto, AI have all sort of—and they all sort of merge into one industry in a lot of ways—have sort of popped onto the scene.

I think the last good count that I saw, about a $1.7 billion has been put into this election. And about a quarter billion of that is just from crypto and sports betting. That’s just the money we know about. It’s a huge, huge, huge sum. But for them to go from two—2020 basically not being on the map to that much money in a midterm, it’s not even a presidential election, is really, really stunning. So yeah, it’s more than a feeling. It’s really happening.

DC: And what strikes me, Russ, is that in the past some big donors have been more—well, sometimes they have wider interests, like, say, the Koch brothers. They want deregulation, they don’t like environmental controls, they want low taxes. It’s basically the conservative libertarian agenda, like, straight through. And we’ve seen that with other major guys who run hedge funds and people like that. The way that George Soros on the Democratic side has a wide liberal, progressive agenda.

But with these guys, it’s highly, highly specific. This is about as quid pro quo–ish as you can get. And I just want to give props to Andreessen Horowitz, the big venture capital fund with Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz. They’ve given over $115 million together to both an AI super PAC and a crypto super PAC.

And these two guys are just bringing this technology, this Big Tech money in in a very direct, very brazen, blatant—I would call it institutional corruption that is undeniable. They tell you what they want. They want to run free with AI and crypto, and they are putting in a lot of money to do this. I mean, to me, that seems almost a little bit different than some of the big money we’ve seen in the past.

RC: Yeah, I think that, like, the Koch brothers wanted to change America broadly, and these crypto guys and AI guys, they’ve got very specific wants. But at the same time, I mean—and I think we’ve seen this through the Trump administration—like, they’re trying to change regulation in general. And they’re trying to just have a broad, open—you know, while she always was lobbying for the carried interest loophole, they want everything, these guys. But yeah, you’re right. It does seem very transactional. They are after very specific things. And the amount of money they’re putting in is—I mean, there’s no subtlety to it.

GH: You know, there’s this sense that whoever raises more money—it’s kind of like the money race. Like, whoever just raises the most money will win. We saw that challenged a little bit in 2024, if I’m remembering correctly, Russ, that Kamala raised—Kamala Harris raised close to $1 billion, while Donald Trump raised, I think, a bit less than that, if I’m remembering correctly. And so is it really that simple, that whoever raises the most money just kind of wins? Or how should we be thinking about that?

RC: Yeah, so, I mean, for decades that was absolutely correct. And both if you were an incumbent and if you raised more money, it was, like, something like 90 percent of the time or more, you won reelection. That has been scrambled, and that does have something to do with Citizens United. It has—I mean, Trump scrambled it in a really big way in 2016. He didn’t raise more money than Hillary, and he won. And so it was scrambled. Part of it is his, as you were referring to before, his personal charisma, as what it is—for what it is.

But, you know, there’s a lot of other things going on as well. And part of it is it’s hard to track the money. So Kamala’s campaign raised a lot of money, but there were also a lot of outside actors who were on Trump’s side who didn’t necessarily get counted in with the Trump campaign money. And that’s sort of the unknown.

And that’s sort of—again, and I think, you know, with Elon Musk, like, the money he put in last time, he put it into specific places, and he put it into Pennsylvania get-out-the-vote. It was a big question mark: Would that work? Seems to have worked in some degree. And so that’s part of the problem with this one is that, you know, I just said $1.7 billion, but there’s also money that we don’t know about that could be coming in.

DC: Yeah, I want to ask you about that. I want to get to some of the most expensive races, but just to put a fine point on this, there’s something called dark money. We’re talking the money—the figures that we just talked about is money that goes to super PACs that have to declare where they’re getting money from and where they’re spending, and to campaigns, and to the Republican and Democratic outfits, the national campaigns, the Senate campaigns run by the Democrats. But there’s something else going on there. It’s like dark matter in the universe that you can’t see, right? There’s a whole possible flow of money that we may never know about.

RC: Yeah. And so one thing is the super PACs have to say that they got money, but they don’t—they can be fairly vague about who they got money from. They can get money from an LLC, and you don’t know who put that money in the LLC. So some of that money, even though it’s technically not dark money, it’s disclosed, we don’t know where it came from.

But then there’s this other class of money, and, you know, there are all these sort of arcane rules that were written for a different era, which have been applied to this one, which have allowed sort of, like, loopholes. And it’s allowed groups who maybe don’t get out and actually give money straight to the campaign but start spending money in other ways.

You know those ads, they’re called issue ads, where it’s like, call Congress and tell them that you don’t want them to, you know, and then it has some absolutely outlandish thing. And it’s not really trying to get anyone to call Congress, but it’s just trying to send, like, a scary message. And there’s—those, for instance, don’t get counted in that $1.7 billion. The things like the get-out-the-vote operation, which is just broadly get out the vote, but if Elon Musk is only targeting it at certain types of people, that doesn’t get reported. There’s all this money, and we don’t know what we don’t know.

And it’s been true every election since Citizens United. But I think the thing is—to what we were referring to before about this big influx of money from crypto and AI—is the money’s coming in on a different scale. So if it’s been there the whole time, we have to assume it’s coming in on a different scale than it’s ever come in on before.

I guess the one sort of counter to that, and this is something as a campaign finance reporter has always sort of, like, tweaked me, is that a lot of the apparent public feelings or shame about putting money into politics has gone away. And this is true on both sides. So it is possible that people are just—I mean, this thing where we have billionaires just opening their checkbooks and writing hundreds of millions of dollars. There was a time, even after Citizens United, where that wouldn’t happen because it was so unseemly. And now it just sort of seems to be the way we do politics. So, I mean, I guess that would be the one possible counter, is that everyone is just so brazen now.

But I do think that it’s very likely that there is quite a bit of money, if only because some of the ways they’re spending money are unsavory. You know, they’re sort of on dirty tricks, they’re on negative—which they might not be ashamed of spending the money, but they don’t want to give away the trick.

DC: So we may never know, really, all the deep money influences that are affecting this election or future elections. Let’s talk about some of the most expensive races that are happening now. We have Texas, we Ohio. Where have you seen the biggest influxes of money?

RC: I mean, the Ohio race is huge, and Texas race is huge. And Texas is always huge. But again, I think that this year in particular—and I think Ohio especially is seen as, like, such—I don’t wanna say bellwether ’cause that’s the cliché about it, but I mean, there’s a lot riding on this, and there’s a lot of big donors who feel very strongly about it, and they’re just spending. And—

DC: And we should say that the marquee race there, as you see on the picture here, on the video here, is James Talarico, the Democrat, running against Ken Paxton, the Republican, for a Senate seat, which once upon a time it would be almost inconceivable to think that a Democrat would be competitive for this seat.

RC: Yeah, no, and I mean, that’s, like you were mentioning before, I mean, we’re seeing money shifting. We’re seeing Republicans pulling out of some states, some of the big spenders, and we’re seeing Democrats going in. But I think there’s also—and there are competing factions as well. I mean, there are donors who don’t care what the GOP thinks, and they’re gonna send money in, and they’re gonna send money in for a certain type of candidate.

And I think that that was what we saw in the Texas primary, in the Republican primary, is we saw sort of different factions within the GOP fighting over that. The president happened to be one of the factions, and his faction won, but the money is not always universal. And—but again, like, that’s where it’s become this thing where very openly we’re using money to sort of settle these things, where I feel like before we—

DC: We should also say that there’s a competitive governor’s race in Texas too, where the Democrat’s been outspent, I think last I saw, 10-to-1, and yet Gina Hinojosa, running against the incumbent, Greg Abbott, is only a few points behind. So to your point earlier, Garrison, this is a place where even though she’s being tremendously outspent, she still has a—you know, she’s still in the fight, although that money differential might be too much for her to overcome.

GH: Yeah, it’ll certainly be challenging, as I understand it. To the point that both you and Russ are making, it’s been, what, 32, 33, 30-something years since a Democrat has won statewide there. And I guess, you know, to the point of our show, which is this idea of stress test, I’m curious, Russ, what we should be stressed about. Yes, you, you have to tell us what we should be stressed about. But, you know, as we think about money in politics, where should, you know, we be placing our attention, and what do you think should really be stressing the American people out?

RC: Yeah, I mean, I find the whole thing extremely stressful, but I think—

GH: Well, there it is.

DC: Well, you have to cover it, Russ.

RC: Yeah, yeah. I think that the—some of the specific things, actually—so here’s the thing that I find stressful, was that, you know, for years after Citizens United, and people would ask me and other campaign finance reporters, well, when are we gonna have some reform? When are we gonna have some change? And I was always very sort of cynical or skeptical about it, and I said, well, the next time we have a big scandal, the next time we have a Watergate, because most of the modern campaign finance rules are derived from Watergate.

Watergate was a campaign finance scandal, and it was one that was so bad that even people in the president’s party agreed we have to do something. And so a whole raft of changes came in, not just campaign finance, but all the big campaign finance rules came from that era. And so I always told people, well, you know, I think we’re going to need a big event, you know, something that really shocks people to get to the point where we want to have some reform and have some new serious rules and some serious thinking. And I think one thing that stresses me out is I don’t think we’re approaching that point.

I think that there are a lot of people who are outraged about this. I think that the numbers are shocking. You know, we’re seeing money come in in unprecedented ways. And I don’t have a feeling that anyone is getting that much closer to saying, all right, after this election, we’ve gotta do something about this. Like, there’s no sign of deceleration, there’s no sign of slowing down, it’s only acceleration. And it’s sort of like everything AI says, you know, it’s sort of accelerant has been put on it, and it’s taken off on a crazy level.

DC: So let’s talk about—you know, we’re talking about the quid here. Let’s talk about the quo. What examples do we see here of money coming into politics, particularly campaigns, and what people are actually getting for that? You know, Elon Musk, he has, you know, multiple, you know, billions of dollars’ worth of contracts with many government agencies, correct? You know, with NASA, obviously, but defense, and he has ideas for building a tunnel across from Alaska to Russia, all this stuff.

So the money he puts in, $100 million is nothing. Andreessen Horowitz has $100 billion in assets that they manage. If they put in $100 million into this campaign, and they’re doing more already, that’s one-tenth of 1 percent, if I did the math right. So what other examples do we see, Russ, of why this is a good investment, why people get good ROI?

RC: Well, I think it’s more than just the contracts. I mean, Elon Musk got an office, you know, and he got basically to control an agency that took apart other agencies. And I think that you’re seeing a lot of these big donors—and this is why I talk about, like, changing the whole landscape, the regulatory landscape—is they’re getting spots on seats of important commissions and rulemaking things. So it’s, you know, it’s not just I’m giving you some money and I’ll get this gift back. They’re getting more than total access. They’re getting inclusion, which is wild.

And again, I think that it seems a little weird to me as a reporter that, you know, both Elon Musk and Andreessen and a few other people, they’re surpassing what, say, George Soros has given. And George Soros has always been—for the right has been a big bogeyman, and the Kochs have been a bogeyman for the left. But I mean, those guys are being left behind by the amount of money that’s being put in. And we’re not quite seeing, like, the outrage over it, but yet they’re also getting so much more than I think that the Kochs or Soros ever imagined they would get.

DC: You just made me think of something, so I’m gonna go off the script we have for a second here. And that is, we’ve seen the Trump years just brazen corruption from Trump himself, right? And from his family. We’ve talked about that. We’ll be talking about that more as Stress Test goes on into the season. And it’s all corrupt, it’s brazen, it’s blatant. Republicans don’t say a word about it. There’s no Justice Department investigation. We know why.

And so compared to Trump making 7 billion, Andreessen Horowitz putting in a mere 100 million, it seems like chump change. I mean, he has sort of enhanced the whole culture of corruption, and maybe that’s why, Russ, we don’t see that type of reaction that you just said was absent.

RC: Yeah, no, and I think that a big thing—and this is not specifically about these midterms, although you’re seeing it play out in the midterms—is that Trump has changed the—what’s acceptable to do. And I think that also the constant headlines about his own corruption and all that, it changes the bar. But that’s a—you know, we are seeing sort of in polls people’s belief that the government is corrupt at an all-time high. And there have always been a lot of people who believe that the government was corrupt, but the problem is that now they’re right.

There’s a lot of corrupt things going on that haven’t—actually, they were the kind of things that people imagined were going on before but weren’t. And now we’re seeing them go on. And, you know, but that in itself is something that can affect the election, because it’s the kind of thing that depresses voters, and it depresses voter turnout when you don’t believe that there’s any point in voting because things aren’t gonna work out for you.

And I’ll say that a big part of campaign finance that I don’t think it’s talked about enough is that the most effective tools that a campaign can spend money on are negative ads. And the negative ads aren’t supposed to make you vote for someone, they’re supposed to make you not vote. And that’s the thing that has been proven. Positive ads don’t have very successful, if any, benefit to a campaign. A negative ad—other than name identification, I suppose. But a negative ad cannot—won’t make anyone switch to your side, but will make people stay home. And that’s, again, the more money there is, the less they’re trying to get people to participate.

GH: That’s the thing that stresses me out, Russ. Russ Choma, thank you so much for being here, joining us today. And listen, if you’re watching this, I hope you learned something. To our viewers and to our listeners, you can follow along for more of Russ’s reporting on MotherJones.com. He’s phenomenal. Thanks, Russ.

RC: Thanks, guys.

GH: All right, David. How are you feeling after listening to our colleague? More stressed or less stressed?

DC: Well, you know, I’ve been covering campaign finance for a long time myself, and it’s just always been frustrating that there’s not much more public revulsion against, you know, basically paying—you know, paying the ump, paying the referee. I mean, if there was one MLB baseball game and you found out that the pitcher was paying the ump, it would be in the news, and it would be a gigantic national scandal. But for decades, we’ve had big-money interests, you know, a lot on the right and some on the left, paying legislators who are supposed to do work for us, serve the public interest. And so it’s been a pretty corrupt, rotten system, and as Russ pointed out, it’s gotten worse.

But I’ll say this, and I’ll take issue with my colleague Russ on this one point. People do see—people are now telling pollsters that they see more corruption, and they don’t like that. And he says that depresses voting, and I think it has in the past. At the same time, though, I think it is adding a bit to voter anger. When you have corruption on one side and a bad economic status on the other side, people start making the connection.

And we just have to look to Hungary, where Viktor Orbán was voted out of office not too long ago after 16 years there and ruling as an authoritarian. And one of the major driving forces was the rampant corruption going on there. His son was driving around a car worth $100,000 or something, and the economy was not doing well, and people kind of melded those issues together.

So I think there is a sense now that Trump, you know, the crypto, the Russian guy, you know, financing Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding, and all this other stuff going on is beginning to register a bit. So I’m still stressed out about campaign financing, but I also think that maybe there’s a ray of light here, that other people out there will start paying a little more attention to the corrupt side of it.

GH: I think you’re spot-on. You know, we’ve been living in the kind of anti-incumbent kind of era in America for at least the last 10 years, maybe a little bit longer, depending upon when you start the count. But people are not enjoying the way things are, the status quo. And I think for the last decade, it’s been very much a, well, it’s the Republicans, and then when the Republicans fail, it’s the Democrats, and then when the Democrats fail, we’ll go back and choose Republicans again.

And I think sooner or later the American people will start to put the pieces together. I’d argue that they are already starting to put the pieces together, that there are these big-money spenders behind the scenes who are often influencing in ways that go beyond the ballot. And I think people will become increasingly sick of that kind of America. And so, you know, there’s always—there are always calls to end Citizens United and all of that. And maybe one day that will happen. But I do think you’re right, David, that we’re seeing a real frustration, a real anger, and people are starting to put those pieces together.

DC: That’s all we have for you on this episode. If you missed the first two episodes of Stress Test, you can go see them at our YouTube channel—that’s youtube.com/MotherJones—or wherever you get your podcasts.

GH: Remember that our great journalism, like the incredible work that Russ leads and does his reporting, and this show is made possible by your support. Yes, you. Your views and your subscriptions keep us going. So don’t forget to like this video or this podcast wherever you get it. Share it with a friend. Subscribe on our YouTube channel. That’s youtube.com/MotherJones. And if you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to leave a comment down below. We’re reading them, even the bad ones—even the bad ones. Or at least our producers are. We will be right back here in your feed again in just a few days with another edition of Stress Test. Thanks for watching.

news.title: Inside Kamala Harris' Stepdaughter Ella Emhoff's Life Years After Her Time as Second Daughter — From Knitting Bikinis to Creating Art
news.text:
Kamala Harris' stepdaughter Ella Emhoff has built a significant online presence after turning a viral coat moment into a mini empire of knit bikinis, runway walks, and art shows.

Over the years, the Los Angeles native went from having Secret Service agents trail her to selling handmade knitwear. RadarOnline.com takes a look inside Emhoff's life post-Biden administration.Inside Ella Emhoff's Early LifeEmhoff is the daughter of Second Gentleman Doug Emhoff and film producer Kerstin Emhoff, who were married in 1992 and divorced in 2008. Emhoff was just 9 years old at the time. 

Her father later married Harris on August 22, 2014, at the Santa Barbara County Courthouse. 

In 2017, Emhoff graduated from Wildwood School, and later left California for the busy streets of New York City. She enrolled at Parsons School of Design at The New School and earned her BFA in fine arts with a concentration in apparel and textiles in May 2021.Ella Emhoff's Iconic Miu Miu MomentOn January 20, 2021, Emhoff turned heads at President Joe Biden's inauguration in Washington, D.C. by showing up in a jewel-encrusted Miu Miu coat over a Batsheva dress. 

Emhoff later signed with IMG Models Worldwide and made her runway debut for Proenza Schouler at New York Fashion Week in 2021. 

Since then, Emhoff has modeled for Balenciaga and Adidas by Stella McCartney and has become a fixture at Paris Fashion Week.Ella Emhoff's Knitting BusinessBut modeling was never the final plan. In 2021, Emhoff launched her company Soft Hands, Inc., a creative hub for fashion, design and events. 

Emhoff started selling unique, hand-knit jackets, vests, hats, bikini tops and ceramics. 

She also built community with her Soft Hands Knit Club, hosting classes in Brooklyn in 2024. Emhoff has said she used modeling to build a platform, aiming to be an artist full-time.Where Emhoff Is Now?Emhoff served as a member of the Second Family of the United States from 2021 to 2025. In January 2025, Emhoff reflected on Instagram, writing that it was an honor being the 2nd daughter.

She's also defended her family publicly. In July 2024, after Senator J.D. Vance's "childless cat lady" comments resurfaced, Emhoff clapped back, saying: “How can you be childless when you have cutie pie kids like Cole and I?”

Now based in Bushwick, Emhoff is working as an artist, designer, and model with thousands of followers on Instagram.
news.summary: Ella Emhoff is now working as an artist, designer and model in Brooklyn after her viral inauguration moment.

news.title: Republicans Hit With Brutal Blow in Struggle to Keep Power
news.text:
Republicans are being bombarded by more bad news as they face down what is gearing up to be a brutal midterm season with just 24 days until Election Day. 

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report on Friday shifted 18 more House races, all in Democrats’ favor, giving them an even greater chance of flipping the majority from red to blue. 

Republicans are also left scrambling in multiple districts that Trump won by double digits, with new polls showing Democrats in the lead. 

Among the shifts by Cook Political Report, five seats that were previously considered “toss-ups” have been moved to “Lean Democrat,” while four seats that were previously “Lean Republican” are now considered “toss-ups.”

Looking at the maps now, their analysis indicates the most likely outcome is that Democrats will pick up nine to 19 seats in the House. They only need to flip three to take the majority. That would give them between 224 and 234 seats in the chamber.

It also means that Democrats only need to win 20 percent of the “toss-up” races to take control. 

Among the seats that are now considered “toss-ups” is the North Carolina 1st congressional district seat held by Democratic Rep. Don Davis. Republicans had attempted to gerrymander that competitive seat to help Republicans, but despite the time and money, their efforts may come up short. 

Among the “toss-up” seats that have now shifted to “Lean Democrat” are the Iowa congressional districts represented by GOP Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks. It comes as Speaker Mike Johnson is set to campaign for Miller-Meeks on Friday afternoon in Davenport, Iowa. 

Johnson also attended a fundraiser for Republican Ralph Alvarado, who is running for Kentucky’s 6th congressional district on Friday morning just as that race was also shifted. It went from “Likley Republican to Lean Republican.” 

Trump won the district by 15 points just over two years ago, but a new poll by House Majority PAC found Democrat Zach Dembo leading Alvarado by three points 48 percent to 45 percent on Thursday. When multiple third party candidates were factored in, Dembo leads Alvarado by six points.

Despite the deluge of bad news, Johnson has tried to paint an optimistic picture for his party as he continues to march lockstep with Trump, but cracks appear in his rosy facade. 

“If we lose the House it will be because the people were misled,” Johnson told Fox News this week while also insisting he did not know how losing the House could fall on him.

He also admitted in a rare moment that he did not know what his next chapter in life would be if Republicans lose the majority. 

Pennsylvania’s 7th congressional district also shifted from “toss-up” to “Lean Blue” just days after Johnson campaigned there with Rep. Ryan MacKenzie. 

Even in districts not shifted by Cook Political Report, Republicans saw warning signs on Friday. 

Up in New York’s 21st congressional district, which Trump won by nearly 21 points less than two years ago, a new poll by Siena showed Democrat Blake Gendebien leading MAGA candidate Anthony Constantino by four points, 46 percent to 42 percent. 

While it showed the Republican gubernatorial candidate up in the district, it had 21 percent of Republicans and 51 percent of Independents backing Gendebien. 

Democrats celebrated the poll, but Constantino’s campaign blasted it as not credible and took issue with it including a write-in candidate in the race.

Trump will be holding a rally on Friday in New York’s neighboring 22nd congressional district. It’s one former Vice President Kamala Harris won by more than seven points in 2024 and the congressional seat is rated “Solid Democrat.”

news.title: Iowa poll SHOCK: Pollster admits how it skewed key race results toward Democrats when GOP really leads
news.text:
Skepticism is mounting about the narrative that a blue wave is set to crash in the midterms. There are, after all, signs that the pollsters may have once again greatly missed the mark.

In a move sure to further shake Democrat confidence, one outfit has openly second-guessed its weighting processes and whether recent polls have properly captured Republican sentiment.

'People want to see the predictive accuracy of the poll,' [but] 'polls can't really do that.'

State Navigate, a nonpartisan organization that engages in election forecasting and public polling, noted on Tuesday that it conducted a poll last week in an Iowa state Senate district that President Donald Trump won by 21 points in 2024 but that flipped to a Democrat in a January 2025 special election.

The polling outfit contacted over 400 likely voters in the district and initially found that Democrat state Sen. Mike Zimmer had a three-point lead over Republican challenger Joe Stutting and that in the Iowa governor's race, Democrat Rob Sand was five points ahead of Republican Zachary Lahn.

These results left the pollsters suspicious.

"We noticed two problems in our survey: 1. There are more likely Trump voters who are lying about their 2024 vote for the president than anywhere else we’ve polled, and 2. Even accounting for this, rural Republicans in Iowa are difficult to reach," said the polling outfit.

A similar miss resulted in humiliation and a career change in 2024 for J. Ann Selzer, whose November 2024 poll showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris with a three-point lead over Trump in Iowa. Trump ultimately ended up winning the state by over 13 points.

RELATED: Vulnerable Ohio Democrat's last-minute flip-flop on trans insanity has LGBT activists crying 

 Scott Olson/Getty Images

The pollster found that fewer respondents recalled having voted for Trump in 2024 than likely actually had voted for him and noted in an analysis that has since been reworded, "Donald Trump carried SD-35 by 21 points in 2024, but in our standard version of this poll, which isn't weighted to recalled vote, likely voters recall a Trump win of just 7 points."

Because of the discrepancy, the pollster ran the results again. However, this time, pollsters weighted answers so that 2024 recall votes more closely resembled the actual heavily pro-Trump results from two years ago. Working on the apparent presumption that Democrats are poised to fare better this cycle, the pollsters then shifted every region roughly five points toward Democrats.

Despite the blue shift, this change in weighting produced a red result — a red result that was partially hidden by an error in the pollster's analysis that also skewed toward the Democrat. The analysis said Zimmer was up by two points, when the weighted poll actually showed a two-point lead for Republican Joe Stutting.

Chaz Nuttycombe, executive director of State Navigate, confirmed the analysis error to Blaze News.

The weighted survey also found Lahn and Sand tied in the governor's race with 45% each.

"That still bodes well for Democrats given the Republican lean of this district, but a 5-point difference shows how weighting decisions can change the outcome," wrote the pollster in the analysis. "Our experience polling this competitive race raises concerns similar to Echelon Insight’s Patrick Ruffini’s: Republicans, particularly rural Republicans in Iowa, are very unresponsive to surveys, at least for now."

"The real surprise here is someone actually admitted a mistake," BlazeTV host and Iowa native Steve Deace told Blaze News. "That’s rare these days."

"Rural voters have always been the toughest to poll, but throw in how reticent Trump supporters justifiably are to respond to polls mostly from outlets who lie daily about them and Trump, and now you know why Trump has outperformed his Midwest polling every election cycle," continued Deace. "Assuming most of these public polls aren’t just Democrat ops, of course."

This is hardly the first splash of cold water to land on Democrats' hopes and dreams.

CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten suggested last week that Republicans in Midwest races may once again be poised to outperform polls — and that if they do so, as they did in 2018 and 2024, then "there's a very, very strong chance that Republicans hold on to the United States Senate, even if Democrats win in places they don't historically win in, like Texas."

Concerns, particularly on the left, that pollsters are missing the mark again have prompted Emerson College director of polling Spencer Kimball to go on defense.

Kimball recently told the NH Journal podcast that the polling industry "has never been stronger. Our analysis has never been stronger."

Kimball emphasized, however, that while "people want to see the predictive accuracy of the poll," "polls can't really do that."

"Sometimes they’ll fall on the right side, and sometimes they come up a little light on that side," continued Kimball. "But generally speaking, they fall within that range about 90 percent of the time."

news.title: Amish Shah's Desperate Debate Flip-Flops Prove His Extremism Is Toxic With Voters
news.text:
Amish Shah wants to represent Arizona's 1st Congressional District, but even he knows his agenda is too extreme for voters, and after ducking out of the August 26 debate with Republican Jay Feely, radical socialist Amish Shah finally showed up to debate Feely last night. Shah, unsurprisingly, spent the debate lying to voters and flip-flopping on issues to hide his extremism — something he knows is toxic with Arizonans.

Shah denied that he campaigned for socialist Senator Bernie Sanders.

"I never campaigned for Bernie Sanders," he said. But that's just not true. Video shows Shah campaigning for Sanders at an "Arizona for Bernie 2020" event hosted by the Phoenix chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Shah is even listed on the event's archived webpage. In his remarks, Shah said Sanders had an "authenticity." 

"There was an authenticity about him that I think so many of us were drawn to; he was coming at it from with his heart," Shah said. "That's what drew me to his campaign." Shah would go on to knock doors for Sanders. 

He also credited Bernie with reforming the Democrat Party. "The message is growing; it's getting louder. What's amazing is that this wasn't really part of the conversation before Bernie came around," he said. "And this has now become a national platform, and he's taken the Democratic Party and, in my opinion, improved our platform."

That's campaigning for Bernie Sanders.

Shah also said it was "misinformation" that he supports single-payer socialist healthcare.

news.title: Trump Voters Are Giving Republicans a Midterm Warning, Polls Show
news.text: Voters who backed President Donald Trump in 2024 are less enthusiastic about voting in November's midterm elections than those who supported Kamala Harris, recent polls suggest, adding to signs of a turnout challenge for Republicans as they try to hold onto control of Congress. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted September 30 to October 5, 48 percent of Harris's 2024 voters said they were "very enthusiastic" about voting in November, compared with 30 percent of Trump voters. The poll surveyed 4,506 US adults online and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points. A separate Economist/YouGov poll found a similar gap using a different question. Asked whether they were more or less enthusiastic about voting this year than in previous congressional election years, 52 percent of Harris's 2024 voters said they were more enthusiastic, compared with 34 percent of Trump's. The YouGov survey was conducted between October 2 and October 5 among 1,513 US adult citizens, including 1,381 registered voters or people who said they had planned to register. The margin of error for registered voters was plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. Democrats Hold a House Edge As Voters Focus on Prices This distinction matters for the midterms, as an enthusiasm gap could affect which party's supporters show up, but it does not confirm how many voters will cast ballots. Meanwhile, a third CBS News/YouGov poll offered a broader look at the potential implications. Its Battleground Tracker estimates Democrats currently have an advantage in the fight for a narrow House majority, citing opposition to the Trump administration's policies and a Republican base that is less likely to turn out. The survey was conducted from September 30 to October 2 among 2,166 US adults and had a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points for the full sample. The House estimate gives the enthusiasm findings added significance. If Republicans have trouble mobilizing their base, that could make it harder to defend their seats. Cost-of-Living Concerns Add to GOP Turnout Challenge Cost of living is also a prominent concern across the polling. In the Reuters/Ipsos survey, 52 percent of respondents said a candidate's position on cost of living would be the most important factor in their congressional vote, including 53 percent of Republicans. The CBS poll also found that many voters felt food and grocery prices were rising and that the administration had not focused enough on lowering costs. It reported that Republicans who thought the administration was not paying enough attention to prices were less likely to say they would definitely vote. For Republicans, the findings suggest a two-part challenge involving addressing an issue voters say matters to their decision and persuading less-motivated supporters that the election is worth turning out for. For Democrats, the polls point to an opportunity if their comparatively higher enthusiasm translates into votes across competitive races. The Reuters/Ipsos poll found other potential signs of Republican vulnerability. Thirteen percent of Trump's 2024 voters said they were unsure who they would support in a congressional election, compared with 7 percent of Harris's voters. Among all respondents who said they were enthusiastic about voting, 62 percent said they were motivated by opposition to Trump, while 36 percent said they were eager to support him. Men, a group Trump won by 12 points in 2024, were more enthusiastic about voting and more certain they would cast a ballot than women in the Reuters/Ipsos poll. Men also favored Democrats over Republicans on the congressional ballot, 43 percent to 39 percent, and had generally favored Republicans in 2025, but since August have leaned back toward the Democrats. Republican strategist Charlie Gerow said the findings raised the stakes for the party's turnout efforts, while predicting the enthusiasm gap could narrow as Republicans focus on the prospect of Democrats gaining power. "The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what's going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections," Gerow said. Republicans also retain an advantage among voters ages 50 and older, who favored the party by 44 percent to 42 percent in the Reuters/Ipsos poll, though that was down from 8 points in December. Together, the results point to a turnout concern for Republicans. Voters who supported Trump may be less motivated to vote than their Democratic counterparts, while the cost of living is a leading issue and men's preferences have shifted in the generic ballot. The polls, however, do not establish why individual Trump voters feel less enthusiastic, or whether they will ultimately stay home. Both parties are competing for control of Congress in the November 3 midterms. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Sam Stevenson and James Debens
news.summary: Polls show Trump’s 2024 voters are less enthusiastic about the midterms than Harris voters, raising GOP turnout concerns.

news.title: A'ja Wilson wins her third straight WNBA MVP and record fifth overall
news.text: A'ja Wilson fine-tunes her shooting touch following every practice. That little bit of extra work has defined her greatness since being drafted first overall in 2018.On Thursday, she received a voice message from former Vice President Kamala Harris congratulating her on redefining greatness leaguewide after she was named WNBA MVP for a third straight year and for the fifth time overall."Obviously, that is an honor," Wilson said. "A woman of our history, and I'm so appreciative to be able to share that moment with her through the phone call and the message of her delivering that I won my fifth MVP."In addition to becoming the first player to three-peat, Wilson won the award in 2020 and 2022.RELATED STORY | Las Vegas Aces star A'ja Wilson makes WNBA history with fourth MVP awardCommissioner Cathy Engelbert, Aces owner Mark Davis and team president Nikki Fargas accompanied Wilson's mother, Eva, who presented her daughter with the trophy."Each one of these has not been taken lightly," Wilson said, flanked by all five of her MVP trophies. "In my heart, they've always been so special. But this one here, I cried a little bit harder. This one here is just a little bit different, and whatever that may look like, or whatever that may feel, my fifth one, I think, is one that's just ... when you dream as a young girl, your dream so big and you write your goals out, and you just never imagine that you were able to just check them off."And when you're able to check them off — small wins, big wins — it truly means a lot. And so I think that's why I cried a little bit harder on this one, because 15-year-old A'ja wasn't sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP. She wasn't dreaming about being a three-time champion. She was dreaming about surviving this world."The 30-year-old Wilson once again led the league in scoring (26.2) while shooting nearly 53% from the field. She averaged 9.4 rebounds, a career-best 3.2 assists and 1.9 blocks.Wilson has the defending champion Aces back in the WNBA semifinals for the eighth consecutive season, although Las Vegas is down 2-0 in the best-of-five series against Golden State. Game 3 is Friday."This is great, I love it, not going to take for granted, shine her up, let's do it," Wilson said. "But tomorrow, when it comes to hoisting it in front of the fans, I love the fans ... but I doubt I will be doing that. I'll be warming up with my team. ... Everyone in this room knows the competitor that I am. Everyone knows what my main focus is, and that is to get a game."RELATED STORY | WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert to retire in December after seven year tenureWilson received 65 first-place votes and nine second-place votes for a total of 713 points from a national panel of sportswriters and broadcasters. Minnesota's Olivia Miles received six first-place votes and 40 second-place votes (442 points), while Indiana guards Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark followed with 287 and 212 points, respectively.No WNBA player besides Wilson has more than three MVPs, with Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson each having a trio. On the NBA side, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar had six and Michael Jordan and Bill Russell each had five."A'ja Wilson is one of one," Fargas said. "She's now standing in a category that no other WNBA player in the history of the league has accomplished. She's in the conversations with the Michael Jordans and the Wayne Gretzkys of the world — where she belongs."

news.title: CNN Data Guru Floored by Trump’s ‘Laughably Bad’ Crisis
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s approval numbers are “laughably bad,” according to CNN data analyst Harry Enten, who warned that no president in modern history has faced a worse position this close to Election Day.

New polling from the Pew Research Center shows Trump’s net approval rating is an astonishing 38 points underwater. The figures triggered disbelief on air as analysts examined the mounting electoral crisis threatening the administration’s legislative agenda and the Republican Party’s congressional majorities.

“No president I’ve ever seen is in a worse position before a midterm election than President Trump,” Enten said. “You go all the way back. You go back to Harry S. Truman, FDR. At this point before a midterm, ever, ever, ever... the worst I’ve ever seen is Donald John Trump, 38 points underwater.”

Enten stressed that the Pew figures are not an outlier, pointing to a string of major national surveys showing virtually identical results. 

Trump is 33 points underwater according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, following an earlier Ipsos survey that placed him at a 34-point deficit. Matching Pew’s record-low benchmark, an Associated Press survey and a CNN poll also show the president 38 points and 34 points underwater, respectively.

“No other president before a midterm election was even at minus 31,” Enten noted. “We are looking at history in the making here for the unpopularity of President Trump.”

The historical comparison underscores the severe political friction awaiting Republicans down the ballot. “It’s historic headwinds in which you are essentially going, ‘Oh my God, how am I supposed to win with numbers from a president this bad?’” Enten said.

The sharpest decline for the administration comes from independent voters, who split evenly between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential contest. Current survey data shows Trump’s standing with independents has plummeted to 57 points underwater. 

“You just never see numbers” like that, Enten said, adding that he struggled to find adjectives adequate to describe the plunge.

The analyst also pointed to Trump’s explicit push for supporters to “vote like I’m on the ballot” during midterm campaigning.

“Democrats, please, pretty, pretty, please, with a cherry on top, they are saying, yes, vote as if President Trump is on the ballot,” Enten said. “Because if he is on the ballot, you can pretty much guarantee that Democrats will take back the United States House.”

He added that the president’s low standing directly explains why Democratic prospects for capturing the United States Senate have continued to climb.

“This president, as unpopular as he is, is dragging Republicans underwater,” Enten said.
