news.title: US Polling ‘Nostradamus’ Predicts Which Senate Seats Democrats Will Flip
news.text: Historian and political forecaster Allan Lichtman has predicted that Democrats will take control of the U.S. Senate in November’s midterm elections, forecasting that five Republican-held seats will flip to the Democrats. Lichtman, dubbed the “Nostradamus” of U.S. election forecasting, expects Democrats to hold Michigan and New Hampshire as well as winning North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas and Alaska. His forecast would give Democrats 52 Senate seats against 44 Republicans, with the remaining seats held by independents. Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member Senate, compared with 45 Democrats and two independents who caucus with Democrats, giving Republicans a 53-47 advantage in party alignment. In a video outlining his predictions, Lichtman pointed to growing dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump, strong Democratic enthusiasm and the party’s performance in recent special elections. But do polling and prediction markets support his ambitious forecast? Newsweek contacted Lichtman's team via online form on Friday for comment. North Carolina: Lichtman’s Strongest Pick Lichtman describes North Carolina as the surest Democratic pickup, arguing that Republicans have withdrawn funding from the race. RealClearPolling’s average of surveys conducted up to October 8 put Democratic former Governor Roy Cooper at 50 percent and Republican Michael Whatley at 43 percent. Kalshi's market listing gave Cooper a 96.5 percent chance of winning, compared with 3.5 percent for Whatley. Both indicators strongly favor Cooper, making North Carolina the most convincing of Lichtman’s five predictions based on those figures. Maine: Can Democrats Defeat Susan Collins? Lichtman predicts Republican Senator Susan Collins will lose despite her history of winning competitive elections. A polling average last updated October 1 put Democrat Troy Jackson at 48.4 percent and Collins at 46.6 percent. A Washington Post-Schar School poll published October 9 found Jackson leading 50 percent to 46 percent. Kalshi’s market listing gave Jackson about a 66 percent chance of winning, against 34 percent for Collins. The figures favor Democrats, but the narrow polling lead suggests the race remains competitive. Ohio: Sherrod Brown’s Comeback Bid Lichtman expects Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown to defeat Republican incumbent Jon Husted, arguing that Brown’s appeal to working-class voters could help him overcome Ohio’s Republican lean. A CNN poll updated October 8 put Brown at 45 percent and Husted at 43 percent. Kalshi’s market listing gave Brown a 62 percent chance of victory, compared with 38 percent for Husted. Texas: Potential Democratic Breakthrough Lichtman believes Democratic state Representative James Talarico could defeat Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton, pointing to Paxton’s controversies and Trump’s declining approval ratings. RealClearPolling’s average of surveys conducted up to October 8 put Talarico and Paxton neck and neck at 45 percent. Kalshi’s market listing gave Talarico a 65 percent chance of winning, against 35 percent for Paxton. The figures suggest Democrats have a credible opportunity, but a victory would still represent a major breakthrough in a state that has favored Republicans. Alaska: Close Race With Democrats Favored Lichtman predicts that Democratic former Representative Mary Peltola will defeat Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, despite Alaska’s Republican-leaning voting history. RealClearPolling’s average of surveys updated October 7 put Peltola at 51 percent and Sullivan at 49 percent. Kalshi’s market listing was more optimistic, giving the Democrat a 75 percent chance of winning, compared with 25 percent for the Republican. Lichtman’s 2024 Prediction Raises Questions Lichtman’s Senate forecast comes after his high-profile failure to predict the 2024 presidential election correctly. He forecast that Kamala Harris would defeat Donald Trump, who ultimately won. Lichtman is best known for his Keys to the White House system, which uses political and economic indicators to forecast presidential elections. However, he says his Senate predictions are based on his experience and understanding of American politics rather than a formal model. He also identified South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska as potential additional opportunities for Democrats, although those states are not central to his forecast. Lichtman argued that Trump’s unpopularity could hurt Republican candidates in multiple states. The polling and market figures offer some support for his predictions, particularly in North Carolina, while the other races remain more competitive. His forecast is a bold prediction of a Democratic wave. Whether Democrats can flip all five seats and secure the 52-seat majority that he expects will depend on turnout, individual candidates and how accurately polls capture voter preferences. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Allan Lichtman predicts Democrats will flip five Senate seats in 2026, potentially reshaping control of Congress.

news.title: Democrats are changing their transgender message. Republicans say they’re just flip-flopping
news.text: South Carolina Democratic Senate nominee Dr. Annie Andrews appears to be distancing herself from her past opposition to restricting transgender athletes in girls' sports, telling Fox News Digital she opposes biological males competing in women's sports and gender transition surgeries for minors. As Democrats fight to regain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, Andrews is among a group of candidates in competitive races in red and swing states who seem to be shifting positions on transgender issues. Meanwhile, Republicans are aiming to use the highly-charged issue as a cudgel to bash Democrats for a second straight cycle. "I don't support biological men playing in women's sports, and I don't support gender surgery on minors," Andrews told Fox News Digital. Andrews, who's locked in an increasingly competitive midterm election showdown with Republican Sen. Darline Graham in reliably red state South Carolina, delivers the same message in a new campaign commercial, adding, "I want you to hear me loud and clear." DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS FORMER - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT But Graham, who was appointed to the Senate following the sudden death this summer of her older brother, longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham, is accusing Andrews of trying to conceal her previous position on transgender athletes. Andrews "has spent years supporting biological males competing in girls’ sports. Now that she’s running for Senate, she’s trying to hide from that radical record," Graham recently charged. Graham and Republicans point to Andrews' opposition to a 2022 South Carolina law barring transgender athletes from competing on girls' and women's public school sports teams. "This is shameful legislation that does nothing to protect or support women or children in SC. In fact, it is actively harmful. I will always support trans youth," Andrews wrote in a social media post at the time. Republicans are seeking to once again make the issue a campaign liability. The GOP effectively blasted Democrats in the 2024 election, with President Donald Trump's campaign targeting Democratic nominee Vice President Kamala Harris with ads declaring "Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you." WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM POWER RANKINGS Republicans spent more than $200 million to run ads targeting Democrats on the transgender issue in the 2024 campaign, arguably helping the GOP to sweeping victories. The latest national polls indicate that most Americans oppose transgender athletes playing on sports teams that don’t match their birth sex. More than three-quarters (76%) of those questioned in a Fox News national poll conducted last month backed banning biological men from competing in women's sports, with one in five opposed. The survey indicated bipartisan support, with 90% of Republicans, 77% of independents and 61% of Democrats backing the ban. Facing a rough political climate amid an unpopular war in Iran and soaring gas and diesel prices as they try to hold their fragile congressional majorities, Trump and the GOP are increasingly looking to replay their transgender political playbook. Trump, at last month's GOP midterm convention, described anti-trans messaging as one of the party’s most effective campaign tools to drive voter turnout and target Democrats in the final stretch leading up to Election Day. "It’s one of our great sound bites of all time," the president said at the two-day confab in Dallas. Tim Scott and Rep. Richard Hudson highlighted the issue in their addresses. Meanwhile, Republican ads on the issue are running for a second straight cycle. But Democrats are recalibrating, and learning to fight back. One of the first to pivot following the 2024 election setbacks was California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate. In early 2025, he suggested that biological males playing in women's sports was "deeply unfair." Also making headlines and sparking a debate among Democrats was Rep. Seth Moulton of Massachusetts, who said soon after the 2024 elections that he opposed transgender athletes competing in girls' sports and that Democrats spent too much time trying not to offend people. Veteran Democratic strategist Maria Cardona told Fox News that "Democrats are being smart on this issue in terms of defining where they are on it so their opponents can't define them and then pivoting back to the issues that they know that voters actually care about." "I have two little girls, I don't want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I'm supposed to be afraid to say that," Moulton told The New York Times. Fast-forward to present day, and while most Democratic politicians remain steadfast supporters of transgender rights, there are an increasing number who have changed course. Texas state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee trying to flip a GOP-held seat in red-leaning Texas, has been targeted by Republicans over his past support for allowing transgender athletes in girls' sports. But he told Fox News last month, "I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In Republican-dominated Iowa, where Democrats are aiming to capture another open-GOP held Senate seat, Democratic nominee state Rep. Josh Turek has expressed opposition to biological males competing in women's sports and gender transition surgeries for minors after facing Republican criticism. Longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, who is facing a tough re-election bid, is running ads saying "boys should not play in girls’ sports" and that she is focused on "making your life more affordable." In her campaign mailers she touts that she "voted to ban schools from touting gender ideology in classrooms," and, "Unlike the far left, I believe boys shouldn't play girls' sports." But the National Republican Congressional Committee pointed out that Kaptur voted against the GOP-led Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act in April 2023 and January 2025. LONGTIME DEMOCRAT GETS HIT FROM THE RIGHT AND THE LEFT OVER THIS ISSUE "Lies from desperate Democrat Marcy Kaptur can't erase her radical record. Kaptur is in damage control, and she must remove herself as a co-sponsor of the Equality Act and disavow her previous votes or remove her lies from the airwaves," NRCC spokesman Zach Bannon told Fox News Digital. Rep. Don Davis of North Carolina, another vulnerable Democrat seeking re-election, was one of only three House Democrats who voted last year for a GOP bill that could lead to prison for health care workers providing gender-affirming care for minors. Davis, who played football at the Air Force Academy, appears alongside a football field in a re-election advertisement, saying, "I believe states should decide what's right for protecting women and girls, and North Carolina has decided." But both Kaptur and Davis have faced pushback from Democrats over their messaging on the transgender issue. And in deep blue Massachusetts, Moulton, who apologized for his past transgender comments, was still trounced in last month's Democratic Senate primary by progressive Sen. Ed Markey, who accused his challenger of throwing transgender children "under the bus." CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Republican strategist Colin Reed, pointing to Democrats who've shifted their positions, told Fox News Digital that "voters should be very skeptical in the authenticity of any shifting policy positions that occur weeks before an election, especially in red parts of America where these types of issues have proven to be so politically toxic in the past." She argued that "Republicans won't be able to weaponize this issue this cycle the way they were able to in 2024 for two reasons. Democrats are fighting about and actually talking about it and defining themselves. But more importantly, when people can't make ends meet, they're not going to be drawn into culture issues which don't make a difference when you go to gas pumps and can't fill up your car to go to work." news.title: MAGA Won’t Die When Trump Leaves. Count on It.
news.text:
Hello, all, and welcome to Friday, Oct. 9, 2026 — the start of Columbus Day weekend, so the mail won't run Monday and the banks will be closed. Plan accordingly.

My calendar says it's Leif Erikson Day, International Beer and Pizza Day, World Egg Day, World Post Day, Moldy Cheese Day, Curious Events Day, Fire Prevention Day, and Sneakers Day. So toast Leif Erikson with a beer and an egg-topped pizza, mail a thank-you note to your letter carrier, and lace up the sneakers before the fire marshal sees what the moldy cheese did to your fridge.

Today in History:

1000: Leif Erikson is believed to have landed in North America, possibly in what is now Newfoundland.1635: Massachusetts Bay Colony banishes religious dissident Roger Williams, who goes on to found Rhode Island.1701: The Collegiate School of Connecticut, later Yale University, receives its charter.1825: The sloop Restauration lands in New York Harbor with 52 Norwegian Quakers, the first organized immigration from Norway.1874: Representatives of 22 countries sign the Treaty of Bern, creating the General Postal Union, today's Universal Postal Union.1888: The Washington Monument opens to the public.1930: Laura Ingalls becomes the first woman to fly solo across the continent, hopping from New York to California in nine stops.1936: The first generator at Hoover Dam begins sending electricity to Los Angeles. There are 17 cranking out power there today, plus two backups, but there's water level problems at Lake Mead. If the water levels fall another few feet, nine of those 17 will shut down.1975: Soviet scientist Andrei Sakharov wins the Nobel Peace Prize.1985: The hijackers of the Italian cruise ship Achille Lauro surrender in Port Said, Egypt, two days after seizing the ship.1992: A meteorite smashes into a family's car in a Peekskill, N.Y., driveway. How'd you like to have been in on the phone call to the Insurance people?2004: Afghanistan holds its first direct presidential election.2006: North Korea announces it has conducted its first nuclear test.2012: Taliban gunmen shoot 15-year-old Malala Yousafzai for advocating girls' education in Pakistan.

Birthdays Today include: Camille Saint-Saëns, composer; Charles R. Walgreen, drugstore chain founder; John Lennon, singer-songwriter (The Beatles); Brian Lamb, C-SPAN founder; Jackson Browne, singer ("Running on Empty," "Take It Easy"); Tony Shalhoub, actor (Men in Black, Monk); and Mike Singletary, Hall of Fame linebacker.

I wrote at some length yesterday about the worldwide swing to the populist right. If you missed it, start there, because today’s argument builds on one paragraph in particular:

I would call what we’re seeing a worldwide gag reflex. A gag reflex is triggered by whatever you’re choking on, and gagging is nature’s way of solving the problem. It isn’t a philosophy. It’s an immune response. Trump and the end of USAID didn’t cause this one. Voters are reacting to what the worldwide Left has tried to force down their throats.

Today, I’m taking that a step further. Donald Trump didn’t create this response. He’s part of it, a symptom of a much larger reaction, not its cause. That’s why I keep saying MAGA won’t end with Trump, because it didn't start with him, either. Indeed, it’s just getting started.

I know what’s clogging social media. The Left has a comforting little mantra that they're spreading like fertilizer. "When Trump leaves, MAGA goes with him." Isn’t that convenient? All they have to do is wait for one man to leave the stage, and the inconvenient voters will come to their senses, apologize, and resume voting for the people who made them angry in the first place.

Sure. And the next time your smoke alarm goes off, just pull the battery. Problem solved. No need to investigate the smoke, let alone the fire.

That attitude confuses the man who gave a movement its most recognizable face with the reasons millions of people joined it. But to extend the analogy I painted yesterday, an immune response doesn’t stand down because one white blood cell retires.

The movement was already on the road before Trump got behind the wheel. I went into this in some detail yesterday. We call these worldwide movements “Trumpian” because Trump is the familiar face and the one the progressives love to hate. 

The chronology, though, says otherwise. The Tea Party wave of 2010 gave Republicans 63 House seats, the biggest midterm swing since 1938, six years before Trump won the presidency. Germany’s AfD was founded in 2013. Britain voted for Brexit in 2016, and both happened before Trump won anything. In Latin America, Bukele took office in 2019, Chaves in 2022, and Milei in 2023, long before Trump’s return, as Sarah Anderson argued.

Understand me here: Trump didn’t manufacture this wave; he surfed it. And because he’s the best-known surfer in the lineup, people started confusing his name with the ocean. In fact, MAGA existed and was growing rapidly before Trump even renamed it. It's just that he was smart enough to identify it and stand in front of it.

If MAGA were a personality cult that needed him in the Oval Office for its survival, you’d expect it to have withered while he was out. In September 2022, almost two years after he left, 38% of Republicans still identified as MAGA, the Economist/YouGov poll reported. By May 2026, it was 62%. Some of that growth came as he returned to power, so I won’t claim the numbers prove independence. What they show is a base that was there before the return.

Is it the whole country? No. It’s about a quarter of adults. But a quarter of the country and a majority of one of its two parties isn’t a fringe that evaporates on a schedule regardless of any fantasy being offered by the progressives. 

Oh, and as for the future, look at who’s lined up for ‘28. At CPAC in March, Vance took 53% in the straw poll and Rubio 35%. CNN, which is always ready to pee on the GOP’s parade, is careful to note the straw poll isn’t scientific, and Vance slipped from 61% last year. But he still leads every recent 2028 primary poll, and Rubio has said he’d back Vance if he runs. The fight inside the party is over who carries the torch, not whether anybody does. And these are a couple of very strong candidates.

Remember, too, that the rest of the world is running the same script. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence. His son Flávio finished first in Brazil’s opening round, about 47% to Lula’s 45%, and they meet in a runoff Oct. 25. In France, Marine Le Pen’s embezzlement conviction was upheld on appeal in July, though the court cut her ban and she says she’s running. Even so, the National Rally had Jordan Bardella ready, and an April poll had him marginally ahead of her, 34% to 32%. And Argentina: Juan Perón was born Oct. 8, 1895, and died in 1974. Peronism shaped Argentine politics for decades after, until voters picked Javier Milei in 2023. And the rest of the world sees the huge turnaround there.

Related: It's Not Just South America: The Worldwide Move to the Right

No movement gets a lifetime warranty. But none of these folded when its founder left the stage. MAGA won't, either.

And before you start, yes, the Democrats are currently leading the polls. I’m not going to insult you by pretending otherwise. Nate Silver’s average has Democrats up about nine on the generic ballot, but not quite as generous across the specific candidates, and one prediction market gives them a 64% chance of a sweep.

Thing is, I don’t really care. That seems a bold statement to make, until you realize that polls have a record. They’re all available on the net these days. The pollsters’ own trade group found 2020’s national polls overstated Biden’s margin by 3.9 points, and Pew says 2024’s errors ran in the same direction, only smaller. Discount accordingly. Are the polls wrong? isn’t even a question anymore, given the last few cycles.

Let's remember that the pollsters were all predicting a Kamala Harris win. You may recall how that worked out.And yes, the numbers being reported currently, even with that four-point or so discount, don't line up to a GOP victory. But think, now: With this much on the line, does anyone with at least two working brain cells figure the leftists are going to get more honest? Spoiler alert: not me. Then, too, they didn't have the DSA splitting the ticket in the last few cycles. They certainly do now. With the races as close as they've been, that is a huge impact. 

Even assuming a loss (which I seriously doubt), we need to understand that losing an election isn’t the same as losing a movement. Republicans lost the White House in 2012, and by 2014 they had their biggest House majority since 1928 and the Senate. Two years later came Trump. The grievances against the progressives won’t leave when Trump does. The crime, the migration, the prices, and the sense that elites stopped listening predate him, and they’ll outlast him. The movement survives only if it delivers. If Republicans lose in November, the answer isn’t to blame the polls. It’s to ask what voters wanted and what the party failed to deliver. That comes back to the Establishment GOP.

It comes down to this: The gag reflex I spoke of yesterday doesn’t care which party is holding the spoon. It reacts to what’s being forced down the public’s throat. So, the answer to all of this is to show up. Pay attention. Check the claims. And if you believe, as I do, that MAGA has a future, don’t assume somebody else will carry it for you. Act. Get your buns to the booths. Period. Full stop.

news.title: Mortgages Hit 3-Year High: How Payments Have Risen Under Trump
news.text: U.S. mortgage rates have climbed to their highest level in nearly three years, adding to affordability pressures for homebuyers as the cost of living emerges as a key issue ahead of November's midterm elections. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 7.40 percent for the week ending October 8, according to Freddie Mac, as reported by Realtor.com, marking the seventh consecutive weekly increase. Rates rose from 7.28 percent the previous week and are now well above the 6.30 percent recorded a year ago. "These elevated mortgage rates have the housing market spooked," says Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner. The latest increase comes amid inflation concerns, a global bond market sell-off and worries about rising government deficits. Federal Reserve officials have also indicated that further interest rate increases may be necessary to bring inflation under control. Newsweek contacted the National Association of Realtors on Friday via email for comment. For Americans hoping to buy a home, rising borrowing costs present another obstacle in a market already made difficult by elevated property prices. How Much Have Average Mortgage Rates Changed Since Trump Took Office? When President Trump took office in January 2025, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.91 percent, according to a report by Freddie Mac. As of September 2026, a typical U.S. home had a median listing price of $419,250, according to data from Federal Reserve and Realtor.com. Assuming that a buyer is purchasing a typical U.S. home taking on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage with a 20 percent down payment, they are now paying an average of $246 more per month, or around $2,954 more per year than they were last year. Overall, compared to when Trump took office, they are now paying $111 more per month, or approximately $1,333 more per year, in principal and interest on their mortgage, assuming the same home price of $419,250 and a 20 percent down payment. How Mortgage Rates Affect Buyers Higher mortgage rates mean buyers pay more to finance the same property, even when its purchase price remains unchanged. The increase can push monthly payments beyond what many households can comfortably afford, forcing prospective buyers to consider cheaper homes or delay purchasing altogether. Mortgage rates are influenced by several factors, including longer-term Treasury yields and expectations about inflation. They do not move directly in line with the Federal Reserve's benchmark rate, although expectations of tighter monetary policy can put additional pressure on borrowing costs. The housing market has already shown signs of strain. Pending home sales fell year over year in August and September, while some sellers have been forced to reduce asking prices to attract buyers, according to Realtor.com. Although increased housing inventory and softer prices may give buyers more negotiating power, those benefits can be offset by higher financing costs. Higher rates can also discourage existing homeowners from selling. Those with mortgages secured at substantially lower rates may be reluctant to move if doing so means taking out a more expensive loan, potentially limiting the supply of properties available to buyers. Cost of Living Looms Over Midterms The mortgage increase comes as affordability concerns weigh on the political outlook for Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published October 8 found that the cost of living was the top issue on Americans' minds as they considered how to vote, ahead of democratic values and immigration. The poll also highlighted a gap in enthusiasm between supporters of President Donald Trump and those who backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. Some 48 percent of Harris voters said they were very enthusiastic about voting in November, compared with 30 percent of Trump voters. Trump's approval rating stood at 32 percent, matching a record low previously recorded in September, Reuters reported. Housing costs add to the financial pressures facing households. Mortgage payments are among the largest regular expenses many Americans face, and rising borrowing costs can leave families with less money for other essentials. Although mortgage rates are influenced by bond markets, inflation expectations and Federal Reserve policy rather than presidential decisions alone, housing affordability remains part of the broader economic picture voters may use to judge the administration. Will Rates Fall Again? The near-term outlook for mortgage rates remains uncertain. Persistent inflation concerns and rising Treasury yields have pushed borrowing costs higher, while the prospect of further monetary tightening could create additional pressure. Buyers hoping for lower rates may therefore face a difficult choice between purchasing now and waiting for financing conditions to improve. Waiting could bring lower borrowing costs, but future rates are not guaranteed to fall, and home prices may also change. For now, the latest rise adds another challenge for Americans trying to enter the housing market. With cost of living a leading concern for voters, the affordability of homeownership could remain an important issue as Americans head to the polls in November. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Trevor Davies
news.summary: The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 7.40 percent for the week ending October 8, according to Freddie Mac.

news.title: Will Indian-American voters who supported Trump in 2024 return to Democrats in the US midterms?
news.text:
Pre-election polls in 2024 showed that between 25% and 31% of Indian American voters intended to support Donald Trump, who went on to defeat Vice President Kamala Harris, the first major-party presidential nominee of Indian descent.
With the midterm elections less than a month away, a key question is whether Trump and the Republicans can retain the level of support they attracted from Indian Americans two years ago — or whether some of those voters will return to the Democratic Party, which has historically enjoyed overwhelming support among the community.
A February 2026 survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace offered a more complicated picture. Although Indian Americans remained predominantly Democratic, the party's identification among the community had declined from 52% in 2020 to 46% in 2026. Republican identification stood at 19% while 29% identified as independents.
The survey also found that Trump’s support among Indian American men under 40 had fallen from 40% in 2024 to 24% in early 2026, suggesting that some of the gains he made among younger voters may have eroded.
The findings underscore a central uncertainty heading into November: whether dissatisfaction with Trump will translate into renewed Democratic support or leave more Indian American voters politically independent.
It’s the economy, stupid
Recent national polling suggests that parts of the electoral coalition Trump assembled in 2024 are under strain amid concerns about gas prices, inflation, the conflict with Iran and the administration’s restrictive immigration policies.
For Indian Americans, those concerns are compounded by an anti-H-1B campaign led by some of Trump's far-right allies, accompanied by growing hostility toward Indian immigrants and the broader community.
Whether these pressures translate into changes in voting patterns will become clearer on November 3.
Early ballot-request data from several key states suggest strong Democratic engagement in several states, although the figures offer limited insight into how voters will ultimately cast their ballots.
In Pennsylvania, Democrats account for 66% of ballot requests, while in Iowa, their share has risen to 67%, up from 54% in the previous election. In North Carolina, Democrats account for 42% of requests, compared with 36% two years ago.
Although ballot choices remain secret until votes are counted, the figures suggest heightened enthusiasm among Democratic voters. Whether that translates into an electoral advantage remains to be seen.
Amit Jani, managing partner at political consulting firm JD Advisory Group, who previously served in the Obama and Biden administrations and at the US Department of Homeland Security, cautioned against reading too much into the early voting trends.
“From several current indicators, including voter enthusiasm and historical midterm voting patterns, Democrats have reasons for optimism heading into the midterm elections,” he said. “But early voting data should be interpreted cautiously: party registration and ballot-request data can tell us something about enthusiasm and participation, but they do not tell us how those voters actually cast their ballots.”
Political analysts are closely watching emerging voting patterns, while some community leaders report growing interest in the midterms among Indian Americans.
Virginia, which voted decisively for Harris in 2024, offers one indication of heightened voter participation. As of October 7, 2026, a total of 448,933 ballots had been cast in the state, compared with 236,405 at the same point in 2022.
With roughly 175,000 Indian Americans accounting for about 2% of Virginia's population, the increase raises questions about whether the community is participating in the broader surge in electoral activity.
However, the statewide figures do not establish whether Indian American turnout has increased or which party those voters favour.
Neha Dewan, national co-director of South Asians for America, an advocacy organisation working to elect South Asian American candidates across the United States, offered a measured assessment of the early voting numbers.
“Democrats tend to vote early, as they did in 2024, when former vice president Harris still lost. Polling has also become less reliable, so the results here deserve close attention,” she said.
Dewan, whose organisation was founded five years ago to strengthen South Asian American political engagement and influence, acknowledged growing political interest among Indian Americans, though it remains unclear whether that enthusiasm favors either party.
“South Asians feel the energy of this cycle on both sides of the aisle. Many South Asians are running for office this year at the local, state, and federal levels,” she said.
“On the Republican side, Vivek Ramaswamy's run for governor of Ohio excites some in our community, even though the party's agenda on immigration and civil rights does not reflect the values most Indian Americans hold. For these voters, the significance of an Indian American winning high office appears to drive their support.”
On the Democratic side, Dewan highlighted two congressional candidates generating considerable interest: Dr. Amish Shah in Arizona and Pia Dandiya in Florida.
“Both are running in flippable districts, and both are engaging the Indian American community in record numbers,” she said.
What about Trump’s relationship with India?
Another factor shaping Indian American political attitudes is the trajectory of US-India relations, which have been far more turbulent than many in the community anticipated at the start of Trump's second term.
The White House has imposed a series of tariffs on India, citing trade barriers, the bilateral trade deficit and New Delhi's continued imports of Russian oil.
The Trump administration has also tightened restrictions on the H-1B visa programme, whose beneficiaries are predominantly Indian nationals. In recent months, anti-H-1B campaigns have gained traction in states such as Texas, targeting Indian companies and workers.
Critics of the programme have accused it of facilitating large-scale Indian immigration, displacing American workers and enabling visa fraud.
“There does appear to be growing dissatisfaction with President Trump among portions of the Indian American community,” Jani said.
“Some older Indian Americans who supported him may have anticipated a particularly strong US-India relationship given President Trump and Indian Prime Minister Modi’s personal relationship during Trump’s first term, while recent trade disputes and broader tensions in the bilateral relationship may have caused some of those voters to reassess that support.”
Dewan, who has worked on South Asian grassroots outreach for the presidential campaigns of Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama, said she has encountered similar disappointment among some Indian Americans who supported Trump in 2024.
“In 2024, we met Indian Americans who voted for Trump because they believed his relationship with Modi would strengthen ties between the United States and India,” she said. “Two years later, some of those voters express regret.”
Immigration enforcement has emerged as another source of concern, according to Dewan.
“ICE detentions have reached families in the community, raising security concerns even among naturalized citizens,” she said. “Rising costs weigh on households, and so does the administration's more hostile posture toward India. For these reasons, some of these voters are returning to the community's traditional Democratic base.”
The immigration question
Yet political observers emphasise that Indian Americans are no longer a monolithic electorate. Although the community remains predominantly Democratic, survey findings reveal differences in political preferences based on age, gender and whether voters were born in the United States or abroad.
Jani pointed to a particularly notable divide: “US-born Indian American men have shown considerably greater openness to Republican candidates than other parts of the community.”
He also emphasised that views on immigration policy within the community are more nuanced than a simple partisan divide might suggest.
“Indian Americans may have a wide range of views on border security and illegal immigration, but rhetoric or enforcement perceived as indiscriminately anti-immigrant can resonate differently in a community where so many families have direct experience with the legal immigration system.”
While early voting figures offer clues about voter enthusiasm, political observers say a more significant development is the Indian American community's growing engagement in electoral politics, regardless of party affiliation.
Dewan captured that generational shift: “Twenty years ago, our parents wanted us to be doctors and engineers, not politicians. Today, they are knocking on doors for Indian American candidates running as Democrats and Republicans.”

news.title: Trump Voters Aren't Fired Up for the Midterms: New Poll Shows Democrats Have an 18-Point Enthusiasm Advantage
news.text: Voters who helped return President Donald Trump to the White House in 2024 are significantly less enthusiastic about participating in November's midterm elections than those who supported former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to a new poll.The Reuters/Ipsos survey, released just weeks before the November 3 elections, found that 48% of Harris voters are very enthusiastic about casting their ballots, compared with only 30% of Trump supporters, an 18-percentage-point gap that could complicate Republican efforts to mobilize their base.Trump's approval rating remains at a record low of 32%, with growing dissatisfaction over the cost of living, rising fuel prices and the war with Iran. The six-day survey, completed Monday, questioned 4,506 U.S. adults online and had a margin of error of approximately two percentage points.The enthusiasm gap is particularly concerning for Republicans because midterm elections typically attract fewer voters than presidential contests, making turnout among committed supporters especially important.The poll also found that Trump supporters are nearly twice as likely as Harris voters to be undecided about their congressional choices. Thirteen percent of those who backed Trump in 2024 said they were unsure which party to support, compared with 7% of Harris voters.Another troubling development for Republicans involves male voters, a demographic that helped deliver Trump's 2024 victory.That four-point Democratic advantage represents the party's strongest showing among men during Trump's second term. Male voters consistently favored Republicans throughout 2025, but their preferences have increasingly shifted toward Democrats since August.The change comes alongside declining support for Trump across nearly every major demographic group. Since his January 2025 inauguration, the president has experienced double-digit approval declines among Hispanic voters, men, evangelical Christians, rural and suburban residents, and Americans without college degrees.Economic concerns appear to be driving much of the dissatisfaction. The cost of living ranked as voters' leading concern ahead of the midterms, followed by democratic values and immigration. Gasoline and diesel prices have surged amid the conflict with Iran, adding financial pressure on households already struggling with everyday expenses.Trump launched attacks against Iran in February despite campaigning on promises to avoid new wars and reduce consumer costs. Republicans retain an advantage among older Americans, a demographic that traditionally participates at higher rates in midterm elections. Among voters aged 50 and older, Republicans lead Democrats 44% to 42%, although that margin has narrowed considerably from an eight-point advantage in December.Perhaps the clearest indication of Democrats' motivational advantage emerged when enthusiastic voters were asked what was driving them to participate. Among those expressing enthusiasm, 62% said they were motivated by opposition to Trump, while 36% said they wanted to demonstrate support for the president.

news.title: A’ja Wilson wins her third straight WNBA MVP and record fifth overall
news.text:
A’ja Wilson fine-tunes her shooting touch after every practice. That extra work has defined her greatness since being drafted first overall in 2018.

On Thursday, she received a voice message from former Vice President Kamala Harris congratulating her on redefining greatness leaguewide after she was named the WNBA’s MVP for a third straight year and for the fifth time overall.

“Obviously, that is an honour,” Wilson said. “A woman of our history, and I’m so appreciative to be able to share that moment with her through the phone call and the message of her delivering that I won my fifth MVP.”

In addition to becoming the first player to three-peat, Wilson won the award in 2020 and 2022.

Commissioner Cathy Engelbert, Aces owner Mark Davis and team President Nikki Fargas accompanied Wilson’s mother, Eva, who presented her daughter with the trophy.

“Each one of these has not been taken lightly,” Wilson said while flanked by all five of her MVP trophies. “In my heart, they’ve always been so special. But this one here, I cried a little bit harder. This one here is just a little bit different. … When you dream as a young girl, you dream so big and you write your goals out, and you just never imagine that you were able to just check them off.

“And when you’re able to check them off – small wins, big wins – it truly means a lot. And so I think that’s why I cried a little bit harder on this one, because 15-year-old A’ja wasn’t sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP. She wasn’t dreaming about being a three-time champion. She was dreaming about surviving this world.”

The 30-year-old Wilson once again led the league in scoring with an average of 26.2 points per game while shooting nearly 53 percent from the field. She averaged 9.4 rebounds per game, a career-best 3.2 assists and 1.9 blocks.

Wilson has the defending champion Aces back in the WNBA semifinals for the eighth consecutive season although Las Vegas is down 2-0 in the best-of-five series against Golden State. Game 3 is on Friday.

“This is great. I love it, not going to take for granted, shine her up, let’s do it,” Wilson said on Thursday. “But tomorrow, when it comes to hoisting it in front of the fans, I love the fans, … but I doubt I will be doing that. I’ll be warming up with my team. … Everyone in this room knows the competitor that I am. Everyone knows what my main focus is, and that is to get a game.”

Wilson received 65 first-place votes and nine second-place votes for a total of 713 points from a national panel of sportswriters and broadcasters. Minnesota’s Olivia Miles received six first-place votes and 40 second-place votes (442 points) while Indiana guards Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark followed with 287 and 212 points, respectively.

No WNBA player besides Wilson has more than three MVPs. Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson each have a trio. On the NBA side, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar has six, and Michael Jordan and Bill Russell each have five.

“A’ja Wilson is one of one,” Fargas said. “She’s now standing in a category that no other WNBA player in the history of the league has accomplished. She’s in the conversations with the Michael Jordans and the Wayne Gretzkys of the world – where she belongs.”
news.summary: Former US Vice President Kamala Harris among those to hail Wilson as Las Vegas Aces centre continues record run.

news.title: John James, a Republican, could become Michigan's first Black governor
news.text:
John James doesn't hold the partisan loyalties of most people who look like him. But on the campaign trail, he emphasizes a shared journey, tracing his family's roots from slavery, sharecropping and Jim Crow segregation to Michigan in search of a better life.

If voters back the Republican congressman over his Democratic rival, Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, James will become the state's first Black governor.

But he would likely reach that historic milestone without most Black voters.

While voters in other states have elected Black governors, they have all been Democrats. As a Black Republican, James is a political minority within a racial minority.

For most Black voters, the Republican Party has not been their political home since the Civil Rights Movement solidified their shift to the Democratic Party. James has argued for Black political realignment, though Black voters have largely opposed his past statewide bids for U.S. Senate in 2018 and 2020. Six years ago in his run against Democratic U.S. Sen. Gary Peters of Bloomfield Township, James received 5% of the vote in Detroit, one of the nation's largest majority-Black cities.

But James has suggested that Republicans have something to offer Black voters.

"I'm humbled because I recognize that I did not get here exclusively on my own," he said in a September interview at his campaign office in Sterling Heights, reflecting on the historic potential of his candidacy. James said he celebrates Black history and those who marched before he ran, but is focused on "Black futures."

"I feel like I have a duty now to honor their sacrifices by making sure that I serve everyone and I do truly believe that good, strong, positive conservative leadership will disproportionately benefit those who have been discarded, disrespected and disregarded for the longest period of time," he said.

State Sen. and Michigan GOP Chair Jim Runestad, R-White Lake, celebrated James as a strong candidate with an impressive business and military background Republicans would be proud to see elected. If James becomes Michigan's first Black governor, it would challenge "the narrative that I hear from within the media castigating Republicans as racist and all this nonsense," Runestad said.

James, who lives in Shelby Township, currently represents suburbs in Macomb and Oakland counties. But he has returned to the Motor City — his hometown and a Democratic stronghold where he received 1,518 votes in the primary compared to Benson's 87,873 votes — for his latest campaign pitch. He visited a home on the city's west side where he said contaminated dirt sits on a vacant lot next door. He stopped by the city's east side after a tornado touched down in early September and left many without power. He appeared on stage with Detroit rapper 42 Dugg at a summer concert at The Aretha Franklin Ampitheatre. The pair later drove around the city together and talked about James' Detroit upbringing and vision if elected.

James is courting Detroit votes now but he once applauded the Republicans who scrutinized them. During his last statewide run for U.S. Senate in 2020, James celebrated GOP election officials' initial refusal to certify the election results in Wayne County, alleging problems with the count in Detroit.

"That same Black community that you're now asking to come out and vote for you to be the first Black governor?" Detroit Branch NAACP Executive Director Kamilia Landrum said of James, adding: "I think if anything, it continues to just show the very transactional nature of his view on Black Detroiters."

Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig, a Republican who campaigned for governor in 2022 but was knocked off the ballot, said during his run, he was advised by "state party fathers" (whom he declined to name) that he shouldn’t campaign in Detroit and other places that don’t typically vote for Republicans. "I just thought it was flawed thinking," he said.

But Bishop Corletta Vaughn, the vice president of Detroit Public Schools Community District School Board and the senior pastor at Holy Ghost Cathedral in Detroit, doesn't see James successfully wooing Black voters in the city.

"He's not going to pull Detroit at all," she said. "Because what he stands for is not what we are looking for, even though yes, he could be Black — could be the first Black governor," she said. "But that's not enough to pull us."

Over the years, James has echoed other Republicans who point to predominantly Black cities to argue Democrats have failed them. State Rep. Tyrone Carter, D-Detroit, said it's an empty appeal. "It's like being an absentee father," he said. "You can show up on Easter with a suit. That doesn't mean s--- for the other 364 days."

More: 2020 election claims loom over Michigan’s race for governor

Nationally prominent Black Republican faces bitter GOP contest

For years, James has been a prominent Black voice within the Republican Party.

During a speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention, he took a dig at the campaign promise former President Barack Obama ran on in 2008 to become the United States' first Black president.

"Black people were sold on hope," he said. But James saw Republicans on the precipice of a major shift in Black voter preferences. "You know, I heard a little bit earlier today, if you don't vote Donald Trump, you ain’t Black," he said to laughter.

The night following his speech, James told the Detroit Free Press, "…Democrats have neglected the Black vote, but Republicans haven't even tried, and right now what I see — particularly at this convention — is Republicans making the effort, and I think that's good."

Between his 2020 and 2024 victories, Trump saw his support among Black voters almost double, according to a Pew Research Center survey, though most Black voters still overwhelmingly backed his Democratic opponent Vice President Kamala Harris. But now, those gains seem to have eroded for Republicans, Pew found.

James faced attacks on race in primary

James sailed through the Republican gubernatorial primary with a 15-point win.

During his primary victory night speech, James described the historic potential of his candidacy as the latest chapter in a story of Black triumph, calling himself "the nominee from the party of Abraham Lincoln 90 days away from becoming Michigan’s first Black governor."

But his win capped what James characterized as a "racially charged" primary. One GOP opponent, businessman Perry Johnson, called the congressman "The DEI Candidate!" in one ad, using the acronym for Diversity, Equity and Inclusion, a framework for tackling inequities that has come under fire by Republicans and the Trump administration.

Johnson denied that it was a racist dog whistle, claiming he only intended to reference that James' family Detroit-based logistics company – James Group – won DEI awards.

Johnson also accused James of "using the race card" after James made a quip about his opponent's age when Johnson criticized him for accepting money from corporate donors. "Perry, I know when you were born, Black people could still be bought and sold in this country," James said during a July debate on WOOD-TV. "But no one owns me."

"There is no question that Perry Johnson ran a racist campaign against John James," said Jimmy Greene, a Saginaw businessman and former Republican who once fundraised for James.

But James called his primary win "an indication that Republicans are rejecting the politics of bile and divisiveness."

More: John James responds to 'Nepo baby' and 'DEI Candidate' attacks

'I understand what it's like to be a Black man in this country'

After fending off the attacks on his race from within his own party, James says his racial identity gives him distinct insight as he tries to reach across partisan lines to beat a Democrat.

James, during the September interview said: "I understand what it's like to be a Black man in this country. Better, certainly, than my opponent."

To improve life for Black Michiganders, James said his goal is to expand access to opportunity, zeroing in on education and entrepreneurship.

James has long promoted expanding access to non-public schools. As governor, he would opt Michigan into a federal education tax credit that could be used to pay private school tuition, tutoring, after-school programs and more.

James said he also wants to tackle barriers to starting and growing a business by expanding access to capital through community banking and axing regulations deemed burdensome; moves he said that would boost Black-owned businesses but also benefit everyone.

For her part, Benson, who is White, has campaigned as a civil rights advocate, highlighting her work investigating hate groups as an intern for the Southern Poverty Law Center, research she undertook as a student on White supremacists and a clerkship with federal Judge and civil rights legend Damon Keith. (James has criticized Benson’s work with the SPLC, noting a federal indictment alleging the organization secretly directed donations to the Ku Klux Klan via confidential informants and other violent extremist groups. The SPLC has denied the charges.)

"We know where Jocelyn Benson stands," Benson's Deputy Campaign Manager Alyssa Bradley said in a statement. "She has dedicated her career to advancing civil rights and opportunities for Michiganders. We'll make sure James is a three-time loser come November."

James not first Black Republican nominee for governor

William Webb Ferguson, elected in 1892, was the first Black legislator elected in Michigan. He was a Republican. In Michigan, Black voters formed a prominent part of the coalition that helped elect Democratic Gov. G. Mennen "Soapy" Williams in 1948, who was White and ran on a pro-labor and civil rights platform. The number of Black lawmakers in Lansing — all Democrats — surged during his tenure.

The 137 Black state lawmakers who have served in Lansing include only five Republicans, according to a Detroit Free Press review of the Michigan Legislative Biography Database.

When it comes to governor, Michigan Democrats have never nominated a Black candidate but James is the second Black Republican to receive his party's nomination. In the 1986 election won by Democratic Gov. Jim Blanchard, Republicans chose as their nominee former Wayne County sheriff and executive William Lucas, after he left the Democratic Party.

James has blazed a campaign trail that runs through Detroit, in the hopes of succeeding where his GOP predecessor failed.

In his recent ride along in the city with 42 Dugg, captured in videos shared on Instagram, James pitched himself to the Detroit rapper as a politician who cares more about the city than its longtime leaders. "The fact of the matter is that Democrats have been running the area that you've been living in for sixty years and nothing has changed, and in fact, many people say it's getting worse," he said in the video. The rapper has since removed the post from his account after the video drew negative comments online, but James still has footage of the ride on his social media. 42 Dugg did not respond to a message on Instagram seeking comment.

Trump backs James

In an election year many describe as a referendum on Trump, James may face the same headwinds confronting Republicans everywhere, but as a Black Republican, James could contend with another elephant in the room.

Greene, the former James fundraiser, said the president has a troubling record on race, one that James should take head on. "I don't think that's an unfair expectation that he speaks out on it," said Greene, who is Black, and said he left the Republican Party, in part, because of Trump.

Asked if he thinks Trump has ever said or done anything racist, James noted his past condemnation of the president’s 2018 comments referring to Haiti and African nations as "s---hole countries."

"But his statements are his own, and mine are mine," James said of Trump.

If James wins, he wouldn't just be Michigan's first Black governor. No Trump-endorsed candidate — Black or White — has ever won statewide.

news.title: Why Does Gavin Newsom Keep Helping the Oligarchs?
news.text:
The billionaire tax doesn’t just raise revenue. It’s a way to both underscore the prodigious, excessive wealth of billionaires in the United States today and limit their ability to use their wealth to influence politics. One of the main reasons our democracy is eroding is the alliance between right-wing politicians and billionaires like Elon Musk. And there is finally a grassroots movement to confront the oligarchy, best illustrated by the nationwide, bipartisan resistance to AI data centers. This ballot initiative being defeated in California, one of the most liberal states in the country, would be a huge blow to that movement. 

That’s why it’s so galling and, again, stupid for Newsom, one of the most prominent Democrats in the country, to be joining the effort to kill the wealth tax. 

Why is Newsom doing the billionaires’ work for them? The main reason is probably ideology. He’s a typical California establishment Democrat. Such Democrats, including Kamala Harris and Nancy Pelosi, tend to be generically “liberal” and supportive of gay rights and abortion rights. But they often aren’t progressive on economic issues, especially when it comes to challenging corporate power and the wealthy.
news.summary:
This year Gavin Newsom has shown that he would be a billionaire-friendly president. Which means he shouldn’t be president at all. In short order, we will all have a huge field of Democratic presidential hopefuls to keep up with, but Newsom has done us a favor and disqualified himself before he even formally launches his expected campaign. 

Newsom has aligned himself with the uberwealthy on two major fronts. He has strongly opposed a ballot initiative that would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the assets of California billionaires. The measure would almost certainly pass if it had vocal backing from Democratic politicians in the state. But lacking that support, polls suggest it might fail. In addition, Newsom pushed Attorney General Rob Bonta and other Democratic attorneys to cut a deal with David Ellison (son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison) and his company Skydance, instead of continuing litigation to stop or stall Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros.
