news.title: The Path to 2028 for Democrats Lies in the MAHA Movement | Opinion
news.text: When Americans say they don’t trust the medical establishment, Democrats have one reflexive answer: defend the science, correct the misinformation and warn about the dangers of the alternative. There is plenty to correct. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has promoted false claims about vaccines, and the Make America Healthy Again movement that formed around him has no shortage of pseudoscience. But on the left, the women drawn to MAHA have been written off as fringe or crazy: conspiracy theorists, anti-vax moms, a punchline. Telling a woman she’s an idiot for asking what microplastics are doing to her body is not an argument for evidence-based medicine, but it is a good way to make sure she stops listening to you. That dismissal is a mistake Democrats can’t afford. These are women the party should be winning, and 2024 demonstrates many of them are women Republicans used to win. Without them, Democrats are putting Congress at risk this November, and the White House at risk in 2028. Corporate America has already noticed. Recently, Sweetgreen CEO Jonathan Neman joined a panel at the MAHA Summit in Washington, an event headlined by RFK and Vice President JD Vance. For a salad chain built on a largely progressive, urban customer base, the move raised eyebrows, but we think it makes complete sense. Sweetgreen has always known where its customers are, and we think the Democratic Party should, too. We say this because we know—and are—this customer. We built two national reproductive-rights campaigns, Vote for Abortion and Hotties for Harris, from scratch, traveling the country talking to women about abortion and politics. We also teach and practice yoga and Pilates, attend wellness retreats, and do the grocery shopping for our families—the exact spaces where MAHA has found its audience. The women in those rooms look nothing like the caricature of the gullible wellness consumer. They are highly educated professionals, activists, and women with serious scientific literacy. Some are into astrology. Some question the chemicals in the food their kids eat, or raise concerns about how little regulation governs our food. Many do all of that while vaccinating their kids and reading peer-reviewed research. The data backs up what we hear in those rooms. In a KFF poll earlier this year, 41 percent of Americans said they supported MAHA. Asked to name their top health priority, 42 percent of MAHA supporters chose lowering healthcare costs and 21 percent chose restricting chemical additives in food. Just 10 percent chose reevaluating vaccine safety. Asked why they backed the movement, only 2 percent mentioned RFK or Donald Trump. The movement’s core concerns reach well beyond its supporters. Large majorities of Americans told KFF there is too little regulation of food additives and agricultural pesticides. That is not a fringe movement, and make no mistake about where these voters are being taken. RFK-aligned groups have poured millions into turning those voters out for Republican candidates. MAHA has basically become a pipeline into the Republican Party. MAHA taps into a distrust of medicine that women rightfully have. For generations, “hysteria” turned women’s pain into evidence of instability. Midwives delivered roughly half of U.S. births in 1900, until a campaign smearing them as dirty and ignorant—aimed hardest at immigrant and Black midwives—nearly erased them within 50 years. In 1977, the FDA recommended excluding women who could become pregnant from early drug trials—a policy that stood until 1993. It took until 2024 for federal regulators to tell hospitals they needed consent before trainees performed pelvic exams on anesthetized patients. Nearly every woman we meet—us included—has a story about a doctor waiving away her symptoms. There’s a reason why “trust the experts” isn’t landing anymore. Two Democrats are already showing the party what the alternative looks like. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said that she meets and works with MAHA advocates, tying the movement’s appeal to real anxiety about a broken health care system. And she publicly documented the process of freezing her eggs, arguing that women need more open conversations about reproductive health. She’s meeting women where they are. In Michigan, Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former public-health director, released a health agenda that takes on pesticides, corporate influence, environmental contaminants and food, while holding firm on vaccines, arguing that the forces making Americans sick are too important to surrender to RFK. Neither has traded away science, and both are proving that Democrats can take voters’ concerns seriously without endorsing the movement's worst ideas. Neither party owns these issues yet. KFF found voters trust Democrats over Republicans on vaccine policy, 41 percent to 25 percent. But on the safety of food additives and pesticides, it is essentially a tie. That matters most with the voters Democrats have struggled to hold. In 2020, Joe Biden won women by 12 points. In 2024, Kamala Harris won them by seven. Trump carried a majority of white women for the third straight election, including more than six in ten white women without college degrees. In a presidential race decided by a few points in a few states, a five-point slide among women is the difference between winning and losing the White House. Yet those same women keep voting for abortion rights. In 2024, abortion-rights measures passed in Arizona, Missouri, Montana and Nevada—all states Trump won. These women aren’t confused. A woman can support abortion rights, distrust drug companies, worry about pesticides, take an herbal tincture, resent the way a doctor treated her pain, and still vote Republican. Democrats have a choice, and they have to make it now. Every time a party strategist mocks a “wellness mom” or rolls their eyes when a woman questions what’s in her food, the right gains a recruit. This contempt for concern and curiosity is a gift to RFK, and Democrats have been handing it over for years. The women drifting toward MAHA are not a lost cause. They are voters waiting for someone to take their concerns seriously, and the party that does it will win them. Ocasio-Cortez and El-Sayed have shown it can be done without giving an inch on science. The rest of the party must follow them and win back the women MAHA has pulled to the right—women who have voted for Democrats before and would again if the party gave them a reason. Or it can keep lecturing them until they stop listening for good. Jenny Kay is a media and communications strategist. Liz Walsh is an editorial advisor and strategist. View expressed in this article are the writers' own.
news.summary: "The women drifting toward MAHA are not a lost cause. They are voters waiting for someone to take their concerns seriously."
news.author: Jenny Kay,Liz Walsh

news.title: Republican congressman tries to outrun a potential blue wave in New York toss-up seat
news.text:
ROCKLAND COUNTY, New York – Photos of children and grandchildren line the wall behind the counter at Sparky's Diner, a local joint that sits on the corner of a busy intersection in Garnerville, New York, about an hour outside New York City.

"I've been in this place 50 years, it'll be 51 in February," said Jeannie Nicolakis, the diner's owner. "I started out – I didn't even have my kids at the time – and then I had my kids, and I raised them in here, in a playpen."

But her pride doesn't stop at her family. It extends to her congressman, Mike Lawler, a two-term Republican running for reelection in New York's 17th district. It is one of the closest races in the country in a seat encompassing a string of commuter towns and suburbs around the Hudson River Valley.

"He's like my own son. That's how I see him," she said, before adding, "not really my son – because I'm old enough to be his grandmother – but I see him as a grandson that's done so much for this county."

To supporters like Nicolakis, no one can take Lawler's place. But this district is far from a Republican stronghold. It's one of just a handful of places that elected a Republican to the House of Representatives in 2024 and also voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris, a Democrat.

Two years later, Lawler's ability to hold onto the seat could be a deciding factor in determining whether Republicans can keep their narrow majority in the House of Representatives. He faces a competitive challenge from Democrat Cait Conley, a military veteran and former counterterrorism official during the Biden administration who has sought to chip away at the broader coalition that's elected Lawler to congress twice before.

Lawler has tried to position himself as a Republican who is unafraid to cross his own party and highlights examples on the campaign trail, including how he broke with the administration over the decision to end a policy that shielded nearly 350,000 of Haitian migrants from deportation. Lawler says he was able to get the White House to temporarily extend work authorizations for beneficiaries of the program, however that has since expired.

He also regularly touts his work to raise the state and local property tax deduction, or SALT cap, a popular issue among his constituents that became a flash point in negotiations over Trump's massive tax and spending bill. Lawler ultimately cast a deciding vote in favor of the legislation, though critics have argued that other key parts of the bill have hurt voters, notably, thesizable cuts to federal healthcare funds.

At the same time, Lawler hasn't shied away from Trump.

"The truth is that the president and I don't always agree, and that's okay. After all, we're both New Yorkers," Lawler said in an address at the Republican National Convention in September. "What I learned about President Trump behind closed doors is that if you're willing to make your case and fight for what you believe in, he's willing to listen."

With less than a month until Election Day, Democrat and Republican-aligned groups have already collectively spent more than $40 million on ad spending in this race.

It comes as national polls show the GOP at a disadvantage, finding that voters are more likely to choose Democrats over Republicans when asked which party's candidate they would back in their district. Plus, President Trump continues to battle historically low approval ratings, with a majority of Americans saying they "strongly disapprove" of his job performance, according to the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll.

Can voters separate Lawler from his party?

Just outside of Sparky's Diner on a recent sunny Saturday afternoon, a lengthy procession of local first-responders and marching bands participate in the annual Rockland County Volunteer Firefighters Association parade. Lawler walks alongside them, frequently stopping to take selfies and shake hands with residents lining nearby sidewalks.

Despite the national stakes of his race, Lawler remains confident in his victory this fall, asserting that his deep understanding of the district makes him the right person to lead it.

"Look, all politics is local," he said in an interview as he neared the end of the parade route.

"My constituents know who I am," he said. "The people who are solely voting on the basis of their dislike of Donald Trump, that's their prerogative, that's their right. But the vast majority of my constituents care about the substance of issues and the policy solutions that we can forge. And I'm proud of the record that I've been able to deliver for this district."

But campaigning as an independent voice within Trump's party may be a tough line for the sitting Republican to walk, especially as voters continue to raise alarm bells about the high cost of living.

Across the Hudson River in the town of Armonk, located within the more liberal-leaning Westchester County, Brett Silverstein is one of many parents trying to keep an eye on their kids as they run around the town's fall festival. He cites high energy prices as a top concern.

"You're paying for goods that are inflated because of how much gasoline is and how much diesel is," he said, adding that while he used to vote for Republicans, he doesn't like Trump and in turn remains doubtful of Lawler's message.

"He's supported Trump and kind of the whole 'MAGA train' over the past 2 to 4 years," he said. "So given how he's affiliated with that, I'm just not a big fan of it in general."

It's an association that's pushed away some of the voters that first backed Lawler in 2022, including self-described moderate Mike Monroe, who ended up casting a ballot against the sitting congressman two years later and plans to again this year.

"He's basically the House of Representatives' version of [Maine Republican Sen.] Susan Collins," said Monroe, who lives in the town of Nanuet, part of Rockland County. "[Lawler] stands up to the Trump administration in certain instances, but only when it doesn't matter."

Democrats here walk their own political tight rope

Monroe now volunteers for Conley, who's tried to appeal to Democrats as well as disaffected Republicans and Independents on the campaign trail by arguing that Lawler's record in Congress has made New Yorkers worse off.

"Whether it's somebody who's a registered Republican, Independent or Democrat, [it] doesn't matter," Conley said in an interview. "The pain they're feeling is real for all, regardless of political affiliation."

"It's harder to put food on the table, keep a roof over their heads, afford health care, or keep the lights on. And they deserve better. And I will be better," she added.

Conley has also tried to differentiate herself from factions of her party that could turn off swing voters, distancing from high-profile figures on the left like New York City Mayor and democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani. She also hasn't publicly campaigned alongside the state's Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, who has faced criticism from Lawler and other Republicans in the state particularly over her economic and immigration-related policies.

It's a strategy that could prove helpful for this district where fewer voters are fiercely partisan.

"A lot of swing districts are just swing districts because they're equal number of Democrats and Republicans. That's not really what's going on in NY-17," said Evan Roth Smith, a democratic pollster who runs the firm Slingshot Strategies.

Polling conducted by Slingshot shows that between 30 and 40 percent of voters in the district are either ticket splitters or are only loosely partisan in their personal identification with the parties.

"One cycle they might vote for a Republican, the next cycle they might vote for a Democrat," Roth Smith said. "So it's a swing district because there are a lot of swing voters."

That's the case for retired builder Michael Alvarado, who lives in Stony Point, a town farther north within Rockland.

"I vote for whoever thinks my way," he said. "I don't really have a party. I'm not a Republican or a Democrat. Actually I would say I'm more of a Democrat than a Republican."

Though he says he supported Lawler last time, he's still deciding this year, and cares most about backing a candidate who is pro union and will cut school and property taxes.

When asked if anyone is currently speaking to those concerns, Alvarado replies, "not really," but added, he always votes.

"I'm just looking. See what happens come November. We'll hear all the promises."
news.summary: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, is in a tight race for re-election in a toss-up district that could help determine control of Congress in November.
news.author: Elena Moore

news.title: 'Different planet' Wilson becomes five-time MVP, but won't celebrate
news.text:
While a ceremony marking her latest historic achievement will take place on Friday night, A'ja Wilson wants no part of it.

The 30-year-old Las Vegas Aces star stands peerless after becoming the first five-time Most Valuable Player (MVP) in WNBA history, and was informed of her unprecedented third-straight award by a former US vice-president.

But recent history means Wilson has no interest in joining the celebrations which will be held on her behalf.

When the Aces held a pre-game ceremony to honour Wilson last year, as is tradition for the MVP winner, they went on to lose game one of their play-off semi-final.

They also lost heavily following similar celebrations after receiving their championship rings in May.

Before a must-win third game in their best-of-five semi-final against the Golden State Valkyries, Wilson is taking no chances.

"I love the fans, but I will not be doing that," she said. "I will be warming up with my team. Everyone knows how much of a competitor I am [and] what my main focus is."

No other WNBA player has won more than three MVP awards.

Having also won in 2020 and 2022, Wilson joins NBA legends Michael Jordan and Bill Russell as five-time MVP winners. Kareem Abdul-Jabbar won six.

"I've said [before] 'Take her off Mount Rushmore, she's Everest," Aces coach Becky Hammon said. 

"Now, I'm taking her off Everest and I just have to put her on a different planet."

Wilson, who received 65 of 74 first-place votes, received a voice message from former vice-president Kamala Harris delivering the news.

Despite her extensive list of honours, Wilson was very emotional after receiving her latest MVP award on the Aces' practice court.

"When you dream as a young girl, you dream so big and you write your goals out and you just never imagine you will be able to check them off," Wilson said

"I think that's why I cried a little bit harder on this one because 15-year-old A'ja wasn't sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP, she wasn't dreaming about being a three-time champion, she was dreaming about surviving this world."

Wilson averaged 26.2 points to lead the league in scoring for the third straight season.

An eight-time All-Star, she registered at least 20 points in 33 games - the third-highest single-season streak in WNBA history, and tied her own WNBA single-season record of scoring at least 30 points in 13 games.

Wilson has won three league titles with the Aces - achieved in the past four years - but they face elimination in this year's semi-finals as they trail Golden State 2-0.
news.summary: A ceremony marking her record-extending fifth MVP award will take place on Friday night, but A'ja Wilson will not take part before a must-win game.
news.author: Harry Poole

news.title: Sublime evenings and empty  downtowns: Democrats threaten comeback in America’s heartland
news.text:
Early October days at Ohio State University in Columbus are arcadia days: warm sunshine, new-term optimism and the green in front of the Thompson library filled with people sitting out reading, having lunch, making the most of a golden afternoon. 

Across the pavilion is “The Shoe”, the century-old football stadium designed in the Romanesque tradition. For Ohioans, it’s not so much a sports stadium as a cathedral. 

On this afternoon, the gates are closed, waiting for the bitterness and snow of winter and the true heart of the season. But from the interiors comes the sound of a lone brass instrument, as if a band player had been left behind from the previous weekend game. 

Near the statue of Archie Griffin, Ohio’s fabled 1970s-era running back, the Piatt family are taking photos. Evie Piatt, a junior from Millersburg, is hoping to attend on Ohio State and her family are on an arranged visit. She has yet to attend a full Ohio game. “But we watch ’em every Saturday. I’ve been to the spring games – defence versus offence,” she says.

“It’s really cool. It just gives you a sneak peek of how they play.”

Craig, her father, inherited his passion for the Buckeyes from his own father. We chat for a bit in the sunshine about their mortal enemy, three hours north, the University of Michigan.

In a county the size of Ohio, a patchwork of 88 heavily agrarian and industrial counties, the performances of the Buckeyes have, for over a century, offered a source of conversation and pastime through Novembers and Decembers. 

The Piatt family has two older boys in college in Capital University, east of Columbus. For Craig Piatt, that has meant five significant intrastate drives within the past few weeks. “That’s a lot of money for gas,” he acknowledges. 

Piatt says he is a registered Republican but doesn’t always vote that way and, right now, is weighing up the various candidates on their own merits.

Although Ohio voted for Donald Trump by 11 points in the 2024 election, it’s one of the many states in which Republican strategists are responding to distant sirens. 

In the Senate election for the seat JD Vance vacated after the 2024 election, Sherrod Brown, the veteran Democrat, is leading Jon Husted by anything from three to eight points in a succession of polls. 

In the gubernatorial election, Amy Acton, the Democrat hoping to beat Republican Vivek Ramaswamy (one of the presidential fantasists steamrolled by Trump early in 2024), has built a 54 to 48 per cent lead over her opponent. More alarmingly for Republicans, Ramaswamy trails his opponent by 57-32 per cent among Independent voters.

“I’m still looking at each of the candidates,” Craig Piatt says.

“I try not to follow through the TV because it so biased.”

It seems a sensible policy. In Ohio, the advertisements are both relentless and relentlessly grim. 

[ Lone star Trump believes he can bend Texas and midterm elections to his willOpens in new window ]

“For 50 years, Sherrod Brown voted how he was told. Higher taxes. Open borders. Sex changes for kids,” opens an attack advert on Brown. 

“He’s been called the face of data centres in Ohio,” begins a counter advert prosecuting Husted.

But the Republican is lagging behind. As a response, the Trump administration sent out a message that the president himself would visit the Buckeye state on Saturday, October 3rd, to rally with Husted. It would be part of Trump’s hastily announced barnstorming tour of Republican strongholds, in defiance of plummeting personal approval numbers.

The messy conflict with Iran is the obvious reason for the high fuel prices that have dismayed Midwesterners and the Piatt family are among the thousands acutely conscious of its cost.

“I don’t,” Craig Piatt says, when asked if he feels the punitive fuel prices are worth it.

“I feel like it is going to be like any other war in the Middle East. It is going to go on, and on, and on. And I’ll be honest with you, as patriotic as most folks are in this country, we are just tired of war. We are tired of being in other people’s business. We have issues here we need to fix. 

“I don’t follow politics that closely, but I would say we are pretty blessed where we live. Housing is high but we are blessed to own our house. Groceries are kind of going up more and more. All in all, it’s been a pretty good place for our family to raise our kids. But I know we’ve got friends all over the state and country that are hurting. 

“I will say this: I think that if he [Trump] could stop spending time on his social media account and making enemies and making dirt and just worry about our country, I think it would be a lot better. And the last couple of months have given me pause for thought – just concerns over his actions and things he said. I think a lot of us are looking forward to the next presidential election.”

Over the course of a few days, I drove across Ohio on Route 40, the fabled “national road”, a narrow, thin ribbon running through quiet villages and corn and soybean fields which, in the October light, looks cinematic. 

This is the land that generations of presidential aspirants have dutifully referred to as “the heartland”. Ohio has delivered a staggering seven presidents born in the state, all Republican, while an eighth, William Henry Harrison, a Whig, forged his political career there. 

Route 40, the first federally-funded road in the United States, is a moseying, peaceful saunter through bucolic countryside, silent towns, churches, car junkyards, antiques shops, well-tended gardens and posters on the telegraph poles honouring local military members from the Civil War through to Iraq. It’s a world of many ice-cream parlours and few bars.

Springfield, Ohio, is about an hour’s drive west of Columbus. After decades in national obscurity, it created a firestorm of controversy during the 2024 election after, first, Vance – who was raised in Ohio – and then Trump made the notorious claim that a local Haitian community were eating cats and dogs. 

When Trump repeated the bizarre idea during his lone televised debate against Kamala Harris in Philadelphia, Springfield officials immediately phoned the broadcasting network to stress that it wasn’t true. But the damage was done. The stigma stuck. 

In its industrial glory years, when it marketed itself as Champion City, Springfield’s population swelled to 80,000. It had fallen to just over 30,000 when Haitians, attracted by job opportunities and the affordable living costs began to arrive in the city. There was a swell of new arrivals in 2021 and 2023, bringing the total number to around 15,000. Almost all arrived through legal pathways. 

The ending of the Temporary Protected Status privilege has led to an intensification of summer Ice arrests and deportations, terrifying the community.

“It has not been huge activity compared to Minnesota, but they seemed to absorb the lessons of that and moved stealthily,” explains Michael McGovern, who works for Innovate Ohio, a Columbus-based non-profit.

“A lot of folks did the right things here and so provided the federal government with all their details. So, it was easy for Ice to arrive in homes and scoop them up. That’s what’s been happening in the late summer period. And one really draconian aspect was that a number of Haitians were forced to wear ankle monitors and there’s a lot of stigma to that.”

Trump’s visit to Vandalia, about an hour west, coincided with the funeral service held in Springfield for Pierre Damas Bel. 

The 20-year-old had excelled since arriving in Ohio from Haiti; a soccer star who had won a full scholarship to study neuroscience at Wright University. He had been forced to wear an ankle bracelet by immigration, even while playing football. 

He detailed his distress in a July post that read: “I came here to this country to pursue my education. I didn’t come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone. Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation I never imagined I would experience.”

On the morning of August 31st, Pierre Damas Bel pulled his 2006 Toyota Avalon on to the hard shoulder of the 1-70. In a harrowing account in The Atlantic, the driver of a tractor trailer explained how he was unable to avoid the pedestrian as he walked out into oncoming traffic in an apparent suicide. 

Mike DeWine, the Republican governor of Ohio, was among those in the funeral congregation on Saturday. DeWine has repeatedly defended Ohio’s Haitians, arguing that they had revivified Springfield’s local economy – and pointing out that as of 2030, Ohioan death rates would exceed birth rates. In other words, the Buckeye state is going to need new people.

A Creole restaurant I visited on lunchtime was empty. The host was smiling and welcoming but said that his boss warned him not to speak and pointed me towards the houses behind the Speedway station. He said that’s where everyone was, at home. Haitians are hiding out.

“They are hearing stories of these deportations back to Haiti – stories of people kidnapped off the plane or hassled for bribes because they know these planes are coming from the US so there are resources,” says Michael McGovern.

“And a lot of people feel in mortal danger if they are deported back to Haiti. It’s under-recognised and it’s a shameful thing for our country.”

Downtown Springfield was, at least on the evening I visited, disconcertingly empty. Like so many Midwestern towns, it expanded quickly with the optimistic certainty that the manufacturing boom would last forever. On a sublime evening – striated sky, warm breeze – its downtown was deserted apart from a tour guide in costume and lantern escorting a small group on a ghost tour and, at the hotel, two guys from Las Vegas who were contracted to work on a nearby data centre. They’d been living in the hotel for months. 

One of the contractors, Valen, compared his turbulent youth in Sin City against the quietness of Springfield. He said he liked to unwind by sitting outside, smoking a blunt and watching the world not go by, which is what he was at when I encountered him.

 “I like it,” he said of Springfield. “People here are ... very ... cordial.”

A short drive north of Springfield is Urbana, one of those dream-factory American towns with a succession of craft shops and coffee shops and candy-striped awnings and a retro-film theatre. I call in unannounced to the branch of the Champaign County Democratic headquarters. 

A group of volunteers has just finished meeting and are immediately welcoming. We talk for an hour about what it feels like to experience life as an American here, in this pleasant, obscure Ohioan town.

As it turns out, Urbana is like a crossroads for the issues that are driving the national sentiment in 2026. The farmers are stressed by months of spiralling fuel costs. Locals are petitioning against a data centre contract signed without public knowledge by city officials. The voting patterns here have been distorted by redistricting, or gerrymandering, over the past 20 years. Champaign County voted for Donald Trump by 74 per cent two years ago (15,344 votes to 4,944 for Kamala Harris) but the group has sensed a dissatisfaction that transcends old allegiances.

“My father is a long-term judge here who was elected twice as a Republican,” Clay Newlin says.

“He is disaffected and he knows a lot of Republicans who are motivated to get out and vote Democrat because they are p****d off. Sorry! Farmers and rural people are very ticked off with what is going on. Tariffs are hitting all the people around us. So, it’s not just Democrats.”

Fears over the energy price hikes, the potential impact of the nearby Cedar Bog conservation area and noise and air pollution concerns for students in the elementary middle school and a senior citizen home are the driving factors in local opposition to a data centre. The issue is subject to a lawsuit that both parties are trying to resolve. A settlement proposal would see Thor Equities waive its $115 million (€102.5 million) damages lawsuit, future tax abatements and agree to pay the city of Urbana some $50 million in several project phases. It’s a lot of money for a small rural community. But a recent meeting drew more than 100 people holding placards that read “No Deal”.

“They want cheap water and cheap land, so we are a perfect site,” explains Kay Nutter.

“They say in their site plan [there will be] one building. But they bought 500 acres, so we fear they are going to build a campus, with eight or nine units and then the generators: it is going to be loud, and bright, 24-7.”

We talk for a while about life in Buckeye state. “I love Ohio,” Suzanne McCoy says and the others chip in. Colvin Bear was raised in New Jersey but gravitated towards the Midwest for college and never left.

“I like the open spaces, but I can still be at an airport in an hour. My house is in the country a mile from my neighbour, but we can get in the car and get to the shops in 10 minutes. While we may wish that many of the residents were more sensitive to others and a willingness to be open to be those who are different, most of them still have a good heart. Even though they may have their blind spots.”

On Saturday last, Carl Ruby, a pastor in Springfield, spoke at Pierre Damas Bel’s funeral. He assured the congregation that they were “a blessing and not a burden” to the town and they had many allies among the traditional Springfield community, some of whom were in attendance.

“You have brought life, energy, love and a renewed sense of hope to Springfield and we not only welcome you, we also want to thank you.”

On the same day, across in Vandalia, president Trump also had Springfield on his mind. Over the course of a 90-minute speech, he called out John Gruden, the former Superbowl winning coach, who was in attendance. “This is rougher than a football game,” he joked about the energy of the crowd. “They have more spirit,” he said, before returning to the theme of enemies vanquished.

“They’ve tried to smear us, slander us, persecute us, demoralise us, they’ve attacked me, they’ve impeached me, they’ve arrested me and they’ve even tried to kill me, I guess. But with you by my side we have always prevailed.”

Then he asked the crowd if they’d ever heard the parable of “The Snake”.

“This is in honour of Springfield, Ohio,” he told them.

“A quaint little town of 32,000 people where they took in 35,000 people and put ’em into Springfield and it didn’t work out too well and they are being removed. It was an idyllic place – that’s a word they use in high scripture. It was an ‘idyllic’ place. ‘Was’ is the better word. Not any more, but it soon will be and they are being brought back to their country.”

So, while the Haitians mourned in Springfield, Trump read a rendition of The Snake with its strange refrain featuring a “tender-hearted woman” who voluntarily takes in a “poor, half-frozen snake”. She feeds him milk and honey before she is inevitably bitten and before dying, asks the snake why, after all her compassion, he had done this.

“Shut up, silly woman, said the reptile with a grin,” the president quoted, deepening his voice for dramatic effect as the crowd in Ohio listened in silence.

“You knew damn well I was a snake before you took me in.”

news.title: How Populist Politics Succeeds and Fails
news.text:
Why is populism, broadly defined, on the brink of historic victories around the world, while populism in the form of President Donald Trump's Republican Party is poised to lose one or both houses of Congress in the United States?

The troubles Trump's Republicans face are not a mystery. It was always unlikely that Republicans would maintain their hair's-breadth House majority.

But the 2026 lineup of Senate seats looked favorable, with only one Republican defending a seat in a state Kamala Harris carried and all but one defending seats in states Trump carried by double digits in 2024. At least two Democrats were defending seats in states Trump carried in 2024, and retirements opened up two other seats in marginal states.

That picture has now changed. Persistent inflation, some of it plausibly triggered by Trump's tariffs, has hurt Republicans. Democrats have sprinted to big polling leads in Georgia and North Carolina, and various combinations of weak Republicans and strong Democrats have left Republicans trailing in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — states Trump carried by double digits two years ago.

Democrats are already planning investigations of Trump's financial shenanigans and drafting articles of impeachment. They have high hopes of a 2028 trifecta: the House, Senate and presidency. Republicans' trifecta hopes are clouded by the prospect of primaries pitting Trump supporters against his opponents.

What a different picture in the rest of the world. Populist veteran Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner for president of France next year, while next month's snap election in Spain is likely to put the populist Vox party into a governing coalition.

Germany's populist AfD just won the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, and it's getting hard to imagine how the traditional parties can keep excluding it from federal coalitions. Italy's Giorgia Meloni, with roots in a populist party that had been excluded from power for years, heads the longest-serving government in post-World War II Italy.

Britain's populist Reform UK party has lost its lead in public polls after the Labour government ditched Keir Starmer and installed Andy Burnham as prime minister. But it's interesting that Labour, founded in 1900, felt obliged to reach beyond the usual parliamentary leadership ranks to select first a professional barrister and then a regional mayor. Reform UK, founded in 2018, is still polling ahead of the Conservatives, whose roots go back to 1846.

The picture is even starker in the Western Hemisphere. In November 2023, free-market booster Javier Milei defeated the Peronist candidate in Argentina after attacking high inflation and bloated bureaucracy. In the 15 months beginning in April 2025, conservative populists defeated leftist candidates in Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Peru and Colombia.

In the first round of elections this past Sunday in Brazil, Flavio Bolsonaro led incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva 47 percent to 45 percent. Bolsonaro's father, Jair, now confined to house arrest, was elected in 2018 and lost in 2022 to Lula, as he is usually called, 51 percent to 49 percent. Lula was previously elected in 2002 and 2006, and his Workers' Party has won five of the last six presidential elections. He was leading in pre-election polls, but Flavio Bolsonaro is considered likely, though not certain, to win the Oct. 25 runoff.

What accounts for the populist wave? In Europe, many voters have recoiled against high levels of immigration, especially of young Muslim men, amid worries that they are not assimilating economically or culturally. Bloated government payrolls and high rates of violent crime are populist complaints in both Europe and South America.

The populist complaint, voiced in loud and raucous terms, is that established parties in government have not just failed to solve these problems but have refused to do so. They have cordoned off populist parties and candidates, as if opposing open borders for immigrants who are difficult to assimilate or supporting tough sentences for violent criminals were morally equivalent to Nazi or communist mass murder.

So how do we explain why populism is on the rise beyond the U.S., even as it seems mired in failure here?

One explanation is that Trumpism is not really mired in failure. Trump has been president of the U.S. for almost six of the last 10 years and has had substantial policy successes. They range from economic growth exceeding that of other major countries to the recent treaty promising American control of Greenland.

That success is part of his problem. After three and a half years of the Biden administration arguing that the law left it no alternative to an open-door immigration policy, the second Trump administration has proved that the border can be controlled.

This success signals to a future administration that it will pay a steep price if it returns to open borders. But for the moment, voters no longer need a Trumpist to close the border. It's been done.

And, given the messiness of everyday life, it's been done with some collateral damage to the populist cause. Consider the heavy-handed Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in Minneapolis choreographed by the oddball Homeland Security appointee Kristi Noem and her consigliere, Corey Lewandowski.

There is something in the nature of populist politics — the willingness to take on and persevere against established media, corporate, academic and party elites — that produces a peculiarly personal kind of leadership. Success in ignoring hoary shibboleths only encourages such leaders to defy warnings they would be better off heeding.

Populist politics has given us the family dramas of the Trumps in America, the Le Pens in France, and the Bolsonaros in Brazil. It has given America a president who threatens the sovereignty of friendly or largely unoffending allies such as Canada and Denmark.

It has saddled the Republican Party with inflation imposed by tariffs for which there is no perceptible demand from even the smallest subgroup of the electorate. Yet Trump supplies them in abundance, driven by idiosyncratic theories he concocted in the 1980s.

The president's party has suffered as well from his choice of suboptimal Republican nominees, which has already cost Republicans several Senate seats and seems on the verge of, amazingly, costing them a Senate seat in Texas as well. A leader who has gotten where he is by defying conventional wisdom that proves wrong gets into the habit of defying it even when, as on many occasions, it is absolutely right.

From time to time, we hear predictions from politicians, both populist and conventional, that their side will govern for the next generation. That seldom happens. The Democrat Party won House majorities in every election from 1954 through 1992. But Republicans held the presidency for 26 of those 40 years, and Democrats were usually split between Southern conservatives and Northern liberals.

In the 32 years since 1994, presidential elections have produced party trifectas — majorities in both houses of Congress and control of the presidency — in six of eight election years. But only once did a trifecta last as long as four years, and in one case, it ended after five months. Populist movements can achieve worthy goals spurned by more conventional forces. But they are subject to the rules that every person's strength is also his weakness and that, in human affairs, success tends to breed failure.

Michael Barone is a senior political analyst for the Washington Examiner, resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and longtime co-author of The Almanac of American Politics. His new book, "Mental Maps of the Founders: How Geographic Imagination Guided America's Revolutionary Leaders," is now available.

news.title: Bam Adebayo Kept A'ja Wilson's MVP a Secret, Heat Center Praises WNBA Star Girlfriend
news.text:
Bam Adebayo can keep a secret. Especially when it involves his girlfriend A'ja Wilson's fifth WNBA MVP. 

According to the Associated Press, "Adebayo—the Miami Heat center and longtime partner of Wilson, the Las Vegas Aces star—was asked last week to record some thoughts about his girlfriend winning the award again, which also meant he couldn't give her any hints about the voting results. The secret was kept, and a fifth MVP award is coming to the home that Wilson and Adebayo share."

Instead, Wilson officially learned she won the award again when she received a message from former Vice President Kamala Harris.

"It's good to celebrate somebody that honestly deserves it," Adebayo told reporters after Thursday's 128-118 preseason win over the New Orleans Pelicans. "You really can't put five MVPs into words. news.title: Ossoff vs. Collins in Georgia US Senate Debate: Key Moments and Polls
news.text: Democrats are fighting to defend U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff’s Georgia seat as Republican challenger Mike Collins faces a difficult path, trailing amid unfavorable polling and a Democratic fundraising advantage. The two faced off in a debate Thursday evening, clashing over tariffs, taxes, immigration and more. Ossoff narrowly won his election in 2020, as the race went to a runoff versus David Perdue. Ossoff won by less than 55,000 votes in a spread of 50.61 percent to Perdue’s 49.39 percent. President Donald Trump flipped the swing state during the 2024 presidential election versus then-Vice President Kamala Harris. He has also thrown his support behind Collins in the U.S. Senate race. In the latest survey by Wedgewood Polls, Ossoff leads Collins by 10 percent as prediction markets also show him as the clear favorite. The Cook Political Report rates the races as Likely Democrat. Newsweek reached out to both Ossoff and Collins' campaigns following the debate for comment Thursday night. Key Moments from US Senate Debate In Thursday night’s debate, the two clashed over key policy platforms like trade, immigration, Trump and more. Below are highlights of the candidates' wrangling for the U.S. Senate seat: Collins was asked about his plan to help make life more affordable for Georgians, saying he wants to continue to be energy independent and export goods out of the port in Savannah. Ossoff said he'd like to repeal tariffs put in place under the Trump administration, while also bashing the rising cost of diesel and ground beef, saying they are crushing Georgia families. Ossoff also pointed to the ongoing war in Iran that is contributing to the soaring price of gasoline. Ossoff was asked about his plan for lowering healthcare and insurance premiums during the debate and he said price transparency is key. He also called for expanding Medicaid, while bashing Collins for voting to allow Affordable Care Act benefits to lapse. Collins called out insurance companies, saying they are the ones "getting rich." He touted Trump RX, the president's platform to combat rising prices for prescription drugs, while also saying there should be price transparency for consumers. Ossoff said there needs to be a federal privacy law in place to protect Americans from Big Tech companies and Flock cameras. Collins also said Flock cameras are being abused and there should be a warrant to access their data. He said he is a big proponent for privacy. He later said, "we're in a race with AI," adding, specifically against China. He said the potential is great, but citizens need to be protected to ensure they aren't being spied on. Collins said people entering the country should come legally, adding that visa programs need to become more efficient. He accused Ossoff's immigration policy of permitting human traffickers in while allowing jobs to be taken away from Georgians. Ossoff said Georgians expect secure borders and a government that upholds human decency and civil rights, saying people have been rounded up at job sites under Republicans. In closing, both candidates ripped into one another for their voting records and seemingly toed party lines on key policies including trade, immigration and healthcare. Jon Ossoff vs. Mike Collins: Latest Poll Results The latest Wedgewood Poll survey shows Ossoff with 55 percent of the potential vote compared to 45 percent for Collins. The poll surveyed 600 likely voters on October 2 and October 3 and has a 4 percent margin of error. A Big Data Poll similarly shows Ossoff leading Collins, with 51 percent to 40.1 percent among registered voters and 52.2 percent to 41.0 percent among likely voters. The poll surveyed 712 registered voters and 678 likely voters in the Peach State from September 21 through September 23. The margin of error was 4 percent. “Senator Ossoff has made a concerted effort to court men who support President Donald Trump over Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, citing his alleged mishandling of the Epstein Files and prioritizing foreign policy over affordability,” Rich Baris, Director for Big Data Poll, said in the survey. “That strategy, which we focus tested back in February, was effective and appears to have worked.” A Quantus Insights poll shows Ossoff with 48.2 percent compared to Collins' 44.4 percent, while 6.5 percent are undecided and 0.9 percent said they prefer someone else. The poll surveyed 645 likely voters from September 14 to September 16 and had a margin of error of 4.3 percent. Biggest Issues Facing Georgia Voters Affordability, the cost of living, inflation and overall state of the economy is top of mind for households across the country. In a Fox News poll over the summer, Georgia voters said that inflation and high prices are their top concerns when picking a U.S. Senate candidate. Healthcare came in second, followed by jobs and unemployment, political divisions within the country, and immigration and border security. Nationwide, Democrats are hoping to capitalize on Trump's dropping approval ratings in state and national polls as the midterm elections loom. The president's overall approval and ranking on key policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are flagging the affordability concerns. Ossoff's Financial Advantage The Democrat's campaign has raised over $77 million from January 2025 through the end of June 2026, according to Federal Election Commission reports, while having spent about $39.7 million. Cook Political Report highlighted Ossoff's advantage, saying in part that he is "so flush with cash that he’s giving some of his massive war chest to a coordinated campaign to help in the much closer race for governor." The forecaster notes that money is part of the factor that makes this race less competitive for Republicans. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. news.title: Trump accused of trying ‘to incite a race war’ with comments about Somalis in Minnesota
news.text:
Donald Trump has been accused of trying to start a race war after he called for people in Minnesota to “fight back” against Somali immigrants.

The US president made the call in a Truth Social post made on Thursday afternoon (Friday morning Australian time).

"The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants," Trump wrote.

"There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State. The people of Minnesota must fight back."

 He then turned his ire to Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, who ran as Kamala Harris′ vice presidential nominee in 2024.

"You have been robbed, and abandoned by your State Government. Your Governor is an incompetent thief who doesn't want to get involved," Trump said.

"He just wants to get out of town with as much as he can steal, and then, lead a quiet life."

Walz is not running for re-election after serving two terms.

Trump then continued to rail against Somali immigrants.

"The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing," he said.

"They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back!

"If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.

“Governor Tim Walz, and Mayor of Minneapolis, Jacob Frey, must immediately ask for Federal help — and leave the rest to us!”

There are an estimated 100,000 people in Minnesota of Somali descent, most of whom are American citizens.

Senior Fellow at the American Immigration Council Aaron Reichlin-Melnick described Trump's comments as trying "to incite a race war against Somalis".

"This is so dangerous," Reichlin-Melnick said.

“President Trump is deliberately inciting race hatred against an ethnic minority, calling on the people of Minnesota to ‘fight back’ against ‘Somali immigrants’.

"This must be a terrifying moment for the Somali community."

In criticising Trump’s remarks, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison referenced the actions of ICE agents in Minneapolis earlier this year.

"We've seen what Trump's government coming to the 'rescue' looks like," Ellison said.

"It ended with two Minnesotans shot dead by federal agents, racial profiling, assaults, and the violation of our rights."

Ellison defended the Somali community in his state.

"Somali Minnesotans are our neighbours," he said. 

"They are part of Minnesota. And the Minnesota I know and love is so much better than this bigotry."

Trump’s comments came after an 18-year-old was arrested after allegedly planning an ISIS-inspired mass shooting at Minnesota’s Mall of America.

The teenager had been corresponding online with an FBI agent he thought was another ISIS sympathiser, federal authorities said.

In a busy afternoon on Truth Social, Trump also described anybody who uses the term "artificial intelligence" as "the enemy".

"The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" the president wrote.

Yesterday he described Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as "Mohammed".

"Mohammed El-Sayed is a terrible Candidate for the Dumocrats," Trump wrote.

"Mohammed goes back to the days of the Jihad. He is a RADICAL Extremist, Terrorist Sympathiser."

El-Sayed is leading in the polls in Michigan and would be the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate.

news.title: Democratic Voters More Engaged in Midterms as Americans Are in a Sour Mood - Pew Research Center
news.text:
The 2026 midterm election is taking place amid deep public dissatisfaction with the state of the nation, near-record low approval ratings of President Donald Trump, and growing negativity about national economic conditions and the ongoing conflict with Iran.

Against this backdrop, Democratic candidates now hold an 8 percentage point edge over Republican candidates in preferences for the House of Representatives among all registered voters nationally.

And while many registered voters will not turn out to vote this fall, Democratic candidates are also buoyed by their supporters’ relatively high levels of engagement and stated motivation to vote when compared with those who are backing Republican candidates. For example:

78% of voters who back their House district’s Democratic candidate say it “really matters” which party wins control of Congress – 9 points higher than the share of Republican backers who say this.

In contrast, Republican candidate supporters were 4 points higher on this measure than Democratic supporters at a similar point before the 2022 midterm election.

The partisan gap is also wide on other measures of engagement: Democratic supporters are 14 points more likely than Republican supporters to say they have given this year’s election “a lot” of thought and 17 points more likely to say they are “extremely motivated” to vote this year.

A new Pew Research Center survey of 5,062 U.S. adults – including 3,917 registered voters – conducted Sept. 28-Oct. 4, 2026, also finds that Donald Trump’s approval rating now stands at 30% – the lowest of his second term. Most voters (63%) consider Trump a factor in their vote for Congress, with far more thinking of their choice as a vote against the president (44%) than for him (19%).

As economic ratings turn more negative and concerns about prices rise – particularly for gas and energy – the economy continues to rank as the top voting issue this year, across the political spectrum: 84% of registered voters – including 88% of those who support Democrats and 82% who back Republicans – say it is very important to their vote.

The midterm race

Democrats currently hold an 8 percentage point edge in national vote preferences, with 44% of all registered voters saying they would support a Democrat for the House if the election were held today and 36% preferring a Republican. Another 5% say they would select a different candidate and 15% say they aren’t sure.

Among validated voters – confirmed to have voted in the 2024 election – those who voted for Trump are less consolidated behind GOP candidates (77%) than Kamala Harris’ voters are behind Democratic candidates (87%).

The difference is even more pronounced among voters who are disaffected with the party they backed in 2024 – who make up a quarter of each 2024 coalition:

49% of Trump voters who have an unfavorable view of the GOP today support Republican candidates for the House this year. While only 12% say they back Democrats, more than a third say either that they are “not sure” (25%) or prefer “another candidate” (14%).

In contrast, Harris voters with a negative view of the Democratic Party are much more solid in their preferences for Democrats this year: 73% say they support Democratic House candidates.

In both 2024 coalitions, these disaffected voters are less engaged with the election than those who have positive views of the parties – but that is particularly the case among Trump’s 2024 voters. For instance, just 36% of Trump voters with an unfavorable view of the GOP say the outcome this November really matters. By comparison, 65% of Harris voters with a negative view of the Democratic Party say it does.

For more on demographic differences in candidate support, jump to “Midterm Vote Preferences by Race and Ethnicity, Age and Other Demographics” and explore the detailed tables.

Trump’s approval rating continues to drop

Three-in-ten Americans now say they approve of Trump’s handling of his job as president, while 68% disapprove – down 4 percentage points from July and his lowest approval rating of his second term.

Much of this decline in his approval ratings over the course of his term is among Trump’s own 2024 voters – 67% of validated Trump 2024 voters approve of his job performance today while 31% disapprove. At the beginning of his term, 95% approved.

Some of the starkest declines have come among Hispanic and younger voters who backed Trump in 2024.

For more on Trump’s approval ratings and confidence in his governing and handling of issues, read “Trump’s Approval Rating Drops as Fewer Americans Are Confident in His Handling of the Economy, Other Issues.”

Trump is more of a factor in voters’ choices this year than Joe Biden was four years ago. While voters in most recent midterms have tended to be motivated more by opposition to the sitting president than support for him, the current gap is wider than it was four years ago – when 36% of voters saw their vote in opposition to Biden and 19% viewed it as in support of him.

Other key findings

Satisfaction with the state of the nation has dropped to 39% among Republicans overall (including those who lean to the GOP). This is the lowest of Trump’s second term (down from 65% shortly after he entered office and 54% at the beginning of this year). Overall, 22% of Americans say they are satisfied with the state of the nation, while 77% are dissatisfied.

Majorities of voters consider the future of democracy (73%), healthcare (68%), education (62%), immigration (59%) and foreign policy (57%) as important to their vote. As in past elections, immigration is a more central issue for Republican voters (72% say it’s very important) than for Democratic voters (53%) – but Democratic voters see it as a more important issue than they did four years ago. For more on the top issues in the election, read “Economy ranks as top issue in midterms for all voters – but partisans differ over the importance of other issues.”

Related: Cost Concerns Dominate as Public’s Economic Ratings Turn More Negative

The U.S. military action in Iran remains deeply unpopular, and most Americans think it won’t end soon. A third of Americans approve of how Trump is handling the conflict – down from 37% in March, shortly after it began. About three-quarters of Americans (77%) expect the conflict to last another six months or more.

Most voters (61%) say they dislike elected officials who support building data centers in their area; just 8% like this. While dislike is especially widespread among Democratic voters (75% dislike), on balance Republican voters also do not like leaders who support data centers (44% dislike, 14% like).

Related: Americans’ Views of Data Centers Have Turned More Negative
news.summary: Democratic Voters More Engaged in Midterms as Americans Are in a Sour Mood - Pew Research Center

news.title: Trump wins again against illegal migration
news.text:
The Supreme Court delivered another victory for President Trump on the issue of illegal migration on Monday. The high court reversed a decision by an Obama-appointed judge that had blocked the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for illegal aliens from Venezuela.

Enacted in 1990, the TPS program grants temporary protection for illegal aliens from being deported to countries harmed by wars, earthquakes, or other life-threatening disruptions. But “temporary” is the key word here; beneficiaries of the TPS program are allowed to remain only for a while before returning home, yet Justice Alito observed that “TPS designations in practice have often lasted for decades.”

President Biden extended TPS to more than 600,000 illegal aliens from Venezuela by misusing this program. All told, migrants from 17 different countries totaling more than 1 million illegal aliens were being harbored by the Biden administration under the TPS program before Trump took office. 

Trump has successfully terminated 13 of the 17 designations, and on June 25 the Supreme Court upheld Trump’s authority to shut these programs down in Mullin v. Doe. This set a clear precedent for Trump to terminate the remaining TPS programs, too. 

TPS does not bring the migrants here. The South American migrants mostly crossed our southern border illegally, and then the TPS program has been used by Democrats to shelter them from being deported.

Venezuela and Haiti were two of the remaining countries with TPS, of which Venezuela poses the greater risk. The terrible Tren de Aragua gang is in Venezuela, and young men associated with that gang sneaked into our country illegally and yet were not deported by the Biden administration.

On Monday, three alleged members of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua were sentenced to 20 years in prison for kidnapping and torturing a Denver man in 2024, and a fourth defendant will be sentenced later this year. They had demanded a ransom from his wife, and when she did not pay it, they cut off the victim’s pinky finger. 

President Biden granted special TPS protection to Venezuelans in 2021 and 2023. But there was no war in Venezuela, or a devastating earthquake, to justify keeping so many Venezuelans in our country.

Instead, there was a socialist regime, as is common in some South American nations, like Brazil today. The response to that is for the citizenry to defeat the socialist in power, as Brazilians took a step toward that on Sunday by voting against its incumbent President Lula.

When a gang of Venezuelan migrants besieged an apartment building in Colorado while brandishing guns, this became a campaign issue in 2024. The management company asserted that the migrants were also members of the notorious Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua.

Time to go home, Trump indicated, by terminating the TPS program for Venezuela, as Trump has done for more than a dozen countries. But an Obama-appointed judge has blocked this.

Federal District Judge Edward M. Chen accused Trump of having “animus” toward the Venezuelans, and of terminating TPS based on an improper discriminatory purpose. He held last year that this issue of animus could go before a jury to decide whether Trump and the Secretary of Homeland Security were improperly motivated by “animus,” which is silly because there is nothing unconstitutional about having animus toward aliens who enter our country illegally.

Trump Solicitor General John Sauer filed a petition to overturn this ruling with the Supreme Court on July 9, while the Court was on summer break. It reopened on Monday, and one of its first actions was to rule in favor of Trump by overruling the lower court decision against him.

The Court also held in favor of Trump on his partial termination of the TPS program for Haiti. Recall that the presence of tens of thousands of Haitians in Ohio, particularly in the town of Springfield, was a winning campaign issue that Trump forcefully spoke about at his debate with Kamala Harris.

Grassroots opposition to migration into Europe has led to success by conservative parties in elections there. The European Union tightened its rules against migration in response to the public opposition to it.

The current riots in the suburbs of Paris are concentrated where there are large immigrant populations, leading some to suspect that migrants are fomenting the unrest. The stated cause of poor school conditions seems unlikely to be the real source of the enormous violence.

Trump has kept that from occurring here by deporting foreign criminals and ending the sheltering of illegal aliens. This has prevented riots by disgruntled mobs that have blighted European countries, and which could happen in the U.S. if the pro-migration policies of Democrats return.

news.title: Las Vegas Aces Player A’ja Wilson Wins 2026 WNBA MVP Award
news.text:
A’ja Wilson has made history by winning the WNBA MVP award a record 5 times since joining the league. 

That’s Miss M’VP to you. 

The announcement came Thursday afternoon, and during the press conference, A’ja Wilson said she received a message from former Vice President Kamala Harris congratulating her on the accomplishment. 

Wilson’s mother, Eva Wilson, presented her with the trophy, and A’ja said she cried a little harder this time. 

“I cried a little bit harder, you know. Uh, this one here is just a little bit different. And whatever that may look like or whatever that may feel. Uh, my fifth one, I think, is the one that’s just, you know, when you dream as a young girl, you dream so big, and you write your goals out, and you just never imagine that you were able to just check them off, Wilson said. “And when you’re able to check them off- small wins, big wins- um, it truly means a lot. And so I think that’s why I cried a little bit harder on this one.”

“Because 15-year-old Asia wasn’t sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP. She wasn’t dreaming about being a three-time champion. She was just dreaming about surviving this world,” Wilson continued. “And so for me to sit up here … surrounded by these trophies and to be able to play the game of basketball um, every single day, it just means a little bit more to me, and it’s something that I won’t take for granted.”

Thursday’s announcement followed the Las Vegas Aces’ 4th-quarter comeback against the Golden State Valkyries in Game 2 of their WNBA semifinal series, as they overcame a 17-point deficit and briefly took the lead with 90 seconds left. 

The Aces ultimately lost by 2 points, but the bigger story was their comeback. Wilson played 36 minutes and led her team in scoring with 24 points. 

The 6’4” center for the Las Vegas Aces came through the Dawn Staley basketball program at the University of South Carolina, where she was the Consensus National Player of the Year during her senior year. Starting in her sophomore year, she was nominated for the Wooden, Naismith, and Wade trophies three years in a row, became a finalist in her sophomore and junior years, and ultimately won all three as a senior. A’ja also won an NCAA championship with the Gamecocks in 2017.

Wilson has shown on and off the court that she is that girl. This latest MVP award is just another acknowledgment that not all kids become goats. 

GOATs aren’t just born; they’re raised. Ms. Eva and Mr. Roscoe raised A’ja. Dawn Staley raised A’ja. Becky Hammon raised A’ja.

A’ja was taught to stay hungry, get loud, and to build others up, even if it means knocking them down. 

She does all of that on and off the court. 

A’ja has stayed confident and stayed humble. 

So when we talk about the greatest of all time in women’s basketball, remember the MV’P. 

If players like Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie, and Cynthia Cooper built the league, A’ja Wilson is the realization of their biggest hopes and dreams, and she stands tall in that legacy. 

She was born into this and raised for it. 

Congratulations, M’VP. 

You make us all proud.

news.summary: A’ja Wilson has won the prestigious distinction for three years in a row, and this latest announcement makes it five times in total.
