Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED’s Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.
Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science. This week we're doing a deep dive into how Elon Musk's America PAC has spent millions of dollars to influence some of the most consequential races this midterm season. WIRED has created a tracker to follow America PAC's support in real time. We're going to take you through why these races matter and how Musk is throwing Republicans all of this cash.
Zoë Schiffer: We're also going to break down the once obscure philosophy that now seems to be everywhere from X threads to The Economist cover, effective altruism. We'll talk about what this ideology is actually all about, why many AI researchers subscribe to it, and how it has been actively shaping the debate around AI safety.
Leah Feiger: And we're going to get into why the designer of Meta's Muse logo has been receiving a ton of backlash. Zoë spoke with her all about it this week and she had a lot to say. Zoë, it's just me and you this week. We've officially pushed Brian off a cliff.
Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, we have. The FaceTime chat has gone live. We will not be talking about any tech conferences this week.
Leah Feiger: Absolutely not. But he'll be back next week. So at the very least, there's that. OK, Zoë, Elon Musk. He's back.
Zoë Schiffer: He's back. He never left for some.
Leah Feiger: He never really left, but he is back and so is his wallet. To refresh everyone's memories a little bit, Musk is the founder and main donor of America PAC, a super PAC that was started in 2024 to help elect President Donald Trump to the White House. They succeeded. Trump is in office. The PAC spent more than $260 million to make that happen. This time around for November's midterms, the PAC has been going about it a little bit differently. WIRED created a live tracker to monitor their donations in real time. You can check it out on the WIRED website. And we learned a lot putting this together. Basically, the PAC is donating to the election's most consequential races. They are not focusing obviously on the presidential race. There is no presidential race this year. But they are all in on the most critical Senate races in the country that are really going to decide the makeup of Congress next year. The PAC is primarily pumping money against Democrats as opposed to for Republicans, which is really interesting. For every dollar that America PAC has spent supporting a Republican candidate, more than two have gone to oppose a Democrat. And that only becomes more extreme in some of these Senate races, right? In Texas where several Musk companies are based, the group has spent tons and tons of money attacking Democrat James Talarico. We're talking like $9 million. Whereas promoting Ken Paxton, around the one million mark. Similar numbers can be found in the Ohio Senate race, in Iowa, really up and down the board. And these races are not random. They represent the path for Democrats to take control of the chamber this November and could open Republicans, Musk included, up to a lot of investigations and regulatory pressure. So this is critical for so many reasons. I'm so excited to talk with you about it. What did you think of the tracker? Did you get a chance to play around with it?
Zoë Schiffer: I did get a chance to play around with it. I was really impressed, not least because you coding something for the internet, an app and web, honestly, groundbreaking.
Leah Feiger: I can take zero, zero coding credit. This all goes to our amazing investigations team who really knocked it out of the park. They did.
Zoë Schiffer: Well, jokes aside. No, I think it's really important. I mean, like you said, the total spending on America PAC's part is less than what they spent previously, but it's much more targeted. They're being really specific. And that's because the stakes are really high. I feel like we should just back up for a second and talk about that. Because there is this chance that Congress flips, that Democrats take control, and it seems like Musk and his associates are taking that very, very seriously.
Leah Feiger: Oh, as they should. Democrats are already telling us, all of our sourcing in Democrats, both on House and Senate side are hungrily talking about all of the investigations and subpoenas that they're going to release the minute that the chamber is theirs. And right now, the polls are looking pretty good for them. This is very much a, if Dems don't mess this up, they have a very good chance of making this happen. I can only imagine that Musk and a similar coterie of fellows are kind of freaking out right now.
Zoë Schiffer: I mean, I am on the record and I'm going to say it again, I think Republicans are going to do just fine. I feel like we've had this conversation before, and I'm sus on the polling. However, you are the politics director, so ultimately I defer to you. That said, I think it is 100 percent true that Musk takes the possibility of investigations and regulations really, really seriously. This was a primary reason why he ultimately decided to go all in on Donald Trump. He said very publicly that if Kamala Harris won the presidential election during the last cycle, the whole country was going to look like California, which was the worst thing that could happen to it, apparently. As someone from California, I disagree, but neither here nor there. It is really hard to build things here. I'll give you that. That said, I find it very hard to imagine a world where really harsh regulations actually do come down on the Elon Musk empire. I think part of the reason for that is SpaceX, and just how dependent the government is on Starlink, on SpaceX technology, on their ability to get stuff into space. SpaceX is the company doing that on behalf of the government now. And so while I do think subpoenas, all of this stuff could happen, will it impact Elon Musk's empire ultimately? I don't know if we have the tools to hold someone like that accountable at this point, frankly.
Leah Feiger: I think that's a really, really good point, honestly. And obviously there's a clear fear that a Lina Khan-esque figure could come in and wreak havoc. But to your point, that havoc will be paperwork. No, I hear you. I hear you.
Zoë Schiffer: I mean, think about it. The one time he was held accountable in a real way was for saying that he had money to take Tesla private. He had funding secured to take Tesla private. What was the outcome of that? He was fined $20 million? How much is Elon Musk worth? Ultimately, even if that number hurts, he doesn't want to pay it, it's kind of a drop in the bucket.
Leah Feiger: No, he's a trillionaire now, again, I guess. And I guess to that point, this is not the first time that super PACs or big money in politics has stirred up a little bit of controversy. We had this big conversation in 2024 about how crazy it was that Elon Musk was just throwing money at the wall, and now he's throwing money again via America PAC, which now feels like a pattern, and it feels like other tech founders and their influence and their PACs are already outsized in this administration. You have PACs from all sorts of groups up and down Silicon Valley that are very involved this election cycle. I'm really interested in what you're hearing about how folks are thinking about this midterm cycle and how they're kind of thinking more future.
Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I mean, Silicon Valley is not a monolith. You hear a lot from the really loud voices in the room, and a lot of those voices are people who have gone all in on supporting President Trump and the Republican Party. And I think those people kind of align with Elon Musk in some of the fears that you have said, that there will be investigations, that if Democrats take control, it'll slow growth, that they won't be able to lead the race in AI and these other areas. And so they need to go all in and protect that future that they want to see happen. Of course, there are a lot of rank-and-file employees who have more liberal values, and they are staying a little more quiet, but they are contributing to different causes. It's an interesting conversation in the Valley right now because there are a lot of newly minted millionaires, people who worked in AI research and now have a ton of money, and they are having active conversations on what is the best way to deploy, to allocate capital right now? Where do we put the money to have the biggest effect? Is it in philanthropy? Is it in politics? If it's in politics, where should we contribute? There's not one defining take right now, but it is definitely a topic of conversation. Leah, as you and our listeners both know, the debate over AI safety has been everywhere lately. It has escaped containment in a big way. And in that debate, there is one central philosophy that keeps coming up again and again, and it's starting to become kind of the center of attention, effective altruism. Last month, AI researcher Jacob Coxon loudly voiced support for one of effective altruism's central concerns, that advanced AI could destroy humanity. This kicked off a wave of headlines and a pretty intense response from the Trump administration. Senior Pentagon officials labeled effective altruism as a, quote, unquote, "dangerous ideology" and an official Department of Defense social media account implored people to choose, quote, "Americanism, not effective altruism." So we're really seeing these dividing lines. But Leah, just to back up a little bit, when did you become aware, because you're not in Silicon Valley, you're in New York, when did you learn about effective altruism?
Leah Feiger: What's amazing is I can actually pinpoint it to, I would say, maybe 16 months ago, and it was from you. We were on a phone call, and you were like, "Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. And this person is all in on effective altruism." And I was like, "I have no idea what that means. I have never heard of this before. I have never heard of this belief." And you should really describe it to our listeners, but it really, really helped me understand that there was a split in Silicon Valley over AI. I wasn't aware of that before. I just though that people were like, "Yep, we work for these companies. We're ready to go." And you took me through the effective altruists in Anthropic and different side in OpenAI, and it was, I'm sure, like the kindergarten version, but it was really, really helpful. So please take it away.
Zoë Schiffer: So at a very basic level, effective altruism is a belief system built around the idea that people should use their time, money, and resources as efficiently as possible to improve or even save the lives of as many people and animals as they possibly can. At its core, it doesn't fundamentally have anything to do with AI specifically. It really is how can we make as much money as possible and then deploy it in such a way to help as many people as possible or save as many people as possible? This concept or these ideas of effective altruism were popularized by blogs like LessWrong, which is fringe, but in Silicon Valley, it did have a real prominence in the early 2000s. There was researchers at Oxford talking about it. The reason that AI has become a part of this is a lot of the AI researchers came up in this philosophy and they see AI as a true existential risk. And if you're concerned with the welfare of humanity, and then you start to engage a lot with a technology that you think maybe doesn't have a huge risk, but nonetheless a substantial risk of killing everyone, then that becomes the central concern. I think one thing though that I wanted to just lay out, far be it from me to come out swinging for effective altruists, but like any movement, it's a spectrum. You have people who are real fanatics. And when you hear their viewpoints and the trade-offs that they would make to save a maximum number of people, that kind of utilitarian belief system, it sounds totally nutty. But I talk to a ton of people who identify as effective altruists who are completely normal. I was going to say rational, but that feels really loaded in this context. But they're thinking about it really deeply. They don't sound like religious fanatics. They don't seem like people who are members of a cult. And it's not like all these people are getting together and talking. It's a movement, it's widespread. There are different groups.
Leah Feiger: And when you apply it to AI, there is something that I find there's an appealing aspect where you're saying, look, we're just saying that we should be concerned about where this technology is going to go and what it could do to people. That's the baseline, right? Is that a pretty decent summary?
Zoë Schiffer: 100 percent. And if you thought that you were working on a technology that might, 10% chance, kill everyone, the rational thing to do would be to quit and warn everyone about it. So in that sense, what Jacob Coxon did isn't completely shocking. But it has been very interesting to see this go fully mainstream. We have seen AI researchers who are really concerned about AI safety go on Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan. And again, the Venn diagram of effective altruists and AI safety researchers, it's not a perfect circle, but there is a fair amount of overlap.
Leah Feiger: So OK, Sam Altman, OpenAI, Dario Amodei, Anthropic. Dario has talked about AI being a risk for the world. So would he be in the EA category?
Zoë Schiffer: OK, this is a very, very loaded question. So Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, worked with Dario Amodei for a while. They were both at OpenAI. Then Dario quit, along with a small group of OpenAI researchers and started a new company specifically to try and build AI safely to benefit all of humanity, etc., etc. And they didn't feel like they could do that at OpenAI. So there you get a clear split between, and this is not how they identify, but this is how people categorize them. Sam Altman kind of represents the growth at all costs, capitalist view of artificial intelligence. Dario represents more of the effective altruism, let's do it safely. We have to be the ones to win because only we understand the real risks involved. Dario has said, I believe, in more recent months and years that he doesn't identify as an effective altruist. That said, a lot of the beliefs do overlap. And I think that you do get a sense from talking to Anthropic researchers that a lot more of them appear to fall into the effective altruism philosophy.
Leah Feiger: Are there Slack channels for this? Are there parties? I'm so curious, now that this has escaped into a mainstream lexicon, I'm very interested beyond just the Pentagon being like, be pro-American, say no, how this is going to kind of continue.
Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I mean, yes, there are group chats. I'm sure there are Slack channels. There's a place in Berkeley called Lighthaven, that's kind of a conference center/group house co-op situation that hosts events. Last time I was there, the possibility of sleeping in one of their bunk beds came up. I was like politely decline forever. No, thank you. But anyway, it's interesting because, as this has gone more mainstream, like you said, the Trump administration has come out and they have really used effective altruism as kind of a overall term to say these people are almost religious fanatics, and they're anti-growth and they're anti-AI progress, and thus they're anti-American. Where of course there is a lot more nuance here. And I think a lot of these people are just trying to take AI safety really seriously. But now you're seeing effective altruism becoming kind of like a slanderous term to say we can't and shouldn't take these people seriously.
Leah Feiger: Why is this controversial? What you're saying doesn't sound that bad. We're just trying to save humanity?
Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. Yes. I think one reason is that it's all about trade-offs. And when taken to the extreme, you can see how if your goal is to maximize good or minimize harm, there is a certain amount of harm you would be willing to take, or be a part of, I guess, in order to save a greater number of people. And I think people, somewhat rightly so, get a little freaked out that in an effort to eliminate the possibility that greater harm will be done, effective altruists would be willing to do somewhat harmful things in the present moment because they think they're protecting people from something that could happen later on. And I think the other part, and this is one that I definitely am thinking about, is if you think that you are the only company that's taking AI safety seriously, then you "winning," quote, unquote, the AI race is really important. And what wouldn't you do to win if you think the stakes are humanity level extinction?
Leah Feiger: I kind of think that everyone involved in this conversation sort of needs to enroll at Oberlin for a philosophy 101 class. That's maybe what I'm feeling right now.
Zoë Schiffer: I think Oberlin is what got us into this mess, perhaps. Oberlin philosophy specifically.
Leah Feiger: 102. Philosophy 102. It's the next chapter. Now that you've moved on from Slavoj Žižek, what comes next?
Zoë Schiffer: Oh my gosh. Moving on, it's been a few weeks since Meta released its new AI assistant Muse, and honestly, it's been kind of an unexpected hit for the company. It is still topping the app charts. But the reason that I wanted to talk to you about this is a really interesting situation played out in the Bay Area a few weeks ago. The designer, a freelance designer and lettering artist, Jessica Hische, who was hired by Meta to help design the Muse logo, told her newsletter subscribers like, "Hey, I did this project." In fact, I think the title of the newsletter was “New Work! (Don't be mad at me).” She kind of knew she was going to get some flack from people. But she basically said, "Look, Meta hired me to do this project. Ultimately, I think a big company should be commended for hiring an independent artist instead of just generating a new logo. Here's how the design process went. Hope you like it." That was kind of the message. One of her newsletter subscribers posted it on Threads. You forgot this was a thing. Threads is still very much a thing in the design world.
Leah Feiger: I did forget. I fully forgot.
Zoë Schiffer: And people flipped out. She had people saying they were disgusted with her, disappointed, that they'd followed her since she was in art school and they could never support anything she did again. People were posting photos of her house and speculating about her finances. She felt like the entirety of Threads was like a mob attacking her for three days for having come out and said she was doing this work. Yeah.
Leah Feiger: That's really intense.
Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, it was a lot. It was really interesting to talk to her because she actually has kind of complicated feelings about AI. She said her husband has worked in this field, and they actually had some disagreements because he was really excited about the technology. It honestly was very AI wife coded, if you read that article. And she was like, "Well, no, this could be really bad for commercial art." Artists who, to support their less highly paid artwork, work for companies occasionally like she does, this could be detrimental. And in fact, that is what Jessica Hische does. She has two shops in Oakland. They're really cute. One is kind of a stationary store. The other one is a space where she hosts kind of kid art workshops and classes and stuff. And she basically fully funds those by taking on corporate work. But she said in the past couple years, her corporate work had really dried up, and that she wasn't getting as many inquiries as she usually does. So when Meta came to her, she was like, "I didn't even feel that conflicted about it. I was like, Oh my gosh, I want to offer one of my employees a health plan. I need to not be so stressed every time Gusto pings me and says I have to run payroll. Yeah, I'll take this." She was paid. Guess how much you're paid if you redesign the Muse logo.
Leah Feiger: I mean, it's Meta. You should be paid half a million dollars in equity.
Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, you would think. No, she was paid $12,500 more or less.
Leah Feiger: No. No, that's the worst part. That's actually the worst part of this whole story.
Zoë Schiffer: I know. Yeah. She was like, "I thought it was kind of amazing for two days of work." Because it was a sprint. She was just talking about designing the M at first, and then she got a bit more for doing the full typeface of Muse. But yeah, it wasn't even that much. And again, she's using the money to support her small businesses in Oakland. But she said there was a huge contingent of people on Threads who seemed like they were really AI purists, and fundamentally were like, "There is just simply no excuse for working on this technology." And they really saw her decision to work on it as a signal of support.
Leah Feiger: I'm mixed here. I don't know. Go after the company, not the artist is sort of how I feel. But I get that that's not as juicy or exciting as yelling at someone personally on a social media app.
Zoë Schiffer: A social media app that is owned by Meta, to be clear.
Leah Feiger: Really important point there. Yep. Does she regret it?
Zoë Schiffer: It's interesting. I asked her that question and she said ultimately no. She kind of weighed like, "Do I regret talking about it?" But she said ultimately she felt like she was doing a good thing for artists by commending a company that had hired an independent artist. She was like, "These big tech companies are not going to hire artists if they feel like that artist is then going to go slam them on social media. Ultimately, these companies exist and there can be some sort of symbiotic relationship with them," which I'm personally sympathetic to.
Leah Feiger: It's not an Uncanny Valley episode if I'm not at least mentioning or thinking about “Silicon Valley,” the TV show. And I can't not think about the artist in the show who is designing Gavin Belson's box and what that took. And I just remember watching it and being like, why are you putting yourself through this? But also everyone needs a salary. It was painful. Oh, wow. That's a complicated one. That's a little bit tough to hear.
Zoë Schiffer: Coming up after the break, we're sharing our WIRED/Tired picks for the week. Stay with us.

It's time for our WIRED/Tired segment. Whatever is new and cool is WIRED. Whatever passé thing we're totally over is Tired. Leah, what have you got for us this week?
Leah Feiger: OK. I want to start by saying everyone should subscribe to Wired.com and everyone should keep reading the news. That's it. No buts there.
Zoë Schiffer: Great.
Leah Feiger: But what I would add is it's tiring. This is a very long election cycle. We just finally finished primary season. We are now in midterm season. There is news from Iran and China and Russian plagues every single day. And sometimes it's really OK to stop scrolling and turn the news off. And I do want to remind people of that. Which brings me to my WIRED, which could help you do that. I am not being paid to say this, though I kind of wish I was, I guess. But there's a new season of Great British Bake Off on Netflix, and I'm really, really enjoying it. And it's just comfort and cozy, perfect for October, highly recommend. So read a couple WIRED articles, get nervous about the state of the world, watch an episode, and then go back and do some other fun things. Zoë, what is yours?

news.title: Howard Kurtz details The “Secret Sauce” To Fox News 30 years of Success
news.text:
Full Episode Below:

Full Transcript:

Guy Benson: Joining us now is Howie Kurtz, media and political analyst here at Fox News, host of the Media Buzz Meter podcast. You can follow him on Twitter or X at Howard Kurtz. Howie, great to have you back.

Howard Kurtz: Nice to be back.

Guy Benson: I would like to read from a tweet that was put out yesterday by Cheryl Atkisson, who’s a journalist who’s been in the business for a long time. She shared an insight into not just her own decision-making as a journalist at another network, but also the reaction that she got for some of those choices. This was something that she shared in alignment with the 30th birthday of Fox News Channel, which was yesterday and we did market here on the show. Here’s what Cheryl Atkisson wrote in part.

She says, true story about Fox News and CBS News. In network newsrooms, they typically had other networks playing on television monitors in the newsroom. That was the way they kind of kept track of what the others were doing. As 24-hour cable news was invented, we began adding them to the repertoire. CNN, MSNBC, CNBC could be seen on monitors in the newsroom and individual reporters’ offices.

Then along came Fox. I had just begun assignment at the CBS News Washington DC Bureau and was interested in the new network. I quickly noticed that Fox had interesting news items, sometimes days before the rest of us would pick them up. It seemed to me that we and the other networks weren’t monitoring Fox News in real time, the way we were obsessively watching other news outlets.

Since nobody else seemed to be doing it, I put Fox News on my monitor in my office. Newsrooms are funny because there’s a lot of group think, and you’d think it would be the opposite. I’m pretty sure I got pegged negatively by some colleagues because I had Fox News on my monitor. The fact is, I was being a responsible news monitor. Nobody else was.

Then she goes on to talk about being in meetings where she would mention a story that Fox was covering, and it would get poo-pooed or played down by people at CBS, and I’m sure this was happening elsewhere, as, oh, that’s a Fox story. No one’s paying attention to that, oh, they’re just pandering to conservatives. Nothing to see here.

And she concluded, I think we all missed an opportunity way back then to recognize we were too often talking past half of America, or at least a sizable chunk. Congratulations, she wrote at the very end, to Fox News for 30 years of work.

I think that assessment, that recollection by Cheryl Atkisson, goes a long way to explain the success of this place, Howie.

Howard Kurtz: It is true that the other networks initially didn’t take Fox seriously. It was Roger Ailes, it was a bunch of right-wing hacks, and we were missing stories. I don’t think that’s true today. I think everybody’s woken up to the fact that Fox has a very good news division as well as high-profile opinion hosts.

But think about it. These mighty networks, you know, Rather, Jennings, Brian Williams, and so forth, and they left a hole in the market. I mean, they thought they were doing a good job. A whole lot of conservatives, even though conservatives like Rush Limbaugh dominated the radio, felt like they weren’t getting what they needed, and the broadcast networks were blind to see this.

Guy Benson: Yeah, I think that’s true. I think some of that blindness very much still does exist today. It might not be the same, to your point, but I think back just to the border crisis for four years of the Biden administration. We were on that story like no one else.

And the rest of the media would occasionally show up, like that sort of Haitians-under-the-bridge moment. They would every so often pop in to do a story, often very slanted, and then run away. And it turned out that the border crisis and the fallout from that crisis was one of the top two issues that shaped a presidential campaign.

And they were playing sort of frantic catch-up, as were the Democrats, by the time that issue was front and center with voters. And I think, to some extent, maybe to a large extent, the reason that our competitors did not cover a giant story the way it needed to be covered is because they still try to ghettoize us and Fox stories as fascinations for the right wing.

I do think there is still some of that, even if it’s not the same sort of dismissive posture that you were just talking about from 20 to 30 years ago, let’s say.

Howard Kurtz: I don’t think it’s always true, and I see now more, I think, a lot of Fox clips on the other networks. If Brit Hume or others say something about the campaign, it’ll get picked up. This interview, because of a lot of exclusive interviews with administration officials, who obviously don’t seem to be speaking to us with CNN or MSNBC.

But the border is a great example. I mean, the border is the reason that Joe Biden lost the election, and other reasons too, but I think it was the principal reason. And sure, Fox was doing it day after day, which sometimes makes rivals say, you know, they’re obsessed with the story. But in the end, it turned out to be an incredibly important story.

Guy Benson: Yeah, the American people were also pretty obsessed with it and the consequences of the policies. And I mean, you said Joe Biden lost the election and effectively he did. Of course, it was Kamala Harris. But that was after they replaced their nominee. What a cycle that was.

I do want to ask you on a personal level, Howie, because you have this incredibly deep history in the news business, in different newsrooms, very well-established newsrooms, whether it’s the Washington Post and then CNN. And then years ago, you came here to Fox.

I just kind of wonder, in your experience and your interactions, and you don’t have to name names if you don’t want to, but just in that other world, what was the perception of Fox? What was your perception of Fox? And did any of that change once you joined us?

Howard Kurtz: Well, at the very beginning, I could get Fox when I was at work in the newsroom, but I couldn’t get it at home because it wasn’t cleared for the DC cable system. So they used to call me all the time to promote, you know, we’re up 0.1, you know, doing their job.

I’d say the perception in early years was pretty negative. And I say, I think as other journalists joined Fox, for example, Bill Hemmer coming over from CNN, I just wrote that out as an example. And as there were some legitimate scoops that they had to follow, and I can think of a few, where, you know, it was dismissed initially and then, as the example on the border, everybody ended up having to follow it.

I think Fox earned more respect, but because, you know, the nighttime hosts, you know, the president knew Trump dropped into attacking Fox now because apparently we should be able to put on Democrats. But the nighttime hosts at that time, not just one, and the book, Bill O’Reilly and Megyn Kelly, who I was intrigued by, it’s easy to say because you don’t wonder if there are very, very liberal people on MSNBC, for example.

You say, wow, that’s good. And when they were very conservative people, that gets a lot of dismissal from the outside world and the outside newsrooms.

Guy Benson: Yeah, I think a lot of the newsrooms enjoy seeing the left-wing people doing their thing because that’s how they view the world. And that shapes a lot of their coverage, which goes to the underlying theme of bias that you and I have talked about ad nauseum for years.

So then you made the jump, right? You were the anchor of a very well-known media beat show at CNN. And you came here. I’d love to get at least a brief version of that story, if you’re interested in telling it. And then once you were here, what was that like in terms of your own perceptions of the place? And of course, you still are a colleague at Fox News all these years later. How you feel things stand 30 years into this media insurgency, media experiment, whatever you want to call it.

Howard Kurtz: Right. Well, I don’t know if that’s going to show. I was taken off the air thirteen years, number one. But here’s the thing: I was stunned by how much freedom I had. CNN has a very corporate bureaucracy, and here I was creating a show from scratch, Media Buzz, and, you know, I’m an executive producer and so forth, but nobody was telling me what to do.

Often I’d go on the air on Sunday morning and, you know, people in New York didn’t know what I was going to do. And I said, this is great. I could sink or swim on my own talent, but…

Guy Benson: And your own news judgment. Cause that’s the other thing. You would sometimes send me a little note or even call me like, hey, we might do this. We’re thinking about that. There’s just never-ending news, especially in the Trump era. And you would just roll with the punches. If something was brand new, you would run with it. And there wasn’t this hierarchical structure telling you yes, no. It was kind of you, right?

Howard Kurtz: It’s a little weird. I mean, ten minutes before airtime, something was breaking that said we’ve got to get this, and maybe we’ll leave a bit, maybe we’re going to get a bump, somebody all the normal things. But it would be my judgment. And also because I talk a certain way, I wrote all the scripts. If somebody had a problem, they can blame me.

But yeah, it was an incredible amount of fun because you can rock and roll in a way that I don’t think is possible at the other networks.

Guy Benson: What do you think about this tiff, this fight between the president and some of the other networks right now? I’ve said I think that he is well within his rights to be angry and bitter about the way he’s covered at a lot of these places, just relentlessly negative, agenda-driven, all of it.

I also don’t love some of these precedents at all, and I know they’re trying to work some of this out. The White House has softened to some extent, but it’s still kind of going back and forth.

I’m worried about how a left-wing administration might try to weaponize some of this against us down the line, potentially. These are all considerations not just from the White House side but from the media side as well, where Fox is kind of figuring out what our role is in this.

Howard Kurtz: Well, as I said, the president is now including Fox. He looks to let out, and he doesn’t mean part for a fact, and he does it in part because he’s angry. There’s a huge amount of anti-Trump sentiment at the other networks and the major newspapers.

However, when he decides he’s going to just ban political MSNBC and CNN, I can’t root for that because my view is, if you let certain journalists in, you can’t pick and choose. And we’ll see how the judge finally rules.

Those who, you know, Trump says are inaccurate and fake news, but to me, it means he doesn’t like the coverage of him and the White House.

So that’s another royal battle. You know, he sued a bunch of papers. This is a battle for supremacy, and the press has never seen anything like it. To some extent, media, many of its members, have brought this on ourselves.

But Donald Trump, who has also gotten very personal with people like Kaitlan Collins at CNN, Donald Trump has certainly played a leading role.

Guy Benson: See, the thing is, if you take him out of it, which I want to do just for a second, take Trump out of this conversation just for a moment, I know it’s hard.

But I feel very confident that, for example, Joe Biden and his handlers would have loved an excuse to stop taking any questions or hearing any questions from, for example, Peter Doocy, who Biden in a hot mic called a stupid S.O.B. at one point and had to apologize, right?

Sometimes it felt like we were the only outlet in that briefing room willing to ask hard questions about anything, and certainly on some specific topics that were not going to get covered at all by anyone else.

Going back to the previous dynamic you were talking about, I don’t want to create an environment where a future leftist administration would say, well, citing this precedent, we are now going to lock Fox out of the room or the plane or whatever it might be.

Because I think that would not only be harmful to us and unfortunate, I think it would be a disservice to the country and the accountability journalism that oftentimes Fox News is virtually alone in delivering.

Howard Kurtz: I think your assessment of the Peter Doocy and others during the administration is right on. But they dealt with it. Of course, Biden was increasingly infirm and the press was very late to that story.

Guy Benson: Another one, right.

Howard Kurtz: But, you know, they may not have been able to turn down the Super Bowl interviews and barely could even be seen. So that was their strategy, and I didn’t like that either.

But certainly, Fox was the unwanted guest at the party for the four years of the Biden presidency.

Guy Benson: Last question, Howie Kurtz, and I asked a similar one yesterday to Steve Doocy. Thirty years in, so much of that at number one. In your view, if you could pin it down, what is the secret sauce here?

Howard Kurtz: Well, you know, the secret sauce, in part, is filling a void that a lot of my friends in the media were just too clueless to understand.

And the other part of it is, I think, not talking down to the viewers and not holding back stories for political reasons. It’s just everybody now knows how dominant Fox is. I mean, Fox’s cable ratings are higher than the other two cable networks combined.

And just in the latest quarter, Fox beat CBS. That would have been unthinkable five, ten years ago. So I think it’s got the biggest mountain right now, but it’s also more willing, and we’ll see what happens on election night, because it looks like a big Democratic year, more willing to take on all kinds of subjects.

Guy Benson: Howie Kurtz, media and political analyst here at Fox News, the podcast’s Media Buzz Meter. Follow him on social at Howard Kurtz. Howie, thanks so much.

Howard Kurtz: Thanks, Guy.

news.title: Dems Have A 'Once In A Generation' Opportunity To Hasten The Fall Of Trumpism
news.text:
Democrats are facing a choice as they stare down what appears to be the best political environment for the party in two decades: Do they go for bare majorities? Or do they try to rack up the kind of wins that could change American politics?

President Donald Trump’s overwhelming unpopularity, fed by voter anger at high prices, an unnecessary war in Iran and a perception of widespread government corruption, has presented Democrats with opportunities to go far beyond their initially modest goals for the 2026 midterm elections.

Victory in the House is seen as close to a lock. The Senate is, in a best-case scenario for Republicans, a toss-up. Those wins would give Democrats the ability to investigate Trump aggressively, put a kibosh on much of his agenda and block his judicial nominees.

Historic victories are seemingly within grasp. Flipping Texas would deal a grave psychic wound to the GOP. Breaking the Republican stranglehold on Georgia, Iowa and North Carolina would help the party in the next round of redistricting battles. Winning Senate seats in rural states could put the GOP on the back foot politically for the first time since Trump’s 2016 victory. Any of these could accelerate a repudiation of Trumpism and a potential splintering of the GOP. 

“You have to focus on 218 and 51,” said Addisu Demissie, a leading party strategist, referring to the numbers necessary for majorities in the House and Senate. “But these opportunities only come along once in a generation. At what point do you play for a wave versus just playing for a majority?”

Operatives in both parties now believe the GOP’s massive money advantage is doing relatively little to blunt Democratic gains. More than $500 million in GOP donor money spent since Labor Day has damaged the reputations of some Democratic candidates but has done little to move polling results in Republicans’ favor.

But there is reason for caution: The Democrats’ financial resources are limited, and party operatives feel obligated to protect incumbents in tough, expensive races. The specter of poll-driven overconfidence in 2016 and 2020 looms over the party. Victories in many deep-red House seats could be quickly undone in two years’ time.

“No one wants to rain on everyone’s parade,” said one Democratic strategist, who requested anonymity to frankly discuss intra-party tensions. “But people need to be strategic, and that means we probably won’t be able to pursue every opportunity that comes up.”

Another strategist working on House races across the country said many of the party’s likeliest victories were still coming in places Trump won in 2024, making it difficult to feel completely confident about November’s outcome. So far, the major Democratic super PAC focused on House races has only cut spending on three contests: Michigan’s 8th District, California’s 48th District and Nebraska’s 2nd District. Not coincidentally, former Vice President Kamala Harris won the latter two in 2024, while Trump won the Michigan seat by just a percentage point.

“It feels terrifying to leave a Pennsylvania 7th or Arizona 1st,” the strategist said, referring to two GOP-held seats strategists in both parties view as likely to flip. “Everything is a Trump district. There’s nothing we can take for granted.”

That focus means the party may not be able to fund challengers in seats like Indiana’s 5th District or New York’s 21st District, two seats that went heavily for Trump but feature weaker Republican candidates. It’s also possible the party could cut bait on Tennessee’s 5th District, where a successful primary challenge to scandal-plagued Republican Rep. Andy Ogles dimmed the party’s hopes of an upset.

“Democrats just don’t have that kind of money,” the strategist said.

The search for additional funds is now dominating the time for many candidates in red territory. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa’s campaign for governor of Texas has seen an unusually public campaign, with Latino leaders around the country lobbying Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the chair of the Democratic Governors Association, to put more cash into what appears to be a toss-up race against GOP Gov. Greg Abbott.

The squeaky wheel has begun getting the grease: The DGA put $1 million into the race on Wednesday, following some comparatively low-cost investments in staff and polling. New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a former chair of the DGA, said the group is trying to put more cash into the race.

“There is a real appetite at the DGA to move things so we have a more immediate response,” Lujan Grisham said in an interview last week. “The DGA recognizes a quality candidate, a quality effort, and we need to do more. So let’s see what we can get materialized.”

The Latino leaders backing Hinojosa say more cash is needed, asking for another $3 million before early voting begins in the Lone Star State.

Many Democrats are keeping close eyes on potential new sources of money. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker donated $1 million to Hinojosa’s campaign, and a PAC funded by him and controlled by his allies is spending in places that could win chits for the billionaire’s likely 2028 presidential run.

Pritzker’s investments in races in New Mexico, Alabama and Arkansas may end up being large enough to allow other Democratic groups to redirect their spending toward other seats, one Democratic source suggested. Similarly, Everytown for Gun Safety, which is backed by billionaire former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, has taken over about $10 million worth of reservations from House Majority PAC.

Cash is also sitting on the sidelines for both parties. MAGA Inc., the super PAC controlled by Trump allies, has hundreds of millions of dollars in the bank, and the Republican National Committee has not spent aggressively on television ads from its war chest of more than $100 million.

Democrats, meanwhile, are closely watching to see what Lower Costs Now, a super PAC linked to the Future Forward network that spent hundreds of millions backing Harris in 2024, is able to do in the final weeks before the elections. The notoriously secretive operation has spent about $9 million but is known to prefer to pour money into races late.

The Senate map has similar dynamics: Even the races Democrats feel most confident about, like North Carolina and Georgia, are in places Trump won, making it hard to abandon them and go after red seats in Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Florida. Senate Majority PAC, which is controlled by allies of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, said in a memo late last month that Democrats “still urgently need additional resources to remain competitive in the final days of the campaign.”

The calculus is slightly different because of the length of a Senate term — a House member who wins a heavily Republican seat could easily lose it in 2028 before a Democratic president is sworn into office, while a senator is safely ensconced for six years, expanding Democratic opportunities and blocking GOP ambitions.

The Democratic super PAC American Bridge has spent much of the past year focused on putting reach districts in play, and announced on Tuesday plans to spend $2 million on Mississippi’s Senate race, plus an additional $1.6 million on GOP-held seats in North Carolina, Virginia, Ohio and Colorado. But Pat Dennis, the group’s president, said the party needs to keep its eyes on the prize.

“You can drive yourself nuts trying to think about what’s going to happen in two years,” he said. “What’s going to happen in five years? Is the Russian plague going to shake up, you know, how everybody polls? You can’t. You got to focus on this election. You’ve got to win the biggest majority you possibly can. The bigger majority you win, the more you can deliver for people on your promises, the better you’ll do next time. That’s as simple as it is.”
news.author: Kevin Robillard

news.title: The week in whoppers: Mamdani inverts reality to push a government takeover, Newsom puts words in Trump’s mouth and more
news.text:
Diary of disturbing disinformation and dangerous delusions

This definition

“Socialism . . . means that you will have whatever you need to live a dignified life and that it is the government’s job to deliver on that.” — Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Friday

We say: This is Mamdani’s pitch to let government take charge of everything. 

Hmm: Has he ever been to a Motor Vehicles office? Does he think living on the dole is dignified

Government has never delivered “dignity,” which comes from pride in doing, not getting.

This warning

“Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million US residents in two of America’s largest cities.” — Calif. Gov. Gavin Newsom, Monday

We say: Let’s be clear: President Trump advocated for no such thing.

The left is portraying his remark that higher gas prices are a small price to pay for ending the Iranian nuclear threat as a sign that he’s deranged — by taking his words out of context and then twisting them.

That kind of desperate attack suggests they’re struggling to find any legitimate criticism. 

This advice

“When you feel powerless, you are powerless. And when you feel powerful, you are powerful. And we are powerful.” — Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Sunday

We say: Kamala thinks wishing hard enough and clicking her heels together will get her to the White House. 

Too bad the Power of Positive Feeling doesn’t extend to winning elections. Maybe she should leave politics and become a motivational speaker instead.

“Our laws do not allow for criminals to have sanctuary.” — Gov. Kathy Hochul, Tuesday

We say: New York state law, in fact, provides sanctuary to thousands of illegal alien criminals — including murderers and sexual predators — by releasing them from custody despite federal requests for their removal. 

How dumb does Hochul think New Yorkers are?

— Compiled by The Post Editorial Board

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed responds to President Trump's Truth Social attack
news.text:
Michigan Senate Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed snapped back at President Donald Trump's late-night Islamophobic Truth Social tirade, where he repeatedly called him "Mohammed" and a "terrorist sympathizer."

The night before the first Senate debate between El-Sayed and Republican Senate candidate Rep. Mike Rogers, Trump on Oct. 7 also called El-Sayed "a RADICAL Extremist," adding that "Mohammed’s Values are not exactly those of Michiganders, or those of our Great United States of America!" The president reiterated his "TOTAL ENDORSEMENT" for Rogers.

El-Sayed, seeking to be the first Muslim U.S. senator, responded Oct. 8, saying Trump knows his "name is Abdul" and that the president says it daily.

"But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us. He thinks so low of us," El-Sayed said about the president in a post on X. "He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better.

"It’s time for change," added El-Sayed, a former public health official who won a contentious Democratic Senate primary against Rep. Hayley Stevens in August to secure the Democratic nomination for Senate.

Trump's comments and El-Sayed's response come as many polls show a tight race between El-Sayed and Rogers, capturing national attention as the Senate election is critical to Democrats' quest to take control of the Senate. Their Oct. 8 debate arrives as more than 200,000 Michiganders have already cast absentee ballots.

Who is Abdul El-Sayed?: The physician's path to the Dems' Michigan Senate nomination

El-Sayed, Rogers finally scheduled for first debate

A day after winning the Democratic Senate primary, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, sent a message to Rogers, Trump and other Republicans during his victory speech ahead of possible attacks during the campaign trail.

"They think they want to use my whole name against me. Mike, listen, man, if you can’t say the name — it’s Abdulrahman — keep the name out of your damn mouth," El-Sayed said. "I’ll be happy to give you lessons." 

Also at that speech, El-Sayed challenged Rogers to five debates. Although Rogers skipped a Sept. 15 debate against El-Sayed in Detroit over moderator issues, the two candidates are scheduled to finally take the stage Oct. 8 in Grand Rapids for their first face-to-face encounter.

A progressive and self-proclaimed capitalist candidate endorsed by former President Barack Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, El-Sayed has energized fellow progressives and young voters. However, El-Sayed has some moderate Democrats concerned about his views, his tense relations with local Jewish communities and his ability to win retiring Democrat Sen. Gary Peters' seat against Rogers.

news.title: Trump Approves WI Disaster Aid, Credits GOP Candidate Rather Than Actual Governor
news.text:
President Donald Trump announced disaster aid for the state of Wisconsin on Wednesday in a decidedly partisan manner, crediting a Republican candidate in the state’s gubernatorial race rather than Wisconsin’s current Democratic governor, who originally made the request for aid. 

“I just spoke with Tom Tiffany, who has my Complete and Total Endorsement to be the next Governor of the Great State of Wisconsin,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. “I told Tom that I will be approving 17.9 Million Dollars for the Severe Storms and Tornadoes that Wisconsin has experienced.”

“18 Million Dollars should help, A LOT,” Trump added. “See you soon, Wisconsin.”

The request was formally made by Gov. Tony Evers (D-Wisconsin) in August, after an EF-3 tornado and its accompanying storms destroyed homes and other structures in Menasha and additional parts of the Fox Valley area of the state in late July. The amount Trump approved is about $4 million less than what the state had requested, and the delay in approval has forced several communities’ residents to launch fundraising drives on their own. 

Tiffany, who is a Republican member of the House of Representatives (and is running for governor against Democratic candidate and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley), thanked Trump for the funds.

“Today, President Trump called to let me know that roughly $18 million in aid for Wisconsin has been approved,” Tiffany said in a statement. “I appreciate the administration responding to Wisconsin’s needs.”

Evers took on a different tone, noting the delay in funding and that the president mentioned a political endorsement as part of his announcement.

“Clearly, President Trump and Congressman Tiffany are continuing to play politics with emergency aid that’s meant to help communities recover in the wake of disasters like tornadoes and floods,” Evers said. “That’s Complete and Total Bullshit.”

Using the announcement of disaster aid funding for political purposes isn’t new to Trump — earlier this year, he made dozens of social media posts following disasters that acknowledged Republican lawmakers or candidates while largely ignoring Democrats who made requests for funds. 

The Trump administration’s decisions on how to distribute aid for natural disasters frequently appear to be politically motivated. 

An Urban Institute analysis in July examining Trump’s second term found that over 84 percent of aid requests from states that voted for him in the 2024 presidential race received approval, whereas only 41 percent of aid requests from states that voted for Democratic candidate Kamala Harris were approved. Additionally, aid appears to be expedited for red states, as funding is typically sent twice as fast to those places as it is to blue states.
news.summary: Trump's announcement ignored the current Wisconsin governor, who had applied for aid back in August.

news.title: Republicans Blame Trump for High Costs in Two Key Senate Battlegrounds
news.text: Many Republicans in Iowa and Ohio are blaming President Donald Trump’s policies for rising costs ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to a new CNN/SSRS poll released Thursday. Fifty percent of Iowa Republicans and 49 percent of Ohio Republicans said Trump’s policies “increased the cost of living” in the new poll, which comes as the two states emerge as critical midterm battlegrounds despite the states backing Trump in all three of his presidential runs. Both states have competitive Senate and governor’s races in this year’s midterms. Control of the House and Senate could come down to these two Midwestern states. Both are former battlegrounds, having given their electoral votes to former President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012 before shifting rightward during the Trump era. Trump’s inroads with white, rural voters helped move these states to the Republican column. But Democrats believe dissatisfaction with the economy during Trump’s second term in office could give them the opportunity to win back voters to make the states competitive again this year. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats when the president’s approval rating is low, and recent polls have found Trump’s numbers falling to their lowest point of his second term, fueling Democrats’ optimism about their chances of competing in states like Iowa and Ohio. The economy has become a “significant drag on Republican prospects” because there is a “very close link” to how people feel about their personal finances and how they vote in elections, Costas Panagopoulos, professor of political science at Northeastern University, told Newsweek. “If even the president's own supporters are blaming him for these issues, there's the likelihood that they will either defect to Democratic candidates in the midterms or not vote at all, which could be equally problematic,” he said. “Voters are connecting the dots.” Cultural issues, which have been used as “wedge issues” in campaigns, have become “secondary” to the “economic pain” voters are dealing with in this election, he said. In Iowa, Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek are competing in a Senate race, while Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn are running in the gubernatorial race. Ohio races are also highly competitive. In the Senate race, Republican Senator Jon Husted is facing a challenge from former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. Meanwhile, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton are running in the gubernatorial race. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Newsweek that nobody “can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement.” “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” he said. Iowa and Ohio Voters Blame Trump Policies for Rising Prices Across all voter groups, 74 percent of voters in Iowa and 76 percent of voters in Ohio believe Trump’s policies have increased the cost of living, according to the new polls from CNN. Fifty-five percent in Iowa and 58 percent in Ohio said they believe that Trump’s tariffs are a “bad thing” for their state, while 70 percent in Iowa and 68 percent in Ohio said the recent increase in gas prices, which have soared amid the Iran war, has caused personal hardship for them. Both polls were conducted from September 29 to October 5. The Iowa poll surveyed 801 respondents and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points, while the Ohio poll surveyed 760 respondents and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. Trump won both states by double digits in the 2024 election. He won Ohio by about 11 points and Iowa by about 13 points over former Vice President Kamala Harris. What Polls Show About Iowa, Ohio Races The polls pointed to competitive races in both states. Hinson held a 2-point lead in the Iowa Senate race over Turek, 45 percent to 43 percent. However, in the gubernatorial race, Sand held a 9-point lead over Lahn, 51 percent to 42 percent. Democrats had an advantage in both statewide races in Ohio. Brown led Husted by 6 points, 49 percent to 43 percent, in the Senate race, while Acton held an 8-point lead, 50 percent to 42 percent, over Ramaswamy in the gubernatorial race, according to the poll. The economic fallout of Trump’s policies gives Democrats a chance to persuade some Republicans to vote for their candidates, but Democrats should not necessarily expect to win “large segments of the Republican population,” Panagopoulos said. Its impact on turnout will be critically important, he said. “What we're seeing is lots of enthusiasm in this election cycle around Democrats, around the prospects of winning in November and putting the brakes on some of these Republican policies,” he said. “That enthusiasm often translates into higher turnout amongst those voters in elections. We're seeing comparatively lower levels of enthusiasm among Republicans.” Why Iowa and Ohio Appear Competitive Again These two former battlegrounds appear competitive in this election cycle as Democrats hope to expand the electoral playing field into more conservative states. The economy is a central reason Democrats believe these states may be competitive. Voter beliefs that Trump’s policies have driven up the cost of living and that tariffs are hurting their states could weaken Republicans in the states. Republicans have long held an advantage over Democrats in terms of voter perceptions of the economy, and Americans often vote based on economic conditions, so a shift in that perception could leave the GOP more vulnerable in places they’ve performed well in recent elections. Trump has done well with white voters in rural areas in both states. This voting bloc was previously more competitive, but the Democratic collapse among them has been a main factor driving them into Republican control. Democrats have gained ground in suburban areas in those states, but have not made strong enough inroads to offset their rural losses. Democrats have struggled statewide in both of these states. Sand and Brown are among the only Democrats who have managed to win statewide races in either state during the Trump era. Sand and Brown running again in 2026, a more favorable national environment, has bolstered Democrats’ hopes of flipping those states. Iowa is a major agricultural exporter of goods like corn and soybeans, and farmers may feel the squeeze from tariffs and diesel prices. Meanwhile, data centers have become a sticking point in Ohio especially, tying into broader themes of affordability that have defined the midterms. The Senate races in these two states are especially important. Democrats are hoping to flip control of the chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, but have limited pickup opportunities in traditionally competitive states. This means they need to compete in double-digit Trump states to win a majority. As these two states do have a history of backing Democrats as recently as the 2010s, they have become some of the most hotly contested races that could ultimately decide whether Democrats or Republicans win control of the Senate after the midterms. Donald Trump Approval Rating Trump’s approval rating was also underwater in both states. In Iowa, his approval stood at -17 points, 41 percent approving and 58 percent disapproving of his job performance. Over in Ohio, his net approval rating was -28 points, with 36 percent approving and 64 percent disapproving. Two recent national polls shed light on Trump’s standing nationwide. Only 36 percent of Americans approved of Trump, while 64 percent disapproved of him, in a new Reuters/Ipsos poll of 3,526 registered voters. Meanwhile, his approval stood at 38 percent, with 60 percent disapproving of him, in a new YouGov/The Economist poll of 1,381 registered voters. His approval among Republicans was still strong in both of those polls. Seventy-seven percent of Republicans in the Reuters/Ipsos poll and 79 percent of Republicans in the YouGov poll approved of Trump. The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted from September 30 to October 5 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.7 percentage points among registered voters. The YouGov poll was conducted from October 2 to 5 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. What Happens Next Trump’s standing among Republicans will have major implications for the midterms. The president will want to retain positive numbers with his core base of supporters to ensure they head to the polls. Issues like the economy, cost of living and gas prices could impact how Americans view his presidency. Panagopoulos said it is likely too late for Republicans to change the narrative about the economy. “Millions of votes have already been cast. These views are baked in the minds of the electorate at this point and what they can do is focus on mobilizing supporters to get to the polls,” he said.
news.summary: Republicans are blaming Trump policies for increasing the cost of living in Iowa and Ohio, a new poll found ahead of the midterms.

news.title: Election Forecaster Moves Kansas Senate Race to Toss Up, Raises Democrats’ Projected Gains
news.text:
The Cook Political Report on Tuesday moved three U.S. Senate races toward Democrats, including Kansas, where it now rates the race between Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Democrat Adam Hamilton a Toss Up.

The nonpartisan election forecaster also moved New Hampshire’s open-seat race from Toss Up to Lean Democrat and North Carolina’s open-seat race from Lean Democrat to Likely Democrat.

With the changes, Cook raised its estimate of Democratic gains to two to six seats. Republicans hold 53 of the Senate’s 100 seats, so Democrats need to net four to win the majority.

“At this point, the question isn’t whether Democrats will gain seats, but how many,” Jessica Taylor, Cook’s Senate and governors editor, wrote in her analysis.

Taylor wrote that Republicans still have a financial advantage in almost every competitive state. She also wrote that Republicans are on the defense even in deep-red states because of rising fuel prices and the cost of living.

Taylor described Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, as a stronger-than-expected challenger with a moderate message. She wrote that Marshall was slow to recognize the threat posed by both his opponent and the political environment.

She also pointed to the GOP’s falling support in the state’s farm economy, which she tied to high fuel and fertilizer prices and to distrust over beef imports. She wrote that Republicans could lose the seat for the first time in nearly a century.

The Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans, launched a $14 million ad buy in Kansas last week. Its first ad ties Hamilton to Hillary Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Taylor called the race a dead heat with four weeks to go.

Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), who chairs the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), said on Sept. 30 that “Kansas is a very competitive state.” He said he expects Marshall to win, but that the race will be “closer than I want it to be,” he said.

NRSC Regional Press Secretary Samantha Cantrell criticized Hamilton in response to the rating change in an email to The Epoch Times, saying he “would vote with Democrats like Chuck Schumer. He will never be the U.S. Senator from Kansas.”

Former Kansas Gov. Mike Hayden, a Republican, endorsed Hamilton on Oct. 2, making him the second former Republican governor of Kansas to back the Democrat, after Bill Graves endorsed him on Sept. 23.

In New Hampshire, Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) faces former Sen. John E. Sununu (R-N.H.) for the seat held by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.). Cook moved the race to Toss Up several weeks ago, and Taylor wrote that recent surveys now show Pappas opening a lead.

Taylor wrote that Sununu, whose family is the state’s best-known political family, will outperform his party’s standing on the generic ballot. She noted that he is one of the few Republican candidates who has broken with Trump in a meaningful way on the Iran war and tariffs on Canada. Still, in a state where she said Trump is unpopular, she called Pappas the favorite.

In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper faces Republican Michael Whatley, a former chairman of the Republican National Committee, for the seat held by retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

Taylor wrote that the Senate Leadership Fund began cutting some of its remaining TV ad reservations in North Carolina on Oct. 2 and moving the money to Kansas. She wrote that Whatley “never caught fire as a candidate” and that Republicans privately don’t see a path to victory, though the final margin could still be in the mid-single digits. With the change, North Carolina joins Georgia in Cook’s Likely Democrat column.

Taylor wrote that Republicans still hope to pick up a seat in Michigan and hold one in Maine. Doing both could limit Democrats’ gains and narrowly keep the Senate in Republican hands.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee promoted the new ratings in a statement the same day. The committee noted that Cook had called Democrats’ path to a majority “herculean” in its first ratings of the cycle following the 2024 elections.
news.summary: Cook Political Report now projects Democrats gaining two to six Senate seats, a range that includes the four they need for a majority.

news.title: Trump voters not excited for midterms as approval rating slips: Poll
news.text:
With critical midterm elections only weeks away, fewer than one-third of 2024 Trump voters say they are enthusiastic about voting in November, a potential sign that the president's base is eroding, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.

The poll, completed on Monday, Oct. 5, found that only 30% of 2024 Trump voters were “very enthusiastic” to vote in November, compared with 48% of people who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted over a six-day period among 4,506 adults online, has a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points.

Monday’s poll is the most recent sign of a crumbling coalition for Trump, who also saw a decline in Hispanic American support in another Reuters/Ipsos poll released the same day.

A continued drop

Since the start of his second term in the White House in 2025, Trump's support among every major demographic group has dropped, including double-digit drops among Hispanics, men, rural and suburban voters, people without college degrees and evangelical Christians.

Among male voters, a group Trump carried in all three of his presidential campaigns, the drop is more notable, with the demographic backing the Democrats over the Republicans 43% to 39%, according to Reuters/Ipsos.

That four-point gap is the largest Reuters/Ipsos has recorded during Trump’s second administration.

More: How Americans rank Trump among US presidents

Cost of living amid opposition to Trump

Monday’s poll also found that cost of living ranks as the top issue on voters' minds heading into November. Democratic values ranked second, followed by immigration as the top three issues voters were concerned with.

Reuters/Ipsos also found that a large majority of enthusiastic voters looked forward to opposing the president, with 62% expressing that sentiment. Meanwhile, only 36% said they were eager to support the president in November.

What do polling averages show?

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump deeply underwater, with disapproval ratings approaching or exceeding 60% nationally.

RealClearPolitics (Oct. 8): 38.3% approve, 59.5% disapproveNew York Times (Oct. 8): 37% approve, 60% disapproveSilver Bulletin (Oct. 8): 37.1% approve, 60.1% disapprove

Reuters contributed to the reporting of this story.

news.title: Trump announces tornado aid for Menasha after CBS News report
news.text: Wisconsin is set to receive nearly $18 million in federal disaster aid after weeks of waiting following a devastating tornado in Menasha.President Trump said on Truth Social that he approved the aid after speaking with Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany, the state's Republican candidate for governor.The announcement came one day after "CBS Mornings" aired CBS News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jon LaPook's report on residents still awaiting federal assistance, which Democratic Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers formally requested on Aug. 26. LaPook's report cited an analysis of FEMA data that found Mr. Trump approved 85% of disaster aid requests from states he won in 2024, compared with only 46% of requests from states won by Kamala Harris. States with Democratic governors also appeared to fare worse. Wisconsin, which Trump won in 2024, has a Democratic governor.The White House denied Wednesday that politics played a role, telling CBS News in a statement, "There is no politicization to the President's decisions on disaster relief and the president responds to each request with great care and consideration."The powerful EF-3 tornado damaged or destroyed more than 1,000 buildings in Menasha in July, carving a 14-mile path of destruction over more than 20 minutes, according to the National Weather Service. Miraculously, no one died.Last weekend, thousands of people came together as filmmaker Phil Johnston and a team of volunteers organized a benefit concert for Menasha, with "Menasha Strong" becoming the rallying cry. Wisconsin's disaster fund does not provide money directly to residents to cover their losses, leaving local governments — which have limited resources of their own — to provide that assistance."People are upset that the government isn't helping a whole lot," Johnston told LaPook at the fundraiser Saturday. "It shouldn't have to be a fundraising concert that is giving you basic needs to live your life. It's not right."Menasha residents described feeling "levitated" and "gobsmacked" by the news, LaPook said Thursday.Comedian Charlie Berens, who emceed the event, said the federal funding was a long time coming."If I was a beer half empty guy, I'd say Menasha deserved this money months ago. But being the beer half full guy I am, I just want to say, when neighbors stick together and help their neighbors, good things can happen," he said.
news.summary: President Trump announced nearly $18 million in federal disaster aid for Wisconsin one day after CBS News reported on residents still waiting for aid following a devastating tornado.

The reality is that there are enough variables in play this cycle that make comparisons to previous cycles very hard and conclusions about future results even harder. Earlier this year, Brendan Fraser starred as General Dwight D. Eisenhower in a delightful movie called "Pressure". The premise, based on a true story, was about when to launch the D-Day invasion on the beaches of France. Tidal flows, the Moon cycle, troop readiness, trickery, deception, and decoys pointing the Nazis in a different direction were all factors in date selection for the invasion, and time was running out to make that decision. The bottom line on the go or no-go order came down to whether the weather, always unpredictable in the North Atlantic, would cooperate or make the most daring military amphibious landing in history impossible. One of Ike's trusted advisors relied solely on almanac data — history. He pulled hundreds of charts of what the weather was on a certain day every year in recorded history and based his guess on how this year would turn out on all that past history. The Brits sent in a weatherman that didn't have all the fancy toys today's weather services have with satellites and computers. Back then, they had weather balloons, wind readings, and human intelligence feeding back telemetry as fast as possible. From that actual data, the Brits called their shot that the original proposed launch day would be heavy rain and wind and would be a disaster for Allied forces. The point is that history can tell you a lot of things.
